News.title: Boy, 13, ‘stabbed’ on seafront and airlifted to hospital as cops launch probe & hunt for ‘group’ spotted at scene
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BLADE HORROR Boy, 13, ‘stabbed’ on seafront and airlifted to hospital as cops launch probe & hunt for ‘group’ spotted at scene







Next

A 13-YEAR-OLD boy has been airlifted to hospital following an alleged stabbing in broad daylight at a seaside town.

Police have appealed for more information following the assault near Eastbourne seafront earlier this evening.



The young boy had sustained injuries consistent with a stabbing and was rushed to hospital shortly after.

The incident took place at 5.10pm in Grand Parade near the junctions with Elms Avenue and Cavendish Place, cops said.



It is believed a group of young people were seen leaving the scene following the alleged stabbing.

Officials are working to locate the individuals.

Sussex Police said: “There will be an increased police presence in the area while enquiries are completed and to provide reassurance.

“Witnesses or anyone with information, such as CCTV, mobile phone, or dashcam footage is asked to come forward.

Information can be reported to Sussex Police online or on 101, quoting serial 1096 of 20.09.”

More to follow… For the latest news on this story keep checking back at The Sun Online

News.title: Two Brits ‘demanded €1m after kidnapping terrified couple & held them prisoners for two days’ in Costa del Sol villa
News.content:
HOSTAGE HORROR Two Brits ‘demanded €1m after kidnapping terrified couple & held them prisoners for two days’ in Costa del Sol villa







Next

TWO “dangerous” Brits are facing 11 years in jail after allegedly holding a terrified couple at gunpoint and demanding a £860,000 ransom.

The accused, said to be drug dealers, allegedly kidnapped, threatened and imprisoned a husband and wife at their Costa del Sol villa for two days.



Their victims were said to be handcuffed during the horror ordeal and told they could only leave if they paid a €1million (£860k) ransom.

Spanish police say three Brit men were involved in the extortion plot, but only two face prosecution.



The third has already been extradited by the UK authorities.

Prosecutors are accusing both men of kidnapping, possession of regulated firearms without a licence and a minor crime of injury.



A trial is set to start next week.

The couple went to a petrol station in Marbella to meet one of the defendants and another man at around 7.30pm on September 7, 2021.

They did not know the suspects, but met them at the suggestion of a friend, who had told them that they could help give them legal status in Spain.

From there, they all travelled by car to a specific address.



At one point, the alleged assailants urged them to stop the vehicle and tied them up after pointing a firearm at them, prosecutors said.

They then untied the man to drive to a remote area, where they picked up the second defendant.

After driving to the victims’ Marbella home, the couple were allegedly held and handcuffed for two days.

During the kidnapping, the defendants are said to have ordered the hefty ransom in exchange for their release.

They allegedly threatened to shoot the couple if they could not get the money together.



The couple’s nationality has not yet been revealed, but they were not Spanish.

One of the victims was able to discreetly Whatsapp a friend while their alleged captors weren’t looking.

The person quickly notified the police, who went to the house, freed the couple and arrested the suspects.

One of the trio was extradited by British authorities in 2023.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Police described all three men as “very dangerous” and “violent drug traffickers”.



Two of them were reportedly on the run from the UK.

News.title: Hunt launched after ‘man caught looking over top of women’s toilet cubicle’ as cops release CCTV
News.content:
COP PROBE Hunt launched after ‘man caught looking over top of women’s toilet cubicle’ as cops release CCTV







Next

A MAN has allegedly been caught peeking over the top of a women’s toilet cubicle as cops launch a manhunt.

The incident took place in West Yorkshire on June 25, cops said.



It is alleged that a man looked over the top of a cubicle in the female toilets at a business premises in Batley.

Detectives from Kirklees Safeguarding have now appealed to the public for help in identifying a man.



In the CCTV picture, the man can be seen wearing a blue shirt and black or navy blue trousers.

He is also carrying a light coloured hat and dark backpack, and appears to be carrying a jacket in his hands.



West Yorkshire Police said: “Detectives are appealing for the public’s help to identify him following an incident where a man is said to have looked over the top of a cubicle in the women’s toilets in business premises in Batley on 25 June.

“If you can assist with identifying this man then please contact Kirklees Police via Live Chat | West Yorkshire Police, or on 101, quoting reference 13260360495.

“Information can also be reported anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555111 or online.”

Police haven’t identified the man as a suspect, and the distribution of his photograph does not imply guilt.

News.title: Key evidence that could have helped Letby’s defence over ‘poisoning’ of babies ‘wasn’t heard in court’, Sun doc reveals
News.content:
Next

THE lynchpin of all the convictions were claims the nurse tried to kill two babies with insulin – the only forensic evidence in the case.

The prosecution proved the poisoning in court by showing Babies F and L had low blood sugar – a key indicator of having too much insulin in their system.



But The Sun has learned lead-accuser Dr Stephen Brearey found 14 normal glucose readings for Baby F around the time of the alleged poisoning, which he left out his original police report.

The results were not included in his witness statement to the court and did not appear in a blood glucose log produced by the prosecution.





This meant no-one explained the “full clinical” picture of the baby, who experts – who have reviewed the case – believe could have been suffering an infection at the time.

The alternative explanation could have been crucial to undermining the poisoning claims against Letby, Sun documentary ‘Lucy Letby: Scapegoat?’ will claim on 5.

Retired Det Stuart Clifton uncovered the insulin poisoning used by killer nurse Beverley Allitt – the original ‘Angel of Death,’ said: “It’s not physically possible to have high sugar and high insulin.

“If you’ve got normal blood sugar, he’s not receiving insulin. It’s as simple as that. That is clear grounds for appeal. It would have cleared her in the eyes of a jury.



He added: “Scientific evidence is central to any murder investigation, particularly where you haven’t got a witness. And in the Letby case, there is no witness of her doing anything.

“If you look at these two insulin cases like a house of cards, these two cards hold the whole house up. If you move those two cards out, the whole house collapses.”

One reading, taken at 5am while the poisoning was taking place, was included at Letby’s trial, but left out of the dossier Dr Brearey initially handed to police.

The blood glucose score of 2.9 was totally normal for the newborn and could have been indicative, on its own, the baby was not being poisoned with insulin as he was comfortably responding to sugar.

It comes as…



The significance of this score – and the other missing scores – was not properly explored during the trial, experts have told The Sun.

The nurse was not on the unit at the time of the poisoning, but prosecutors claimed she spiked one, if not two, feed bags before they were given to Baby F.

The Sun has learned discrepancies also exist around the evidence for the other Letby poisoning, Baby L.

Lab results were available to the court on all days from April to 8 to April 12 2016 – but the day of alleged insulin poisoning result, on April 9, was missing.



After Letby’s trials in 2023 and 2024 the lab reading was confirmed in nurses notes as being 2.8 – a normal blood sugar reading that undermined the insulin poisoning claims.

It also undermined prosecution timings on what happened to the baby that day, suggesting the baby’s blood sugar was fine even before it was given sugar.

A source said: “The inclusion of these readings for the trial could have been crucial for undermining the prosecution case against Letby.

“In some respects they show the babies may not have been poisoned at the times the prosection claimed they were.

“In other cases the results help build a clinical picture of what was actually going on with the babies at the time.



“The results could have helped prove these were naturally poorly babies, but the jury were never given that information.”

The Sun can also reveal Letby’s main accuser, Dr Stephen Brearey, failed to report a needling of Baby O during the tragic newborn’s collapse and death.

The consultant inserted a cannula in the baby’s stomach to release bloating as they fought to save the triplet’s life, in June 2016.



But instead of releasing gas, he pulled out blood – suggesting he must have hit something else.

There is no suggestion Dr Brearey called the child’s death – but he failed to report the incident to the coroner, until AFTER Baby=O’s post mortem had been completed.

Stephanie Davies, who was the senior coroner’s officer for Cheshire at the time, told The Sun: “It meant the coroner could not investigate whether or not the procedure had contributed to the death.

“If death happened shortly afterwards, then that has to be investigated by a coroner, and it wasn’t.”

The Sun has learned records of the needle insertion and the babies levels of haemoglobin falling may have been reordered in Dr Brearey’s notes.



The handwritten note he based his evidence in court appears to record the time of the needle insertion as 5.53pm.

But a document seen by The Sun shows the needle was inserted at 5.25pm.

Stuart Clifton said: “He should have disclosed everything that he did.

“So you couple that with the fact that he didn’t report the needling to the coroner, and you begin to get a picture that things are not quite right here.

“The whole thing makes you feel that Lucy Letby was unjustifiably convicted by people who should have known better.”

The prosecution applied to put the insulin cases first, aware that once the jury were persuaded someone was poisoning children they could tie it to Letby.



In the judge’s summing up, he told the jury it appeared beyond doubt someone had poisoned the babies.

The judge told the jury if they convicted Letby over the insulin cases they could use that as evidence in the murder charges that she was prepared to harm babies.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Det Supt Clifton reviewed Letby’s crimes for The Sun in January and claimed her to be the victim of “the biggest miscarriage of justice”.

News.title: ‘It’s IMPOSSIBLE Letby’s “victims” died that way’ – top surgeon’s damning verdict undermines prosecution star witness
News.content:
Next

NONE of the babies died from the method of murder used in court to convict Lucy Letby, an exclusive Sun documentary will reveal.

Leading experts have raised serious doubt over the theory the nurse injected the six or seven victims with air – put forward by prosecution medical advisor Dewi Evans.



Anyone who dies from the condition – known as air embolism – will have air visible in the heart, where bubbles create a lock and stop it pumping, experts claim.

However, an exclusive Sun documentary being aired on 5 tonight will reveal NONE of the murder indictment babies had air found where researchers would expect.





The evidence has been reviewed by a team made-up of a vascular surgeon, neonatologist, and diving medics.

It raises the serious possibility no known method of murder now exists for all the babies Lucy Letby is behind bars for killing.



Vascular Dr Colin Ferguson, who spent his career treating blood vessels and blood flow, began examining the case after following Letby’s ten-month trial.

The former director of professional affairs for the Royal College of Surgeons said: “These babies have not died from air embolism.

“The fact that six, if not seven, babies are meant to have died from air embolism and in none of these cases was air found in the heart at post-mortem means that this is just not true.

“There isn’t any evidence that it’s happened and somehow they have managed to convince a whole range of people that there’s a possibility that it did.”

Letby was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others at the Countess of Chester Hospital.



A major part of the prosecution case was that she deliberately injected air into the bloodstream of babies, causing potentially fatal air embolisms.

The Crown’s medical expert Dr Dewi Evans described injected air travelling through the veins to the right side of the heart.

He and neontologist Sandie Bohin, who peer reviewed his reports for the court, agreed a sufficiently large volume could obstruct circulation in the heart and cause rapid death.

It comes as…

A whistleblower says Lucy Letby may have been ‘scapegoat’ to cover up failures at the unit

A mum says she believes her boy died of a sewage-linked bug that came from the taps months after Letby was removed from the unit

Evidence that could have helped Letby’s defence ‘wasn’t heard in court’

An unseen bombshell email sent by a doctor who was the only Letby eyewitness CONTRADICTS his evidence to jury

The Sun has seen Dr Evans witness statement to the court. In it he reviewed all the known cases of air embolism in the world – meaning he was aware air had always been found.



Yet, as the prosecution’s medical advisor and key witness, he dismissed that “real-world data” claiming the air must have been “absorbed”.

Experts have now blasted it is “impossible” for air to be absorbed in the way the court relied on to convict Letby.

Research has never shown this before. During the trial the claimed causes of deaths of the babies were bizarrely unclear.

But for five of the babies Dr Evans and his co-witnesses relied on air embolism.

Evans incredibly changed his mind on the stand in relation to Baby C and since the trial now relies on air embolism.



He has also reviewed the cause of death of Baby P. The Sun now understands he relies on air embolism in that case too.

Asked by The Sun if he had found the first seven cases of air embolism in the world with no air found in the heart, Dr Evans declined to comment, insisting air could have been “missed”.

Colin Ferguson said: “When the Lucy Letby trial was underway, I seemed to be not hearing any obvious evidence of guilt.

And I was waiting for the killer blow to occur or the smoking gun to appear.



And it never did.” He said: “I spent my career dealing with blood vessels and blood flowing in blood vessels. It didn’t seem to make clinical sense to me that these babies had died of air embolism.

There didn’t seem to be the evidence to support that assertion.

By far the commonest way that an air embolism would kill a person would be if it’s injected into a vein in sufficient volume that the air would then obstruct the right side of the heart.

So that the outflow from the right side of the heart, the pulmonary artery, becomes blocked by the air.



And when that happens, circulation suddenly stops and blood pressure disappears and the person will die quite quickly.”

Dr Ferguson disputes the prosecution explanation that air responsible for a fatal embolism could subsequently have been absorbed.

He said: “That can’t happen. Air cannot be absorbed from the heart once a person has died.

“It’s a physical impossibility. If somebody has died from air embolism, it is inevitable that you will find air in the heart.”

He added: “In every single case that he’s reported in his literature review and witness statement, air has been found in the heart.



“The real-world data says that in order to die from venous air embolism, you have to have those features.

“And unless you can explain to me how a baby died without that being apparent, I’m struggling to understand.”

In response Dr Evans suggested the volumes of air could have been small and therefore overlooked.

Neonatologists have said they do not support this claim as an explanation for air not being seen in the heart of all the babies.

Retired Det Supt Stuart Clifton, who snared Angel of Death nurse Beverley Allitt, said: “The whole case is based, or was based, on presence. Nothing else. There was no actual proof.



“There was just evidence of opinion. There is nothing that suggests that she did anything to create situations where she was left alone with the children.

“There’s nothing that suggests that she’s manipulated staff. Quite honestly, there is nothing that you could term evidence that would be sufficient to convict.

“Not only do I believe that Lucy Letby is not responsible for any criminal acts, I’ve got to go one step further and I’m going to say there never were any crimes for her to commit.”

In response to the air embolism claims, Dr Evans said his work was peer reviewed for the court by neonatologist Sandie Bohin.

He said: “Air may pass through the pulmonary vessels and, particularly in a newborn infant, through the foramen ovale [FO], which is an opening between the right and left atria.



“A patent ductus arteriosus provides another route by which air may leave the heart. Once air enters the pulmonary circulation, it may dissipate through the very thin pulmonary vasculature into the airways.

“All of the babies received vigorous resuscitation. In addition to the inevitability of air dissipating because of robust cardiac massage a standard x-ray would be unlikely to detect tiny air bubbles, especially if the bubbles were found within the thorax, which is naturally full of air within the lungs. “

In a face-to-face meeting, Dr Evans became visibly flustered as before taking off his microphone and walking out when confronted with the claims.

He claimed with authority that there were no known cases in research papers of babies with air embolism.

But he became visibly subdued when confronted with the fact that EIGHT cases are known to exist.



Similarly, Dr Evans balked at claims air cannot be absorbed – which he had relied on in his evidence to the court.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Having discussed the matter for 90 minutes, Dr Evans stuck by his medical opinion.

News.title: Did Lucy Letby really kill those babies the way they say she did? The more we dug – the more doubt we uncovered
News.content:
Next

FOR a year I have been investigating the Lucy Letby case and the one question that refuses to go away – did she really do it?

Our aim was clear when we started – we set out to prove the neonatal nurse was the “wicked” monster a jury found her to be.



We wanted to end the hurtful debate and prove Letby wilfully killed seven babies in her care and tried to kill seven more at a hospital in Chester.

It seemed impossible Britain’s biggest child serial killer could actually be innocent – that our courts could have bungled the biggest murder trial in history.



But the more we dug – the more doubt we uncovered.

It was clear we couldn’t turn our backs on everything we were seeing.

As the new evidence kept coming we knew the only way to explain such an important case, with so many twists and turns was to produce a documentary.

We wanted the country to see and hear from the experts and whistleblowers we tracked down first-hand – to consume it all with their own eyes and ears and decide for themselves.

What we have presented is more extraordinary access to this case than has ever been achieved anywhere before.

An insider from the hospital at the time – a consultant no less – claims he fears Lucy Letby was scapegoated, if only unintentionally.



His explanation the unit she worked on had too many babies, that were too unwell – and not enough staff, space (or even a safe building) – is born out in a papertrail of documents.

There are conflicting accounts from the only eye witness in the case, whose story was what sparked the police investigation.

What cops heard may not have been accurate.

The confession note evidence has been critically undermined by the world’s leading confessions expert.

He left his job to back the Letby case.



The rota chart has been exposed as biased and misleading by the statistician employed to examine it by police.

It turns out the forensic evidence contained a string of missing readings – the reality of what was happening with those babies medically was never explained to the court.

The trial might have been halted in the first week – or perhaps never reached court with proper use of that evidence.



Fundamentally, the prosecution’s lead medical advisor appears not to be able to adequately explain why no air was found in the hearts of all the murdered babies.

According to the method of murder he relies on for them, it should be. He knows that – he told me as much – but it wasn’t.

We can’t say if Lucy Letby is innocent or guilty.

Only a court can decide that.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But after everything we have learned, it has become increasingly difficult to believe Letby killed those babies the way they say she did.



And if you take that away, what do you have left?

News.title: They said babies stopped dying when Letby left, but I believe my boy died of sewage-linked bug – it came from the taps
News.content:
Next

THE claim babies stopped dying after Lucy Letby was moved from her neonatal unit has been slammed by a tragic mum – whose newborn collapsed just months later.

Annalise McClements says baby Archie suddenly deteriorated at the Countess of Chester Hospital six months after Letby had been taken off the unit.



And she says Letby’s key accuser – consultant Dr Ravi Jayaram – told her at the time that babies could deteriorate rapidly because they were so weak.

Annalise told The Sun documentary Lucy Letby: Scapegoat? – broadcast tomorrow night at 10pm on 5: “Even if he didn’t die at Chester because they very quickly moved him out, he collapsed there.



“But that’s not been included. So how many others aren’t being included?

“How many other babies started to decline or collapse and were shipped off to another hospital?”

A key component of the original accusers’ claims against Letby centred on their belief babies did not suddenly collapse or die without warning.

It comes as…

But Annalise claims that’s not what she was told.



The mum-of-two, of Crewe, Cheshire, said: “I asked Dr Jayaram why he declined so fast, and he just said, well babies can decline fast.

“It’s quite normal for a baby to rapidly decline because they are so weak.”

Annalise has blasted the care Archie was given and claimed the poor state of the unit is a likely cause of his death.

Archie’s cause of death was lethal bug enterovirus, which can be transmitted by fecal matter. The hospital told Annalise he likely caught it from HER during labour.

It was only later the mum learned the unit had suffered sewage and plumbing problems – making it entirely possible he caught the infection on the unit.



She now blames the poor state of the unit is a likely cause of his death.

His mum blasted: “They said it was me – but they knew full well Archie could have caught it from the unit.

“I can’t forgive them for making me feel like that – for letting me take the blame.”

She added: “I think he’s got the virus from the dirty sewage in the unit.

How many deaths are because of that? How many deaths are the uncleanliness?



“It’s an explanation that makes far more sense than the alternative given.”

She added: “You could tell it was an old building. It felt run down. The toilets, the showers, all the facilities were just worn.

“It didn’t feel the cleanliness that you’d expect from a hospital. The unit was quite well known to have sewage coming up from the taps.”

Archie was born at the Countess and transferred to its neonatal unit shortly afterwards. He later died in Manchester after being transferred there, in December 2016 [checking].

His mum said she became concerned almost immediately by his condition — and by what she described as a lack of staff.

She said: “The first thing that was alarming to me when I did go to see Archie was the lack of staff.



“I couldn’t ever remember there ever being more than one person available at the time. I think I saw the consultant or a doctor once that week, and that was by chance.”

Annalise said Archie was extremely sleepy, did not wake to feed and had not cried. She said: “I don’t think he was a well baby.



“I expressed that and other family members expressed that and we were completely dismissed. Until he collapsed.”

Archie’s blood then stopped clotting properly and his stomach became distended.

Annalise was woken on the post-natal ward and told he was being blue-lighted to St Mary’s Hospital in Manchester.

She recalled a senior nurse telling her: “I’m sorry, we can’t save him. He’s going to pass.”



Annalise said: “I just remember screaming.”

A spokesperson at the Countess of Chester Hospital NHS Foundation Trust said: “We understand the significant public interest in these matters and recognise the importance of providing reassurance to our patients and the local communities we serve.

“However, it is equally as vital that we continue to recognise and cooperate with the ongoing legal processes and we are unable to comment on issues that remain subject to an ongoing investigation by Cheshire Police.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“When it is appropriate to do so, we will provide further information about the actions we have taken to strengthen patient safety and governance and about any further actions we take or have taken to address the Thirlwall Report’s findings and recommendations.”

News.title: Unseen bombshell email sent by doctor who was only Letby eyewitness CONTRADICTS his evidence to jury, Sun doc reveals
News.content:
Next

THE Sun’s investigative documentary will tomorrow night reveal a bombshell email undermining the ONLY eyewitness account against Lucy Letby.

Consultant Dr Ravi Jayaram told jurors he walked into a nursery after becoming worried about leaving Letby alone with extremely premature Baby K.



He said he found the nurse standing beside the infant as her oxygen levels plummeted and her breathing tube was dislodged – but claimed Letby had neither sounded the alarm nor called for help.

The prosecution said the chilling encounter amounted to Letby being caught “virtually red-handed”. But an email written by Dr Jayaram before police began their investigation gives a fundamentally different account.



In the May 2017 he messaged to fellow consultants: “Staff nurse Letby at incubator and called Dr Jayaram to inform of low saturations.”

It means his original account recorded Letby herself summoning the doctor as the baby’s oxygen levels fell – and is fundamentally DIFFERENT to what he told the court.

It is not suggested this was intentional but it is another factor which could cast doubt on the safety of Letby’s conviction.

Former Assistant Ch Con Dr Steve Watts – who wrote the manual on murder investigations in hospital settings – said the differing accounts needed to be looked at.



He told The Sun: “On the one hand, he’s saying that Lucy Letby was standing there and inappropriately taking no action whatsoever.

And on the other hand, he’s telling us that Lucy Letby called him in. I would be asking why his accounts were different.”

Beverley Allitt cop, retired Det Supt Stuart Clifton – who has reviewed the Letby evidence for The Sun – said: “This is not a smoking gun at all.

“It’s not even a damp squib because he’s confirmed it in his own words.”

He added: “Dr Jayaram, you would have expected, if he thought that there was a murderer around, that he would have… done something, called her out. He would have taken some positive action in respect of that.



“The reaction of Dr Jayaram on this particular day does not lead me to believe that he had come across somebody that had attempted to murder a baby. He didn’t take any course of action that suggested that.

It comes as…

A whistleblower says Lucy Letby may have been ‘scapegoat’ to cover up failures at the unit

A mum says she believes her boy died of a sewage-linked bug that came from the taps months after Letby was removed from the unit

Evidence that could have helped Letby’s defence ‘wasn’t heard in court’

A top surgeon’s damning verdict undermines the prosecution star witness

“He didn’t even write that in the notes. And yet here he is, some considerable time later, giving this evidence to a court.”

The discrepancy in Dr Jayaram’s account is so stark that the Thirlwall Inquiry has now highlighted it in her final report into the scandal at the Countess of Chester Hospital in 2015 and 2016.

Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall wrote: “That Dr Jayaram had gone into the room because he was called by Letby was different from what he had said in evidence.”



She added: “No questions were asked about that.”

Thirlwall found: “In the event, he told no one for over a year.”

Dr Jayaram never claimed he actually saw Letby interfere with Baby K’s breathing tube.

And despite later describing the incident as so troubling that it would remain in his “nightmares”, he made no medical note recording his suspicion, filed no Datix incident report and did not report his suspicion to police at the time.

The incident nevertheless later became important as consultants pushed for police to investigate the extraordinary rise in deaths and collapses at the Countess of Chester Hospital.



By March 2017 Dr Jayaram had told a senior manager about an incident in which a “baby deteriorated and LL at end of cot”.

Weeks later, he and fellow consultants were assembling information to put before police. In his May email, Dr Jayaram said the purpose of the document was “for the police to have their interest piqued”.

He suggested they should “highlight explicitly” cases where Letby had been in attendance and close to babies’ incubators.



But the account recording that Letby called him to Baby K was not included in the final document sent to police, according to reports.

Neither was his observation that events surrounding her subsequent death could be explained by extreme prematurity.

The revelation is significant because Baby K later became one of the most dramatic allegations against Letby.

At her 2024 retrial, prosecutor Nick Johnson KC asked Dr Jayaram whether he had received “any call for help from Lucy Letby?”

He replied: “No, not at all.”



He told jurors he had instead gone into the nursery because he already felt uncomfortable about Letby being alone with the child. Letby was convicted of attempting to murder Baby K by deliberately dislodging her breathing tube.

The jury at her original trial had been unable to reach a verdict on the allegation.

Questions are now also being raised about how narrowly the subsequent police investigation focused on the nurse.

Former Assistant Chief Constable Dr Steve Watts has claimed detectives appeared to settle on Letby as the culprit at an early stage rather than adequately testing competing explanations.

He said: “At a very early stage, it appears that Cheshire Police decided these children had been injured deliberately, and that Lucy Letby had done it.”



Cheshire Police strongly dispute criticism of their investigation.

The force says the six-year Operation Hummingbird investigation was painstaking and extensive, involving almost 70 officers, around 2,000 people being spoken to and multiple independent medical experts.

And police were not persuaded to investigate by Baby K alone.

Consultants presented them with a much wider picture involving unexplained deaths and collapses, unusual clinical features and their belief that Letby’s presence was a common factor.

Former Detective Chief Superintendent Nigel Wenham later described hearing the consultants’ concerns as an extraordinarily powerful moment.



He told the Thirlwall Inquiry: “I can’t describe how powerful it was.” The consultants, he said, had “lived and breathed these events” and finally had the opportunity to speak to someone who would listen to them.

A police spokesman said: “Cheshire Constabulary will not be commenting further in relation to this case.

We strongly refute the allegations made and remain confident in the integrity of the investigation, the conduct of the prosecution, and the decisions reached by the courts.

Our thoughts remain with the families of the babies – who have always been at the heart of this case.”

A spokesperson for the Countess of Chester Hospital said: “We understand the significant public interest in these matters and recognise the importance of providing reassurance to our patients and the local communities we serve.



“However, it is equally as vital that we continue to recognise and cooperate with the ongoing legal processes and we are unable to comment on issues that remain subject to an ongoing investigation by Cheshire Police.

“When it is appropriate to do so, we will provide further information about the actions we have taken to strengthen patient safety and governance and about any further actions we take or have taken to address the Thirlwall Report’s findings and recommendations.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Dr Stephen Brearey and Dr Ravi Jayaram both declined to comment.

News.title: Harry and Meghan could return to US 'for good within a few weeks'
News.content:
Harry and Meghan could return to US 'for good within a few weeks'

A source close to Harry and Meghan has reportedly claimed the couple could soon leave the UK if the outcome of a review does not go their way

View 3 Images Harry and Meghan could 'move back to the US within weeks' a source claimed (Image: Getty Images)

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle could return to California for good in just a few weeks, insiders have reportedly claimed.

‌



The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stunned the world when they returned to the UK in August, six years after their royal exit and move abroad. The couple had moved from their Montecito, California, home with their kids Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5. It is said the family moved into a home in the Cotswolds.

‌



At the time of their move back across the pond, sources close to the couple said they were coming back to the UK for an "extended period" on time. Despite this, sources close to the pair have claimed one thing could force them to fly back to the US.

‌



View 3 Images Harry, Meghan and daughter Lilbet in a recent Instagram post

Security concerns could also lead to the royal couple moving back to the US "within weeks", sources have claimed. Prince Harry, since his split from the royal family, has had his requests for taxpayer-funded security denied.

The Royal and VIP Executive Committee - known as Ravec - oversees Royal and VIP security in the UK. The committee however met again to discuss the couple's level of police protection now that their two kids are residents.

‌



Sources close to the pair have reportedly claimed Harry and Meghan could move back to California if the Ravec review does not go their way, according to the Daily Mail.

A friend of Prince Harry's reportedly said: "If he doesn’t get [security] then I believe he will go back to Montecito for good, and that could be as soon as half-term.

"The view is that if they don't get security then it will have to mean that Ravec has been nobbled. The need is so clear, what else could be the explanation?

‌



View 3 Images The couple moved back to the UK in August (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

"So if he doesn't get it then he will take that as a sign that there are deeper elements at play. In that case then he will be safer in the US than in the UK, so he will return."

Harry and Meghan enrolled Archie and Lilibet into a private school and the kids started the new school year in the UK. The couple however moved their kids to another school just two days after they started, due to security concerns over the school run.

‌



Sources close to the couple said this was due to the distance between the school and their home as well as heavy traffic which raised concerns about whether the school run could be done safely.

A spokesman for Harry and Meghan said this decision to moved schools "was taken following a discussion with the family's security team".

This comes as Princess Diana's brother Earl Spencer said he worries about Harry "not having any police protection".

Article continues below

The Earl, who is releasing a controversial memoir next week, in an interview with the BBC said: "I would say that I personally worry about the fifth in line to the throne who's served in the military not having any police protection.

"As an uncle who's seen his sister die in very, very preventable circumstances, that I would veer towards protection."

News.title: Incredible 180 year history of household gadget that changed fashion forever
News.content:
As the sewing machine celebrates its 180th anniversary this year, the world is enjoying a needlework renaissance, driven by younger generations pushing back against fast fashion and learning to make do and mend. Only last week, 27-year-old Anna, an amateur sewer from York, won the 12th series of the The Great British Sewing Bee - which often attracts more than 4 million viewers for the BBC.

But when American machinist and inventor Elias Howe patented the practical lockstitch sewing machine in 1846, it was to promote fast - or faster, at least - fashion. It revolutionised manufacturing, replacing hours of painstaking hand-stitching with precise stitches, delivered mechanically in seconds.

How two refugees created Britain's iconic Corgi cars 70 years ago READ MORE :

It was the first truly modern sewing machine - wiping the floor with previous attempts, which could only make a single stitch. Elaine Taylor of Hobkirks Sewing Machine Museum in Blackburn, Lancs., says: “British inventor Thomas Saint designed and patented the first detailed blueprint for a sewing machine in 1790, but never built a working prototype.”

View 7 Images Elias Howe (1819-1867) inventor of the sewing machine (Image: Bettmann Archive)

‌



Then, the first practical sewing machine that successfully made stitches using a single thread and a hooked needle provoked a violent backlash, when it was invented in 1829 by French tailor Barthélemy Thimonnier. Elaine says: “Fearing that the fast machines would put hand-sewing tailors out of work, an angry mob of 200 tailors ransacked the workshop and destroyed the machines in 1831.”

Then came Mr Howe’s groundbreaking lockstitch machine. Dominic Macey, founder of the Gates Museum of antique sewing machines in Street, Somerset, says: “He made the first sewing machine that made repeatable stitches and that itself was reproducible from his design.”

Thommonier’s machine could not be reproduced and had to be adjusted for each stitch. In contrast, Dominic says: “Elias Howe made his machine have timing, like a watch. The parts worked in time to make the stitch.” Set to revolutionise the garment trade, it also sparked competition, legal battles and saw sewing machines become the precursor to modern status symbols like expensive cars.

And while Singer is now the biggest sewing machine brand in the world, its American founder, Isaac Singer, became embroiled in a tangled legal battle when he copied Mr Howe’s design without consent. Dominic says: “Howe sued Singer and other manufacturers for patent infringement in 1954 and won, forcing Singer and others to pay him substantial royalties on every machine sold.

‌



View 7 Images First lockstitch sewing machine, constructed by Elias Howe (Image: Getty Images)

“Singer subsequently redesigned his sewing machine. Then everyone copied his redesigned sewing machine, which is what made Singer famous.”

The next leap in innovation came via bobbin technology, when US innovators Wheeler & Wilson invented a sewing machine with a round bobbin at the very beginning, rather than a shuttle that went backwards and forwards.

Dominic says: “This was groundbreaking, because it eliminated the noisy, vibrating, back-and-forth movement of traditional shuttles and replaced it with a continuous, smooth, spinning circular motion.

‌



“Fifty years later it was outselling Singer, so in 1905 Singer bought them. Fast forward to today and Singer still has the monopoly on sewing. Domestic, industrial, commercial, everywhere you look at it, it's all Singer.”

View 7 Images A woman operating a Singer patent sewing machine, USA, circa 1860. The machine sits on a crate labelled 'Singer's patent sewing machine'. (Image: Getty Images)

But it was a German sewing machine that became probably the most famous of all time , when it was given to Queen Victoria’s daughter Vicky, as a wedding present in 1865.

Dominic says: “It was a highly ornate model from German firm Pollack & Schmidt. In 1997 The Princess Vicky machine sold for £23,500 - the most expensive sewing machine ever purchased. It now resides in the London Sewing Machine Museum in Tooting.”

‌



The Royal seal of approval turned sewing machines into status symbols, also elevating the standing of certain dressmakers. Sir Norman Hartnell was knighted in 1977 for his services to the Royal household, having designed custom made clothing for the royal family, including Queen Elizabeth II’s wedding dress and her 1953 coronation gown.

More recently, Vivienne Westwood became a dame in 2006 for her services to fashion - having found fame as the first punk designer, before earning renown as a master craftsperson of structural corsetry and British tartan.

View 7 Images Esme Young on The Great British Sewing Bee (Image: BBC/Love Productions/James Stack)

Elaine says: “Then there’s Esme Young. A prominent contemporary British fashion designer and sewing icon, who co-founded the cult 1970s brand Swanky Modes and became widely known as a judge on The Great British Sewing Bee.”

‌



But perhaps the most famous seamstress in history was fictional. Dominic says: “No history of the sewing machine could be complete without a mention of Bertha the Sewing Girl. She appeared in an article in a New York newspaper in 1871, and her story was made into a very early black-and-white silent film.”

Away from the glamour of haute couture, Bertha’s story told of the gruelling 12-to-15-hour working days of thousands of real 19th-century sewing girls.

Seamstresses in New York even used her fictional story to justify getting union recognition. Dominic says: “Although sewing machines arrived, the seamstresses were being asked to work ridiculously long hours. Her story was written to be emblematic.”

View 7 Images Bertha the Sewing Machine Girl became the subject of many films (Image: LMPC via Getty Images)

‌



In the early days, sewing machines were so expensive that neighbours would club together to buy one for the whole street. In 1856, Singer machines cost around $125 and became the first major consumer product to be sold using a hire-purchase plan - dubbed buying "on the never-never."

Singer's lawyer and business partner, Edward Clark, created the hire-purchase system, so that ordinary working families could buy them.

Elaine says: “Customers paid a small deposit and made regular monthly instalments with interest, until the machine was fully paid off. This pioneering ‘buy now, pay later’ approach turned an elite industrial tool into an affordable household item and tripled Singer's sales in its first year.”

There remains a kind of romance to sewing machines that makes people want to hold on to them, according to Elaine. She says: “We see people with sewing machines that belonged to their grandmas. They still want us to keep them going. There’s a magic to them, they have stories.”

‌



View 7 Images The chain-stitch sewing machine invented by Barthelemy Thimonnier (1793-1857), a French tailor, was the first to achieve any practical success. (Image: SSPL via Getty Images)

The oldest machine at Hobkirks Museum is a US Grover & Baker from 1860. Elaine says: “I have had stitches out of that machine. It’s worth about £1,500.”

Dominic adds: “The oldest we have at Gates Museum is from 1865 - and it still works. And our latest addition made Cilla Black’s wedding dress, Emma Peel's catsuit in The Avengers and Sandie Shaw's dress for the Eurovision Song Contest when she won it.”

Elaine also says that, after its launch in 2013, she definitely noticed a Great British Sewing Bee effect. Running her own shop in Preston at the time, she says: “The first Saturday after it aired, I sold six Janome machines that were featured on the show. When I phoned on Monday to order more, they had sold out.”

‌



Modern machines cost from as little as £30 to £15,000 for the Brother Aveneer. But, despite having everything from embroidery to buttonholing machines, some with computerised displays and automatic threading, 180 years since their invention, the underlying mechanism of the sewing machine remains unchanged.

Dominic says: “First and foremost, it aims to hold two pieces of fabric together.”

News.title: Can Andy Burnham build a strong US-UK relationship? Take our poll and have your say
News.content:
Can Andy Burnham build a strong US-UK relationship? Take our poll and have your say

The Prime Minister will meet the US President next week in New York City but Andy Burnham has previously shared strong remarks against Donald Trump

View 3 Images Andy Burnham will meet Donald Trump next week (Image: ADAM VAUGHAN/POOL/EPA/Shutterstock)

Andy Burnham is set to come face-to-face with Donald Trump for the first time next week.

‌



The two leaders will cross paths at the UN general assembly in New York, as Burnham's steps up his presence on the world political stage. Trump and Burnham have spoken to each other at least twice on the phone since the new PM entered Downing Street in July.

‌



The US President even described Burnham as "a very nice guy" last week but the PM made unflattering comments on Trump in the past.

‌



In a post from 2021, Burnham, who was the Mayor of Greater Manchester at the time, said: "Any UK politician who gave Trump the time of day should be ashamed right now." This was after the January 6 Capitol riots.

North Korea launches double ballistic missiles into the sea as Pyongyang escalates weapons testing READ MORE :

View 3 Images Trump and Burnham have spoken over the phone twice (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

In 2017, Burnham, who was also the Manchester Mayor at this time, said the US leader would not be welcome in the city.

‌



Labour chair Bridget Phillipson however suggested these past comments will be not get in the way of a strong UK-US relationship.

She said: "Look, I think what you've just described there is politics, and the President knows that. And this is not far from unique, and people will express views at different points on different topics, and that's no bar to having a strong relationship."

‌



Phillipson added: "But of course, like there are differences of opinion, we don't have the same political outlook, but the relationship between the UK and the US goes beyond any one President, any one Prime Minister. It's something that has stood the test of time over many centuries."

The Prime Minister has previously defended his old remarks on Trump. Last month, the PM said: "I've had a habit of saying what I feel over the years, and I'll continue to do that.

"But, at the same time, I am somebody who works with people, tries to find common ground, and obviously that's what I should be doing in this job in the British public's interest, and I will always take that approach.

‌



View 3 Images The relationship between Starmer and Trump was strained over Iran and Greenland (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

"I'm looking forward actually to my first meeting. We had a good phone call on my first day in office and looking forward to meeting in person."

Relations between the White House and Sir Keir's government later became increasingly strained over the Iran conflict and disagreements about Trump's threats to annex Greenland.

Article continues below

Liberal Democrats leader Sir Ed Davey, an outspoken critic of the US president, urged the Prime Minister to take a firmer line in his dealings with the White House.

He said: "There is a danger that the new prime minister could be Keir Starmer, but with just better social media, that's not going to help anybody, is it? We need to see some teeth in his relationship with the White House. I want him to stand up to Trump. It's really clear that’s the only language the president respects."

News.content:
Aldi's new £18 boots that look like £70 Mountain Warehouse pair

The discounted set will be on offer in stores this week (September 24)

View 3 Images Aldi will be adding new items to the SpecialBuy section this week (Image: Getty)

Aldi shoppers could pick up a new set of boots that are "built for adventure" in the outdoors without spending a small fortune. For less than £20, customers could get a pair of shoes that look very similar to those from a more expensive brand.

‌



Coming to stores on Thursday, September 24, Aldi is selling pairs of Trekking Boots for £17.99 as part of its clothing event. Customers will be able to choose from two colour schemes (brown or black) as well as adult sizes ranging from four to 12.

‌



The budget supermarket claims that these boots are "built for adventure" and come with a promise of "all-day comfort". The shoes have memory foam insoles and built-in heel shock absorbers.

Every pair is listed as having "waterproof protection". The shoes are made from "premium suede leather combined with water-based PU and durable PES", offering "comfort and a stylish finish", according to Aldi.
