News.title: North Korea launches double ballistic missiles into the sea as Pyongyang escalates weapons testing
News.content:
North Korea launches double ballistic missiles into the sea as Pyongyang escalates weapons testing

North Korea has launched two ballistic missiles into the sea off the east coast of the peninsula, South Korea's military said, amid an escalation in weapons testing

View 4 Images North Korea has launched two ballistic missiles (Image: AP Photo/Ahn Young-joon)

North Korea has fired two short-range ballistic missiles towards the sea just days after Pyongyang threatened to strengthen its nuclear programme and respond to what it called US hostility.

‌



The missiles were launched about three hours apart from the eastern coastal city of Wonsan on Sunday, South Korea's military said. The first travelled around 450 kilometres (280 miles), while the second flew more than 600 kilometres (370 miles) before both landed in the sea.

‌



The launches are the latest in a series of weapons tests by North Korea, despite US president Donald Trump scaling back a joint military exercise with South Korea last month in an apparent bid to restart talks with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

‌



View 4 Images The missiles were launched towards the sea, South Korea's military said (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

South Korea's presidential office urged North Korea to immediately stop launching ballistic missiles, which are banned by UN Security Council resolutions. Its military said it stands ready to respond to any threats under its alliance with the US.

Japan's Defense Ministry also detected a suspected North Korean missile on Sunday, but said it did not land in Japanese territorial waters.

‌



The latest launches follow a warning from Kim Jong Un's sister and senior official, Kim Yo Jong, who dismissed the US decision to shorten the military exercise with South Korea. She said the move would not change its "provocative, aggressive nature."

North Korea's military later launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea, apparently following through on a threat to respond to the US-South Korean drill.

View 4 Images The launches come despite Donald Trump scaling back a joint military exercise with South Korea in an apparent bid to restart talks with Kim Jong Un (Image: Getty Images)

‌



On Friday, Kim Yo Jong also condemned another US-led military exercise involving six countries, calling it a "frantic military move" aimed at prolonging American hegemony in the Asia-Pacific.

The "Pacific Vanguard" exercise involved the US, South Korea, Japan, Australia, New Zealand and Canada. She claimed that "regular U.S.-led war rehearsals" are the main source of rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula and across the region.

"Our will to defend our sovereignty will be expressed in clearer action and there will be never ever change in the course of intensifying the nuclear war deterrence," she said.

‌



Earlier this month, North Korea also held a large live-fire drill involving missiles, artillery and drones. The exercise came a day after the US, South Korea and Japan completed a five-day military drill, which North Korea described as a provocation.

Pyongyang said it fired different types of weapons at the same time, in a likely attempt to practice overwhelming the air defences of South Korean and the US.

View 4 Images North Korea held a large live-fire drill involving missiles, artillery and drones earlier this month (Image: KCNA VIA KNS/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Kim Jong Un has focused on expanding North Korea's nuclear arsenal since high-stakes talks with Trump broke down in 2019.

Trump later ordered the Pentagon to "substantially reduce" its Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise with South Korea, pointing to what he called a good relationship with Kim. Kim has repeatedly called the exercises rehearsals for an invasion of North Korea.

Experts say Kim may now feel he has more leverage if talks with Trump resume, thanks to North Korea's growing nuclear arsenal and closer ties with Russia and China.

Article continues below

Earlier this year, Kim said he would be willing to return to talks if the US drops what he calls its "hostile policy" towards North Korea.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, a liberal who advocates improved ties with the North, said on Friday that a resumption of US-North Korea talks would be "an important starting point" toward peace on the Korean Peninsula.

"What is clear is that President Trump wants dialogue and I've also been encouraging President Trump to seek dialogue" with Kim, Lee told reporters.

News.title: GP says three 'overlooked symptoms' could be sign of food allergy - including 'subtle' ear issue
News.content:
GP says three 'overlooked symptoms' could be sign of food allergy - including 'subtle' ear issue

You might not think your ear would show a symptom of a food allergy - but you would be wrong

View Image Dr Arif lsited three symptoms that people might be overlooking (Image: BBC)

A doctor says three surprising symptoms could be indicators of a food allergy. Dr Nighat Arif, a GP, said that most people associate food allergy symptoms with 'hives and swelling'.

‌



But she said that there were actually other subtle symptoms which people might be experiencing without realizing they were also linked to food allergies.

‌



The NHS says: "A food allergy is where your body reacts to certain foods. It's often mild, but can be very serious for some people."

‌



Three signs

"If you think food allergy symptoms only mean hives and swelling, then these three signs might surprise you, especially number three - you'll want to stick around for that one," Dr Arif said.

"That post-lunch brain fog or feeling dizzy, and that gets easily brushed off, think again, because there might be more to it. And for some, it could be a delayed reaction to a trigger food. Your body releases inflammatory chemicals that make you feel mentally and physically drained. In some food allergies, your immune system responds by affecting your blood pressure and your inflammatory pathways, leaving you feeling light-headed and woozy or unsteady after eating.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



"Allergic reactions can irritate your vocal cords, leaving your voice raspy, tight, or weaker than usual. But if it keeps happening after certain meals, your immune system is trying to tell you something, and it could be reacting to something that was on your plate at that dinner time or lunch time.

"Likewise, a runny or a blocked nose that shows up after eating can be a food-triggered reaction. Your nasal linings swell as part of the immune response; many people treat the symptom, not the trigger.

"And this one is the most overlooked: an itchy feeling deep inside your ears after eating. That strange, deep itch in your ear canal or throat can be early, subtle signs of an oral immune reaction. Yep, your ears are connected to your oral pathway, but it can signal your immune system is reacting to a food, and reactions are becoming more and more severe with repeated exposure—keep an eye out for that."

‌



What does the NHS

The NHS lists the following as common symptoms of food allergies:

feeling dizzy or lightheaded

itchy skin or a raised rash (hives)

swelling of the lips, face and eyes (angioedema)

coughing, wheezing, breathlessness, noisy breathing or a hoarse voice

sneezing or an itchy, runny or blocked nose

feeling sick or being sick

tummy pain

diarrhoea

These symptoms can kick in straight after eating, or sometimes several days afterwards. A food allergy is different from a food intolerance, which causes symptoms such as bloating and tummy pain, usually a few hours after eating the food you're intolerant to.

‌



What should you do?

Most allergies are not serious. However, you should see a GP if you think your child has a food allergy. You should call 999 if:

your lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly become swollen

you're breathing very fast or struggling to breathe (you may become very wheezy or feel like you're choking or gasping for air)

your throat feels tight or you're struggling to swallow

your skin, tongue or lips turn blue, grey or pale (if you have black or brown skin, this may be easier to see on the palms of your hands or soles of your feet)

you suddenly become very confused, drowsy or dizzy

someone faints and cannot be woken up

a child is limp, floppy or not responding like they normally do (their head may fall to the side, backwards or forwards, or they may find it difficult to lift their head or focus on your face)

"Food allergies don't always scream; sometimes they can whisper for hours, and they don't always come as dramatically as we think," Dr Arif said. "Reoccurring tummy troubles, random rashes, or that tingly mouth after certain foods—please don't ignore it. Mild reactions can get worse over time.

Article continues below

"If this sounds familiar, track your symptoms and keep a good food diary before seeing a specialist. And share this with someone who's always "just tired" after a meal—it could be that they're eating something that's triggering their immune system."

News.title: Tesco and Asda selling 15p fruit that lowers cancer risk
News.content:
Tesco and Asda selling 15p fruit that lowers cancer risk

Lowering your risk of cancer doesn't have to be expensive.

View 2 Images There are several foods being sold in UK supermarkets which can help lower your risk of cancer (Image: Getty)

More than 403,000 people are being diagnosed with cancer each year in the UK, according to Cancer Research UK. This means that 1,100 people every day in this country are being given the devastating news — and that’s before you include their families.

‌



It is a record high figure and while the number one driving factor is the UK’s growing and ageing population, as well as the fact that doctors are now better at diagnosing cancer, we’ve also seen a rise in preventable cancer risk factors like obesity.

‌



There are ways to lower your risk of getting cancer, though you can never eliminate the risk, and these will be familiar and obvious to most of us: eating a healthy and balanced diet, minimising your alcohol intake, exercising regularly and not smoking are among them.

‌



But it is perhaps less well-known that specific foods can help protect you against cancer. In particular, fibre-rich foods have been associated with lowering the risk of cancer. The World Cancer Research Fund says there is “strong evidence” that “eating plenty of fibre can lower the risk of bowel cancer. It can also help protect against weight gain, overweight and obesity, which are linked to at least 13 types of cancer.”

It adds: “Because of this, we recommend that you make fruit, vegetables, wholegrains (such as brown rice) and pulses (like lentils and beans) a main part of your daily diet.”

In a 2018 report , the World Cancer Research Fund said: “For wholegrains and foods containing dietary fibre the evidence shows that, in general, the more people consume, the lower the risk of some cancers.”

‌



How can fruit and vegetable lower cancer risk?

The simple reason for healthy foods like fruits, vegetables, wholegrains and pulses (or legumes) lowering your risk of cancer is that they provide a range of nutrients, including fibre, vitamins, minerals and natural plant chemicals, which together can help lower the risk of some cancers. They also contain different compounds, chemicals and properties which also have their own cancer-preventing properties.

View 2 Images Bananas cost around just 15p each in supermarkets and evidence suggests they can help lower your cancer risk (Image: Getty)

This principle is broadly applicable to virtually all commonly-available fruits and vegetables. But to pick out one example, take a banana. A single banana currently costs around 15p at Asda. Not only do bananas contain fibre (one medium banana contains around 10% of your total daily fibre needs) but an international 20-year study involving the University of Leeds also found that a starch found in bananas can reduce some cancers by more than half.

‌



The university said the study showed a “major preventive effect from resistant starch among people with high hereditary risk of cancer”. Resistant starch is found in a wide range of foods including oats, breakfast cereal, pasta, rice, peas, beans and slightly green bananas.

Another study found that properties in bananas “have been shown to exhibit cancer preventative and anticancer activities in breast, cervical, colorectal, esophageal, hepatic, oral, prostate, and skin cancers”.

The good news is that several fruits contain more fibre than bananas. Among the most fibre-rich fruits are raspberries. And, according to a study in the Journal of Agriculture and Food Chemistry, “overwhelming evidence suggests that edible small and soft-fleshed berry fruits may have beneficial effects against several types of human cancers”.

Article continues below

The study didn't just include raspberries but looked at several widely available berries, including blackberries, blueberries, cranberries and strawberries.

News.title: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King
News.content:
Earl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Charles, was his "duty...as an eyewitness to history".

In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the memoir's release on Tuesday, Earl Spencer said he wanted "to put things down once and for all that were true".

Among claims made in Swan Song about the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, was that he said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Here are the key moments from Earl Spencer's interview, which include his first account of how he was told about Diana's death and criticism of press coverage of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

News.title: Watch: Emotional Earl Spencer says he misses sister Diana every day
News.content:
Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, said he misses his sister every day during an interview with the BBC.

"That's the thing with sibling loss, you never get over it," he told Laura Kuenssberg.

His book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published on Tuesday and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family.

He said one of the reasons the book is called Swan Song is because it is his "sign off" as Diana's brother and "final take on the situation".

"This is my swan song too. I'm not here to bang on about Diana, this is my final word, celebration of her," he added.

The full interview, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story, is available on BBC iPlayer and will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday.

News.title: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of expected first Trump meeting
News.content:
"Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted since the 1950s," he said at a Q&A with members at party conference.

"So let Donald Trump try to pretend he's had a victory. The truth is, Europe, Nato, countries like Canada stood up to him and won."

Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.

In the wake of the deal, Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week.

The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.

The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted.

Burnham has spoken with Trump at least twice since entering Downing Street and No 10 said he intends to use the UNGA to "drive forward work on issues that matter to people at home" including the cost of living and the war in Ukraine.

News.title: Kelsey Parker welcomes baby after 'devastating' stillbirth last year
News.content:
Kelsey Parker, the widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker, has welcomed a baby after last year announcing a "devastating" stillbirth.

The podcaster and author, 35, had two children with British boy band star Tom Parker before he died in 2022, aged 33, after being diagnosed with terminal brain cancer.

She is now in a relationship with Will Lindsay and last June revealed the "earth-shattering news" that they had lost their baby Phoenix.

On Sunday, a post on her Instagram account showed a photo of a newborn baby's arm next to a pink sign with the word River. "Welcome to the world, River. Our little bit of hope," the caption said.

Celebrities including The Saturdays singer Rochelle Humes, TV presenter Susanna Reid and reality TV star Holly Hagan-Blyth have congratulated Kelsey Parker on social media.

"Congratulations angel," Rochelle Humes wrote.

"Oh my goodness â this is so wonderful â welcome River," Susanna Reid said.

Hagan-Blyth commented "I am SO happy for you xxxx".

Kelsey Parker's Instagram bio says "turning life's hardest moments into hope".

Last year she posted a poem online after the loss of her stillborn baby.

It was called Born Sleeping, Forever Loved, and began "the world grew quiet as you arrived, So loved, so longed for, yet not alive. Our precious boy, our angel light, Born with wings, took silent flight".

News.title: Ed Davey calls for immediate 10p cut to fuel duty
News.content:
Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cutting the cost of living.

The Liberal Democrat leader is also urging the government to scrap a permanent increase in fuel duty which is set to take effect in January.

Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.

The Lib Dems claim cutting 10p from fuel duty now would mean fuel would drop by 12p per litre at the pump.

Sir Ed claimed drivers should be supported and a temporary three-month fuel duty cut would pay for itself by stimulating the economy.

"Petrol and diesel prices are higher than they've been for a long time because of Trump's mad war with Iran, and people need help now," he said.

The policy would cost about Â£2bn, he said, adding: "It's a three-month package, a temporary package, but if you look at the extra money the government will get through the energy profits levy, from gas taxes, from VAT and fuel duty, it's self-funding."

In a speech to his party's conference on Tuesday, Sir Ed will make further calls to cut the bus fare cap from Â£3 to Â£1, and reduce rail fares by 10%.

He will also call for VAT to be dropped from public charging points for electric vehicles and a review of network costs the Lib Dems have labelled unfair.

Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending at his Budget next month, amid soaring government borrowing costs.

Asked about Sir Ed's call for a fuel duty cut, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson told Laura Kuenssberg: "I'm sure John Healey will be open to any and all suggestions ahead of the budget but actually this is an area where the Labour government has taken action on fuel duty already.

"Whilst I recognise what the Lib Dems have to say on this topic, this is the element of politics about it - they've got their conference, they're making their pitch, good luck to them."

Sir Ed also ruled out scrapping the state pension triple lock after party grandee and former business secretary Sir Vince Cable said at a fringe event it was unsustainable and should be "phased out".

Speaking at Q&A on the conference stage, Sir Ed said the policy had been introduced by the Lib Dems during the Conservative coalition to address inequalities and there was still work to do to tackle pensioner poverty.

"It has not finished the job," he told party members, who were split in a show of hands about whether the triple lock should be scrapped if the Lib Dems win power.

The triple lock guarantees that the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but critics say it is unaffordable and unfair to younger people.

News.title: Man rearrested after missing mum's remains found
News.content:
A 56-year-old man has been rearrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and further arrested on suspicion of murder after human remains were identified as a missing mother-of-three.

Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019.

Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham, London, on 12 August after bones were found in shrubland damaged by a fire a week earlier.

The man, from Southampton, first arrested in 2020, has been released on conditional bail. Another man, also 56 and from Southampton, was released on bail after being arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder.

News.title: Top Gear star Richard Hammond thanks emergency crews 20 years on from crash
News.content:
Former Top Gear presenter Richard Hammond has thanked emergency services for their help on the 20th anniversary of the crash in which he was nearly killed.

Hammond was seriously injured in September 2006 when the 320mph (515km/h) jet-powered Vampire dragster he was driving veered off the track at Elvington airfield, near York, during filming for the BBC show.

In an Instagram post, Hammond said he wanted to thank the members of the staff who rescued him and supported him following the accident "from the bottom of my heart".

In the post, he spoke of the events of that day and said he would be "forever grateful" to all those who helped him in the aftermath of the crash.

He wrote: "Twenty years ago today, I came to an abrupt stop upside down in a Yorkshire field, convinced I was about to die."

He said he recalled having pulled the lever to release the car's parachute before trying to steer it away from disaster, "but disaster was, it seemed, my fate".

"Having done everything I could to avert it, I gave myself over to that fate," he said.

News.title: Kuenssberg: I asked Earl Spencer who we should believe - him or the King?
News.content:
When I arrived at Althorp on Thursday to speak to Charles, Earl Spencer, only a handful of people were in evidence in the vast stately home, where Princess Diana had once tapdanced in the hall and rollerskated in the cavernous library.

It was only hours after Buckingham Palace had sent out its blistering statement in response to the explosive claims made in a new book by Earl Spencer. From the particularly English peace of this grand countryside setting, Diana's brother had provoked a storm.

That Palace statement, questioning Earl Spencer's account of the days after his sister's death, was a total contrast to its normal "never explain, never complain" mantra. But it meant that as we sat down, with oil paintings of Earl Spencer's aristocratic ancestors staring down at our TV lights, the interview was not just about his recollections of his sister. It had become about whether the earl, or the King himself, was telling the truth. As we asked Earl Spencer: which Charles are we meant to believe?

News.title: Homes evacuated over fears fire at seaside hotel weakened building's structure
News.content:
Speaking to the BBC, John Dighton, who was evacuated from Pavilion Court, said that he was told to leave his flat at about 19:00 on Saturday.

The 50-year-old said: "We don't know how long we will be out for but we have grabbed stuff for a couple of days.

"The worst thing is the not knowing. We are at a hotel over the road from the flats."

Ross Honeycomb, 39, was staying at the hotel with his family and told the BBC on Saturday how they were woken by fire alarms at about 01:00.

He said: "I thought I was dreaming, it was horrifying.

"We looked out and there was smoke billowing from the underground car park. Later we started hearing explosions."

Kevin Crawford, 91, and his wife Kathleen, 82, said they had booked in for a two-week stay at the hotel.

The couple, from London, told the BBC that they were in their room on the sixth floor when they heard a fire alarm.

"We saw the fire but we thought the fire brigade had it under control," said Kevin.

"We managed to sleep through it. At the time, we didn't realise how bad the fire was."

The council's chief executive, Susan Priest, said on Saturday: "The extent of support of organisations, including Three Hills, Morrisons and the Salvation Army, has been amazing and helped to ensure that visitors and residents were looked after, supported and had food and hot drinks.

"This was an extremely difficult day, firstly for the hotel guests and this evening for our residents who have had to move out of their homes."

News.title: Billionaire Man United owner loses moral high ground after tax exile, Labour chair says
News.content:
The Labour Party chair has said Sir Jim Ratcliffe loses "the moral high ground" by making statements about the UK while living in tax exile.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Bridget Phillipson said she would take the billionaire businessman's comments that the UK was "on the slide" with a "pinch of salt".

Sir Jim, the founder of petrochemical giant Ineos and Manchester United's co-owner, told the BBC he has lost confidence in the UK due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.

He has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020 and said "things would have to get better" in the UK for him to return.

When questioned over the remarks, Phillipson said Sir Jim loses "the moral high ground" by "making these kinds of pronouncements while choosing to make decisions, that he is within his rights to make, to become a tax exile".

Pushed on whether it bothers her that people who create jobs and pay a lot of tax were leaving the UK, the minister said she was "optimistic about our country's prospects".

Other high profile billionaires have left the UK, including including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently the UK's third biggest taxpayer, hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.

But, Philipson argued the country was in a good position ahead of the Budget next month, and Andy Burnham has shown a "sense of hope and optimism whilst recognising that many families are still struggling and there is more to do."

"Of course, there are challenges, including big international headwinds, but I fundamentally believe that we are in a strong position going into this budget because of the decisions taken over the last two years, and I believe our country's best days lie ahead of us," she said.

Philipson declined to speculate over whether there would be tax rises in the Budget on 28 October, and said the government remained committed to being disciplined about its spending rules.

News.title: The deadly new drugs making Scotland's fight against addiction even harder
News.content:
Efforts to bring down Scotland's sky-high rate of drug deaths are being frustrated by the arrival of hundreds of powerful new synthetic substances that experts warn are making the deadly drugs crisis even more dangerous.

In the past three years, there has been an explosion in the supply of new synthetic cannabinoids and opioids, transforming the illicit drugs trade and increasing the risk of fatal overdoses.

Annual figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show a rise in the number of drug-related deaths in Scotland, which already has an unenviable record as the drugs death capital of Europe.

"The illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more and more dangerous," said Dr Lorna Nisbet of Dundee University's Leverhulme Research Centre for Forensic Science.

News.title: JLR suppliers call for shift to aerospace
News.content:
Major Jaguar Land Rover suppliers have urged the government to help automotive manufacturers move into aerospace and defence, warning that large-scale car production in the UK faces long-term decline.

In an open letter to the prime minister, chancellor and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, industry leaders argued Britain's automotive supply chain was "not in decline" but "in the wrong market".

The intervention comes nearly a fortnight after JLR announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs.

The Treasury said it recognised the uncertainty facing workers and was supporting the automotive sector through grants, lower energy costs and investment in electric vehicle production.

JLR has its global headquarters in Coventry and plants in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Halewood.

Signatories to the letter said the redundancies were "the first visible crack" in a UK automotive supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs.

News.title: Maddy Cusack 'more than a number on a shirt' as anniversary falls during inquest delay
News.content:
Sitting on a bench dedicated to her memory, Maddy Cusack's sister and cousin fondly remember her as their sunshine and someone with a real sense of fun.

Olivia Cusack says her big sister was the person "I looked up to my whole life", while for Emily Reilly, her cousin Maddy's the one who "used to get us in trouble with my dad".

But as they come to remember the former Sheffield United footballer on the third anniversary of her death, they're still waiting for answers.

An inquest examining what happened to Maddy Cusack, who was 27 when she was found unconscious at her home in Derbyshire, started in June and should've finished in July.

But it has been paused for months while her former club Sheffield United looks for documents linked to her medical records.

It means her family will have to wait until at least December to hear more evidence, a wait Olivia describes as "extremely overwhelming".

"It is very emotional and you can find yourself frustrated at times," she tells BBC Newsbeat.

"They're very difficult days."

News.title: Tens of thousands of fridge freezers left at docks as household collections suspended
News.content:
People have reported storing broken fridges and freezers in their gardens for months because some council collections have been suspended.

It follows the closure of specialist treatment facilities and a wider shortage of capacity to process cooling appliances, the Local Government Authority (LGA) said.

Recycling company Unimetals, which had dozens of sites in the UK, filed for liquidation in 2025 leaving tens of thousands of fridge freezers at Newport Docks.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it was working to manage the capacity shortages.

Almost a quarter of Welsh councils say they have suspended household collections of fridge-freezers due to a shortage of space at disposal sites.

Cardiff is one of these and Lee Young, who lives in the city, has been trying to get rid of his broken fridge-freezer for two months.

"I tried to take it to the recycling centre in July but was told it wasn't accepted. Someone said the council would collect it, but they won't either."

It has been sitting in his back garden ever since and he does not know when council collections will resume.

News.title: Michael Marra announced as new Scottish Labour leader
News.content:
He went on to thank his opponents, Joe Fagan and Monica Lennon, and praised them for their ideas about how the party needed to change.

He said: "Joe argued for a politics rooted in people and place, for less control in the centre and more control for local communities. That should be the case in our country and in our party.

"Monica was right to say we need to reconnect with the trade union movement that birthed the Labour party.

"Her record delivering change through parliament is also a template for how Labour should behave in opposition â robust in our criticism of the SNP, yes, but also making our own change."

Marra continued: "Scots know what we are against. They can't tell you what we are for... Social justice. Eradication of poverty. Good work. Good housing. Good public services. The good life for working people. An economy where everyone has a fair chance in life, which redistributes power, wealth and opportunity."

News.title: Strictly returns with new hosting trio as celebrities find out dance pairings
News.content:
Writing in the Independent, external, Rachel McGrath and Lauren Morris ask if three hosts is "truly a crowd" but decide the trio are "certainly off to a good start".

"Emma Willis is undoubtedly doing the heavy lifting, but that makes sense as she is the presenter with the most experience," they note.

"At times, when the three of them were all together, it did feel a little crowded - but there is more than enough presenting to go around..."

The pairings "as usual, seem very well matched", they add, singling out Antonia and Xu.

"Did it take three to tango?" asked Michael Hogan in the Guardian, external's live blog.

"It will take some getting used to, of course, but I thought it worked pretty well. Emma Willis seemed completely at home and smoothly steered the ship. Johannes Radebe was a legend and his understanding of the contest from a pro's perspective will prove invaluable. Josh Widdicombe was enthusiastic and entertaining, although the loud laughing into his mic might need to be turned down...

"An even sterner test will come next weekend, of course, as we go live for the first time. No pressure, you three. But a promising start."

In her analysis of the show for the Guardian, external, Emine Saner says "the presenters look terrified and some of the celebs are hard to identify, but Strictly remains a rare refuge of joy".

"The vibe" the new presenters are "going for is can't-quite-believe-we-got-the-gig humility combined with superfan credentials, which is absolutely the right note", she says.

But she suggests "the pro dancers must now be better-known than some of their celebrity partners" to "which the response can only be 'no, me neither'".

Writing in the Telegraph, external, Anita Singh clearly sees Willis and Radebe as the company, and Widdicombe the crowd.

"Why has the BBC hired jokeless Josh?" she asks.

"Can someone come and collect little Josh from the Strictly studio, please? The poor thing got left behind after the Year 7 school trip and accidentally found himself on Saturday night TV."

By contrast, her initial concerns about Radebe's ability to make the jump from dancing to presenting now look misplaced as he is "so at home in the studio, and so genuine in his interactions with the celebrities and professionals".

And Willis is "great, a pro who could do this job in her sleep", Singh writes.

But both male presenters clearly must do better if they are to impress Sasha Morris of the Express, external who declares that "Strictly's new Tess and Claudia are total car crash".

"Just seconds after seeing the three new hosts... bumble onto the set together, my hope died, and quickly," she writes.

"Poor Josh... looked like a deer in headlights and was completely out of his depth from start to finish...

"Backstage with the stars, both male hosts were too often wide-eyed, nodding and smiling as if they were being held hostage, while charismatic Emma showed them up, moving seamlessly from one position to the next."

"Having three presenters seemed unnecessary, too, as if the bosses didn't feel they could trust Josh or Johannes to hold a role on their own," she adds.

However, for Morris too "the real test will be next week".

The sneaker company Converse has removed a social media ad that sparked outrage among critics who viewed it as evoking the Ku Klux Klan and lynching.

The Instagram ad photo showed K-pop singer Karina wearing a skirt and holding a pair of Chuck 70 X sneakers. Critics lashed out online, saying that a white triangular image created by lighting on the skirt resembled a KKK hood and that the way she held the sneakers made them look like the dangling feet of a lynching victim.

Converse, owned by Nike, issued a statement apologizing and saying it removed the ad.

“We’re sorry,” said the statement, first released on Friday. “We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong. We removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared. This should not have happened and we will do better.”

Converse, based in Boston, declined on Sunday to answer questions seeking additional information, including how the company screens ads before they are posted and how the ad was approved.

Karina and her management company, SM Entertainment Group, did not immediately respond to messages through their Instagram accounts.

Retailers and top fashion brands have issued a string of apologies over the years for products criticized as being racially insensitive.

Last month, retailer Target pulled a children’s Halloween costume from its shelves after widespread social media backlash, apologizing for selling a garment that critics said evoked racist minstrel caricatures.

The Converse photo sparked swift criticism, including calls for staff involved in the ad to be fired and for a boycott of the company. In a slew of comments on social media, posters questioned how the ad could have cleared the company's advertising vetting process. Other commenters defended Converse, saying they didn't believe it was intentional.

Lee Merritt, a civil rights attorney based in Texas, posted on Instagram that Converse’s apology “doesn’t undo what got past legal, marketing and leadership at every step.”

“We keep having this conversation because corporations keep failing the same test,” he wrote. “Do better means catching this before it airs — not after we’re offended.”

Converse, founded in Malden, Massachusetts, in 1908, makes the iconic Chuck Taylor All Star sneaker. It was first released in 1917 as a non-skid basketball shoe, adding the signature of Taylor — a basketball player who promoted the sneaker — in 1934, according to the company's website.

Manchester United avert a crisis, but can’t really avoid criticism. Michael Carrick got lucky against Fulham, and consequently got away with one. For now.

A game that had looked like it was edging towards a first Alvaro Arbeloa win, courtesy of Lisandro Martinez’s bizarre own goal, instead saw another wicked deflection divert it to a 1-1 draw.

Neither club is completely unhappy, but this could have been a lot worse for both.

An exuberant Fulham at least climb off the bottom of the table, ensuring it is Tottenham Hotspur who sit there going into this three-week international window. They look the closest to the “crisis club” enduring all manner of external criticism and introspection going into an unusually long break. That was so close to being United.

open image in gallery Bruno Fernandes struck the post in the first half in United’s best opportunity to score ( Reuters )

open image in gallery A fortuitous own goal scored by Lisandro Martinez gave Fulham the lead in a dire contest with Manchester United ( Reuters )

Matheus Cunha’s deflected late strike, however, shouldn’t put off bigger discussions.

This was another underwhelming display, completely lacking in any kind of convincing attacking football. There is just so much off with the team right now.

An irony is that the calamitous own goal actually came in the one period of the game where what United were doing actually made some sense. Fulham are one of the most aggressive teams in the Premier League in how they push forward, almost absurdly overcommitting.

After that contributed to an entertainingly open first half, Carrick evidently realised his team should just try and hit the home side on the counter. It was logical… until your team just does something illogical.

An Alex Iwobi shot was eventually deflected into the path of Martinez, who instinctively reacted and helped the ball back towards goal. With Senne Lammens wrong-footed by his initial save, however, he didn’t reach across and somewhat meekly allowed the ball to go past him.

He might have been conscious of a back pass or maybe was just too far away, but it all added up to another hapless moment.

Carrick might well feel that’s just what happens in football when it seems that everything is going against you.

It is almost the total opposite of last season, where it was like everything – right up to the calendar – was going United’s way. They had a positive momentum. Now, certainly until that late strike, it was a negative momentum.

And that’s also why he might feel the equalising goal was so important. It was a stroke of fortune when United badly needed it.

Rather than intense discussion of Carrick losing his job, the talk could be about how this might be a turning point, that this is something to build on, that it will psychologically settle a team that had looked tense.

That would also be a bit much, though.

open image in gallery Man Utd were too passive and lacked the desire to win the game ( Getty )

open image in gallery Matheus Cunha's goal earned United a point at Craven Cottage ( PA )

United do look to have visible structural problems. They don’t properly construct attacks that aren’t almost set-piece moves. So many passages of play end with hopeful long shots, or hopeless crosses to a striker who isn’t even there.

That is where the main discussion should lie.

Put bluntly, they don’t even attack in the way that Fulham do. The 19th-place position of Arbeloa’s side does seem like it doesn’t fully reflect performances, given they have had an enjoyable intensity about all of their games. But the issue is a clear inability to close anything out.

There’s a vulnerability there that doesn’t look like it’s going to go away any time soon.

Is it a naivety about the Premier League from a young manager who does have something about him?

Can they grow from fully committing to the idea?

It is at least an idea. United don’t really seem to have one going forward, and that should be the real concern out of this match, regardless of result.

The wife of top Trump administration official Stephen Miller says she fears looming legal bills if Democratic wins in the crucial midterm elections lead to congressional subpoenas for the president's inner circle.

”After the first Trump administration, my family spent money we did not have on lawyers because of multiple partisan Democrat led investigations into President Trump,” Katie Miller said Saturday on social media. “I watched as many of my friends also had no idea how to pay expensive legal bills because they simply served their country.”

She added: “You can’t convince me Democrats won’t do this again.”

Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia of California, ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, told Bloomberg Government in April that Stephen Miller was among several people the committee would subpoena if Democrats take control after the midterms.

Garcia also mentioned former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, her former associate Corey Lewandowski, FBI Director Kash Patel and now-Attorney General Todd Blanche.

open image in gallery Katie Miller with husband and Trump administration official Stephen Miller during the Congressional Picnic outside the White House in June last year ( AFP/Getty )

“They would all be in front of us pretty consistently,” Garcia said at the time.

Katie Miller’s comments came in response to a Bloomberg podcast in which New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman put the likelihood of billionaire Elon Musk being subpoenaed at “100 percent.”

“People have privately told me that’s what they plan to do. I think that they will,” said Haberman, co-author of the best-selling book Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump.

Katie Miller served as an adviser to Trump's ad hoc, Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency before leaving the administration in May 2025 to work for Musk, whose estimated $946.5 billion net worth makes him the world's richest person.

Three months later, she told Axios that she'd left that job to launch a podcast for conservative women. It now has about 73,000 YouTube subscribers.

open image in gallery Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia of California, seen referencing a photo of Stephen Miller during a February 23, 2026, public forum in Washington, says he’s among the current and former administration officials who will be subpoenaed if Democrats win control of the House Oversight Committee ( Getty )

In April 2022, Stephen Miller — a two-term Trump aide who's now his deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser — testified by video for more than eight hours after receiving a subpoena from the Democrat-led House January 6 select committee.

He also testified in April 2023 before the federal grand jury that later indicted Trump for allegedly conspiring to prevent Congress from certifying his 2020 electoral loss to Joe Biden.

Special counsel Jack Smith dropped that case, and another in which Trump was accused of illegally hoarding classified documents after leaving the White House, following Trump's 2024 victory over Biden's vice president, Kamala Harris.

Katie Miller, who was an aide to Vice President Mike Pence during Trump’s administration, avoided having to testify about the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol by Trump supporters because she was on maternity leave at the time.

Republicans hold a narrow, 219-214 House majority with two vacancies, and the GOP also controls the Senate, 53-47.

Polls show Democrats leading in the so-called generic congressional race, 50.4 percent to 42.3 percent, according to Real Clear Polling, but the Cook Political Report rates future control of both chambers as a toss-up.

Sunday afternoon at Wentworth Club in late September, where the sun is low and the leaves are beginning to rust. Everything is still and pristine, and into the light step two of the most aesthetically pleasing swings in golf. Rory McIlroy bounds to the first tee with a spring in his step, where Adam Scott is waiting with sleeves rolled up, sporting a deep tan over perfectly pressed cream trousers, with the air of a man who just berthed his yacht.

These golfers on this golf course on this beautiful late summer day? No wonder fans stacked three or four deep on all sides to catch a glimpse as the pairing moved through the grounds. McIlroy alone carries a magnetic attraction, of course, and here the entourage included a string of sweaty photographers and reporters, some burly security personnel, two police officers, the Everton midfielder Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and half the population of Surrey.

In the pleasant hubbub it was easy to forget the stakes here. McIlroy has not won at Wentworth since 2014 and desperately wanted to repeat the feat at this BMW PGA Championship, the DP World Tour’s flagship event. There was considerable prize money of more than £1m for the winner. And perhaps most significantly for McIlroy was the opportunity to close the gap to Patrick Reed in the Race to Dubai. It is a title McIlroy virtually owns having won it seven times, and there cannot be many people he would less like to watch take his crown than the American.

open image in gallery McIlroy was the star attraction at Wentworth Club ( Reuters )

Reed, one of the gurning faces of LIV Golf before his exit in January, arrived here at Wentworth more than 800 points ahead of McIlroy, before pulling out with a hand injury. It opened the door: McIlroy needed to finish in the top two to move ahead of the American in the standings with only a handful of events remaining.

McIlroy began the day on 11 under par, two shots back from the overnight leaders in the thick of a packed leaderboard with 25 players inside five shots. After a disappointing Irish Open in which McIlroy finished tied-45th, he has refound some of his touch, particularly with his irons. But he ended this compelling Sunday tied second after wasting a series of makeable putts.

It had been a morning for extraordinary shots before McIlroy’s round began. Tyrrell Hatton hit a blind approach from the rough to within a couple of inches of the cup after piercing a gap between low-hanging branches and a bush. Frederic Lacroix aced the 14th from 163 yards to win himself a BMW iX5 xDrive 60 M Sport, to remind everyone who the sponsors are and that car names are getting out of hand.

McIlroy himself hit one for the highlight reel, manufacturing a banana hook from the trees on 12 reminiscent of his famous approach on the 15th at Augusta, arms wrapped around his body to generate that extreme right-to-left turn through the air, and it landed travelling sideways just shy of the green.

But the world No 2’s challenge frittered away with putter in hand. McIlroy had earlier missed good opportunities at two, three and five, and finished the front nine with two birdies when it might have been four or five. Then came a disastrous moment on 11 when he fatted a chip into a bunker as the clubhead snagged in soft, sandy soil where he expected firm ground.

open image in gallery McIlroy hits his approach to the 18th green ( Reuters )

McIlroy rallied, hitting that enormous hook to birdie the 12th. But he was always chasing and stretching to catch leaders who were a shot or two out of reach. A birdie putt on 16 slid by the hole and McIlroy pulled off his hat in frustration as his challenge effectively ended. McIlroy finished ranked 76th in the field for strokes gained putting and was left to rue so many mistakes with the flat stick.

It was a familiar story, reminiscent of the 2024 US Open at Pinehurst and the 2022 Open Championship at St Andrews, when McIlroy spurned prime positions on Sunday with too many missed putts inside 10 feet. Here he recovered masterfully from wayward tee shots and the occasional missed green, but there is no recovery when the ball burns the edge and rolls by.

“I had my chances out there,” McIlroy said. “I wish I had some of those putts back, but I have to be encouraged with where my game is at.”

At that point it looked like Aaron Rai would triumph, until a late-round stumble. Then it seemed Spain’s unheralded 30-year-old Manuel Elvira might break clear of the rest. Elvira has played much of his golf in the shadow of older brother Nacho, a winner of three events on the DP World Tour, and this was the biggest day of the younger brother’s career.

Unfortunately, nerves told as he missed putts on 14 and 15, and despite a brilliant eagle on 17, Elvira made a disastrous strategic decision to adopt a conservative approach on the par-five 18th and lay up on one of the easiest holes on the course. He made the cardinal sin of finding the fairway bunker, then duffed a chip and ended with a double bogey.

“It was devastating that I hit the wrong shot at the right time on the lay-up and left myself the toughest shot in the fairway bunker, and wasn’t able to pull it off,” Elvira said.

open image in gallery JJ Spaun celebrates with the trophy ( PA )

Watching on was clubhouse leader JJ Spaun, who hugged his wife in celebration as the par Elvira needed to force a play-off slipped away. It has been an inconsistent season for Spaun since victory at the Texas Open in April, and a so-so day until a run of three successive birdies on 14, 15 and 16 propelled him to the top of the leaderboard on 16-under par. A birdie at the last earned Spaun a win by two strokes from McIlroy, Scott, Elvira and Rai.

“I played with a huge chip on my shoulder,” Spaun said of being overlooked as a captain’s pick for the Presidents Cup next week outside Chicago. “I definitely had something to prove this week, but everything happens for a reason.”

Tied second was enough for McIlroy to halve the points gap to Reed heading into the last events of the year. There may not be a Middle Eastern swing to this season’s European Tour at all, in the shadow of the war in Iran, so the Race to Dubai may in fact be a race to the final tournament of the season in – checks notes – Cheonan, South Korea, next month. Just as they did once upon a time in their epic Ryder Cup rivalry, McIlroy and Reed will fight to the bitter end.

The grunge aesthetic of the 2010s made a comeback last autumn/winter with the revival of tartan midi skirts and chunky leather.

But this season it seems the indie sleaze aesthetic is set to continue as Roksanda Ilinčić sent loose threads, leather gloves and dresses covered in trailing fabric down the runway at London Fashion Week.

But while this return might bring to mind threadbare denim and distressed T-shirts, Roksanda offered a rather more glamorous interpretation of grunge.

The Serbian-born designer staged the show on an outdoor terrace at the National Theatre on London’s South Bank, where the early autumn sunshine caught the colourful threads against the building’s concrete walls.

Backstage before the show, Roksanda said she had been inspired by Swiss-born artist Françoise Grossen, known for her large-scale sculptures made from braided and knotted rope.

“I love her beautiful monumental sculptures, usually made in this braiding technique and I loved the element of earthiness about it but also something very crafty, very arty and very connected to the women,” she explained.

“And I wanted to take the female gaze and thread it throughout the whole collection from shirts, daywear, all the way into the eveningwear.”

While the designer took the idea to extremes in her finale gowns, there were plenty of more accessible trends to take away from the collection.

open image in gallery Loose threads and leather opera gloves were key motifs from the show (Joss

The first model emerged in a fitted black jacket and wide-leg trousers, with a silk scarf draped over her shoulders and a shaggy fringed accessory tucked under one arm.

Scarves continued to appear throughout the show, tied at the neck, thrown over shoulders or left hanging from the waist.

They offered a relatively simple way to bring movement and interest to otherwise understated outfits – particularly when worn with Roksanda’s oversized tailoring.

One model wore a brown pinstriped shirt and trousers with a bright pink collar and purple gloves, while another appeared in an enormous striped coat layered over a shirt and tie.

Ilinčić brought a loose but smart edge to traditional suit tailoring.

open image in gallery Roksanda put a spin on pinstripe suiting (Joss Wild for Authentic Beauty Concept/PA)

The beauty look, meanwhile, was much more reminiscent of the signature Roksanda sleekness.

Rather than styling every model’s hair in the same way, lead hairstylist Anna Cofone, working with Authentic Beauty Concept, said she wanted to celebrate their individual textures.

“Each model’s own texture has been elevated,” she explained backstage.

“Lots of, like, hydrating textures, not a lot of product, just really effortless, and just really looking at the models’ face shape and looking at their texture, and then just enhancing it.”

Some models wore their hair straight and tucked behind their ears, while others had their natural waves, curls and tighter textures defined, with the hair kept close to the head.

open image in gallery The models wpre mostly natural hair to showcase the collection (Joss Wild for Authentic Beauty Concept/PA)

Cofone said the team paid particular attention to the hairline, rather than automatically smoothing away the small curls and kinks that can give a hairstyle its character.

“I think that’s what enables each model to look like themselves rather than going in and approaching it all in the same way,” she said.

For wavy and curly hair, the team used hydrating products like the Authentic Beauty Concept Glow Spray Serum to add moisture, while straighter hair was given a little extra body without losing its natural movement.

Cofone said they avoided blow-drying most of the models’ hair, as applying heat could change its natural shape.

And for anyone attempting the look at home, her advice was less about perfecting the hair and more about feeling comfortable showing your face.

“As soon as you tuck your hair behind the ears, it’s like you’re saying, ‘Look at me – I feel good and I feel confident.’”

The minimal and natural hair textures worked well with the organic movement of the natural threads on the runway.

open image in gallery Hair was simply worn down in most cases to let the clothes take centre stage (Joss Wild for Authentic Beauty Concept/PA)

The palette of the show also played a huge part, as the collection began with black, ivory and chocolate brown before introducing hot pink, turquoise, yellow and lime green – sometimes all within the same outfit.

Several pieces featured abstract, painterly prints, with faces emerging from splashes of colour on silk scarves, dresses and oversized tops.

“I also introduced these wonderful faces […] they are reappearing as almost a woman peeking through to this quite abstract world, and I wanted to bring that intimacy back into the collection,” Roksanda explained.

As the show moved into eveningwear, the loose-threaded trend became less practical.

A series of dresses appeared covered in dense layers of multicoloured strands, some gathered tightly together and others left hanging freely.

One dress combined pink, grey and cream fibres in a rounded skirt, while another had long red and orange threads trailing from a bright pink bodice.

The effect was closer to the sculptures that had inspired this Roksanda collection rather than the usual pieces you see on a hanger.

Roksanda said she was particularly interested in the contrast between Grossen’s tightly braided sculptures and the strands the artist allowed to hang loose.

She described the work as “very cautiously braided but then left loose to live and breathe life of their own”.

That contrast carried through to the final looks, where the trailing threads gave way to gowns with enormous skirts that stood away from the body.

One strapless oxblood dress had a tightly fitted bodice and two great curved panels extending from the hips, while the final black gown featured an asymmetric neckline and a similarly exaggerated silhouette.

They may not offer much inspiration for an everyday wardrobe, but they showed how far Roksanda was prepared to take an idea that began with a loose thread.

News.title: Fulham v Man United LIVE: Pressure on Carrick continues as Neville labels performance ‘a disgrace’
News.content:
Why Michael Carrick’s Man United ISN’T Working

Manchester United were spared some blushes after a deflected strike from Matheus Cunha earned them a 1-1 draw with Fulham at Craven Cottage.

In a week that has seen Michael Carrick’s team lose to rivals Man City and be dumped out of the Carabao Cup by Brighton, United needed a positive result in London but trailed the Cottagers with mere minutes remaining in the match.

In a game that lacked quality and intensity, an error from Lisandro Martinez sent the hosts into the lead as the defender deflected a Senne Lammens save into his own goal. Both sides had previously wasted opportunities to score with 26 shots coming in a goalless first half.

United’s lack of urgency threatened to be their undoing before Cunha struck in the 89th minute to salvage a draw but the woeful nature of their performance will increase the pressure and scrutiny on Carrick as the teams head into the international break.

Follow the reaction from Fulham v Man Utd, below:

News.title: Man Utd earn barely deserved point after comical own goal
News.content:
Michael Carrick may have had a point when he said it was “ridiculous” to question his future this early in the season, but this afternoon’s game at Fulham will shape the mood at Manchester United for the next three weeks.

A tally of four points from their first four games of the season is a disappointing start, and Brighton added to the sense of gloom in the League Cup by becoming the first side in 50 years to win from 2-0 down at Old Trafford.

With Champions League football on the agenda, that competition was at the bottom of United’s priority list but the ragged nature of the performance prompted boos around the stadium.

The no-show at Hull and defeat to 10-man City also fall into the “it’s how you lose” category of defeat, while there are widening fissures between the fanbase and the club’s hierarchy over ticketing policy and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s political interventions.

The mood has also been sour at Fulham in the first few weeks of the season. In fact, they start the game bottom of the Premier League with one point, but do have the incentive of knowing a draw would take them above Spurs.

Following reports of friction between some established players and new head coach Alvaro Arbeloa though, they produced their best performance of the season in a goalless draw at Anfield last week when they had chances to win the game.

Fulham made nine changes in the League Cup in mid-week, but still ran out 3-2 winners at West Ham. Despite the west London club being an established mid-table Premier League team for a number of seasons, and United’s vulnerable state for the past few years, Fulham have beaten their opponent’s just once in the league since December 2009.



Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Alisson’s brilliance takes the breath away to show way forward for Liverpool
News.content:
It proved to be the foundation stone from which Liverpool were able to build and inflict Bournemouth’s first home defeat since January. There are plenty of [valid] questions to ask of Liverpool’s attack at present but, defensively, it is starting to come together.

“It was a really good fight,” Alisson said, in that self-effacing way of his. “But we have to improve a lot – on the ball and sometimes off the ball as well but we improved in the second half. We adapted to the opponent and that’s what we are doing.”

Any manager with a well-drilled defence stands a chance of improving and that is what Liverpool are doing. Only four weeks ago the discussion was about how easy it was for teams to play through their middle – remember that chaotic afternoon at Newcastle to start? – but that is changing swiftly.

Since Iraola replaced Jeremie Frimpong with Araújo at right-back, three consecutive Premier League clean sheets have followed. Araújo, the Uruguayan on loan from Barcelona, revels in doing the dirty work while Jacquet, the £60m signing from Rennes, oozes quality.

“He’s [Jacquet] very young and adapted really well to the Premier League,” Iraola said. “The first games, he was physically feeling the change of rhythm and I had to sub him. This was a step forward. He looked solid until the end. He’s in a good place physically and I hope he can continue his development.”

News.title: All that money spent and Spurs do not have a proper striker or goalkeeper
News.content:
It was an excellent goal, but Kinsky got a good hand to it and a top goalkeeper would have pushed it around the post. On the evidence of the first half, when he made four saves, Suzuki would have also stopped the ball creeping into the net.

Suzuki cost Villa in the region of £30m and he looks a more than able replacement for Emiliano Martínez. Spurs, on the other hand, have not had a top-class goalkeeper since Hugo Lloris and it is a puzzle that so much faith has been placed in Kinsky.

Spurs spent most of the summer firmly denying any links to Jackson before Villa signed him from Chelsea for an initial £47.5m that could rise to £65m. Given the London club paid an initial £75m for Sávio and committed to a £60m obligation to make Omar Marmoush’s season-long loan permanent, Jackson might have been a relative bargain for them.

Asked if Tottenham had made a big mistake by failing to sign a proper number nine, head coach Robert De Zerbi said: “The transfer market was long. The situation changed many times. There was also the financial rules, at the end of the transfer market. And we had to respect the rules.

“We didn’t sell the players who we thought, in the beginning, there was the possibility, the chance to sell. There are a lot of reasons. I think the club and the coach, we are not sleeping, we know the characteristics of the players, we know everything. And if we didn’t make any different decisions, it was because we couldn’t.”

News.title: An A to Z guide to what’s in your laundry detergent
News.content:
Laundry is one of those jobs that most of us do on autopilot. Throw a load of washing and your favourite detergent into the drum and wait for the machine to work its magic. Perhaps you’ve never even thought to ask yourself what chemicals you’re putting in with your clothes.

In the UK, detergent brands are legally required to state the use of surfactants and enzymes (the main ingredients for stain removal) in a way that is easy to understand, but you may see additional compounds that leave you scratching your head.

Here, I break down the words on the back of the bottle to help you understand exactly what you’re putting in your washing. Given that I’ve just tested 26 laundry detergents and developed an app to help you clean your clothes better, I’m the best woman for the job.

Below, you’ll find the most common detergent ingredients listed A to Z. If you’ve got a burning question about a laundry buzzword, I should be able to help. Add any in the comments section below.

Anionic

There are two main types of surfactants: anionic and non-ionic. A surfactant has a hydrophilic head that loves water and a hydrophobic tail that hates it. Anionic surfactants have a negative charge on their head, which is what helps lift soils and stains from the fabric, though they’re not so good at getting rid of oils. They create a lot of foam but their effectiveness can be limited by minerals found in hard water, which is why they are paired with non-ionic surfactants.

Bio

Short for biological, this label means that a detergent contains enzymes. These are proteins that break down fats, starches and grease, so use bio formulations when you need to tackle stubborn food stains. They are effective at lower temperatures but they can be abrasive on sensitive skin. If your skin is easily irritated, opt for non-bio, instead.

News.title: Spitting row mars feisty Millwall-West Ham clash
News.content:
Millwall manager Alex Neil said after the game that fourth official Lewis Smith had confirmed a spitting accusation had been made.

Asked if he had spoken to Marschall about the claim, Neil replied: “I haven’t asked him about it. But it’s like anything else; I’m sure there’ll be footage of it, or not of it, if it didn’t happen.

“I’d be extremely surprised if Fil’s made an accusation and nothing’s happened. But that’s not really for me to deal with; I’m sure the authorities will deal with that.”

West Ham manager Nuno Espírito Santo said: “I’m aware of the allegation. I didn’t see the image; I didn’t speak with Taty. I cannot go much further on that.”

He added: “I’m going to try to look at the images.”

There were also ugly scenes at full time when players had to be separated at the end of a derby that had been at the centre of an unprecedented police operation.

There were six arrests as of 4pm on Saturday for offences including tailgating, assault on a police officer and entering or attempting to enter a stadium while intoxicated.

News.title: Bloodthirsty Brighton feast on rattled Arsenal
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of today’s Premier League 3pm kick-offs, with Brighton vs Arsenal the pick of the three matches.

Brighton are the league’s top goalscorers so far this season and have amassed the most expected goals, but the champions have the league’s best defence and are seeking five wins from five to start their title defence. There is some welcome needle between Fabian Hurzeler and Mikel Arteta, dating back to Declan Rice’s contentious second yellow for delaying the restart two years ago, as well as the Brighton manager’s comments about Arsenal’s style of play in March.

That 1-0 Arsenal victory at the Amex coincided with Man City dropping points at home to Nottingham Forest on a pivotal night in the title race. Bukayo Saka scored a deflected shot in the ninth minute, and Arsenal held on from there in an ugly but resolute display.

With Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz fit and firing, as well as the introduction of Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes to Arteta’s midfield stable, Arsenal’s football has been more technical and enterprising so far this season. Brighton are one of the few teams who will back themselves to play through Arsenal’s press, which should make for an absorbing game.

Elsewhere, Newcastle are looking to bounce back from their shellacking at Leeds at home to surprise package Hull City. Mattias Jaissle’s team took four points from Liverpool and Spurs but there is concern about how many shots they are conceding. Hull remain unbeaten and continue to confound the odds and underlying data, but that surely cannot last forever.

Everton are also one of the division’s unbeaten teams, but will be targeting three points from a home game against Ipswich after three consecutive draws. Ipswich are sitting comfortably on six points after their win at Crystal Palace, though they did have the extra man for the majority at Selhurst Park.

Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Red Roses’ 39-match winning streak brought to end in Canada draw
News.content:
The record books will show that this meeting, a proper Test full of ebbs and flows, was neither. And, no matter the pre-match belief of England head coach John Mitchell, Canada are not on the same level of professionalism and funding as his side. Mitchell had brought back nine players, many of whom featured in last year’s World Cup final victory, after the thrashing of Australia last week with the expectation that the history of 2025 would repeat itself. Canada had other ideas.

“The plan on the field at the last scrum was to go for the win,” Canada captain Sophie de Goede said. “And then the message came on from the sideline to kick it out. In that moment you have to trust your coach and your coaching staff, and we’ll have a discussion about it later. If we had given away a penalty off the next breakdown, we’d be sitting here going, ‘Why didn’t you kick it out?’”

England’s downfall came at the set-piece, where their line-out malfunctioned and their scrum never gained dominance, in a tale which was not too dissimilar to last week. The hosts came second in the physical battle, too, which was uncharacteristic of them; losing Hannah Botterman to a shoulder injury did not help, either. All told, Canada just looked as though they wanted it a little bit more and maybe this was the wake-up call the Red Roses needed: when you are at the top, and at the top by a margin, every team want to be the one to dethrone you.

News.title: GPs summoned in Frankfurt as third malaria death reported
News.content:
While malaria is treatable if caught early, the patients were likely not considered to have the disease because they lacked travel history to countries where malaria typically circulates, meaning treatment was delayed.

“This is why we alerted the medical people in Frankfurt, if you have odd cases presenting at your clinic, please also consider that there might be malaria around,” Dr Tinnemann said.

“There is this assumption that people who get sick with a nasty fever in places like Frankfurt and elsewhere that have not travelled cannot have malaria, and we don’t bother to investigate. That’s got to stop. That’s why these people die,” Joe Lines, Professor of Malaria Control and Vector Biology at the London School of Tropical Hygiene and Medicine, told The Telegraph.

Before the two cases in Schwanheim – both of which occurred at least 3 miles from the airport where the first malaria cases were reported – investigators were working on the hypothesis that just a single mosquito was responsible for the outbreak, but the new cases have cast doubt on that theory.

“We expect mosquitoes to live between one and three weeks on average,” said Dr Tinnemann.

“We had five cases in the beginning of July, then another in August - at that point, there was a good chance that potentially it could just be one bug. But now it seems at least there must be one other,” he said.

Frankfurt’s public health board have now shipped blood samples from all eight patients to a specialised lab in Antwerp, Belgium, where scientists can carry out DNA analysis to indicate if the infections came from one or multiple mosquitoes, and are awaiting results.

As temperatures warm, experts fear that several tropical mosquito-borne diseases – including malaria, dengue fever, Zika virus, and chikungunya could become established across Europe.

Earlier this month, a colony of Aedes aeypti mosquitoes – the bugs responsible for transmitting dengue and Zika virus – were found breeding in a residential area in East London for the first time.

Airfinity, the disease-monitoring company, said of the malaria outbreak in Frankfurt: “the risk to the wider public remains low but non-zero.”

“Continued vector surveillance, rapid diagnosis, and ready access to antimalarials are critical to prevent further severe outcomes.”

Sports.title: Wayne Rooney stays off booze ahead of I’m A Celeb stint after quitting for World Cup as he aims to ‘make his boys proud’
Sports.content:
Next

WAYNE Rooney is on the wagon ahead of his stint on I’m A Celebrity — to help him at least equal wife Coleen’s second place on the jungle show.

The ultra-competitive former England and Manchester United striker packed in the booze to be on top form as a BBC World Cup pundit.



Wayne, 40, has told pals he is “feeling great” and is keen to emulate Coleen’s success in 2024.

A source said: “Wayne sees I’m A Celeb as a huge chance to make a fresh impression.



“The wider public maybe don’t know how hard he’s been grafting on his punditry and in his managerial career.

“Wayne so impressed BBC bosses that they’ve commissioned him to host a new quiz show.

“He wants to bring that same professional approach to I’m A Celeb and really make Coleen and their four boys proud.”

The Sun on Sunday revealed yesterday talks are at an advanced stage for him to join the ITV show.



Coleen, 40 is likely to support him in Australia alongside their youngest three sons Klay, 13, Kit, ten, and eight-year-old Cass.

Insiders said Wayne has been keen to take part after seeing how much Coleen enjoyed it — and will be getting some helpful advice from her on how to cope.

As well as Wayne, other celebrities approached this year include Gavin & Stacey star Joanna Page, TV presenter and former Team GB Paralympian Ade Adepitan, and Kaiser Chiefs frontman Ricky ­Wilson.

After a spell in management, Wayne landed a role on BBC’s Match of the Day last summer.

He has signed up to host a ­podcast, The Wayne Rooney Show, plus a gameshow called Can You Beat Wayne Rooney?.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick reacts to Man Utd fans booing Kobbie Mainoo sub in show of defiance at Fulham
Sports.content:
Next

MICHAEL CARRICK insists he was not offended by Manchester United supporters booing his decision to substitute Kobbie Mainoo.

Mainoo was replaced by Mason Mount in the 80th minute of United’s 1-1 draw at Fulham, with the hosts 1-0 up.



United supporters loudly booed Mainoo’s removal and broke into a rendition of his chant before Matheus Cunha claimed a deflected 89th-minute equaliser.

Carrick accepted emotions were running high with United staring at a third successive defeat before they nabbed a late point.



He said: “There’s always going to be certain reactions when you’re making changes.”

“I think Kobbie played well to be honest, so it was just more of at that stage of the game we’re trying to make something happen and Kobbie understands that.

“He’s fine, I spoke to him after the game, he’s absolutely fine. He’s all about the team and what’s best.
