'The pressure here is like something out of the 1980s. Trujillo, the VAR official, called him over for the first red and didn't call him over for the second, which was even clearer. This Trujillo has a history with Real Madrid: last year in the Copa final, Osasuna, Girona...

'If the poor referee has no experience, no stature for a derby, then this man is either under no pressure, or under a kind of pressure we know nothing about.

'I would have liked to leave here with the win or without having to speak. I arrived here three months ago and you know I'm not usually one to go in this direction.

'Two reds against Elche and we won. Two reds today, that's already more difficult. It's a referee with only small matches behind him and a VAR official who has a history.

'Congratulations to the Refereeing Appointments Committee.'

Mourinho was in disbelief at a referee he is adamant will never make it to the highest level

Mourinho is an expert at making his point in press conferences and this was one of his finest since returning to Spain.

Goals from Grimaldo, who scored from the penalty spot, and Jonathan David ensured Diego Simeone's side won it 2-1. Antonio Rudiger's late goal was merely a consolation.

But it was the fact that Atletico Madrid kept all 11 players on the pitch en route to victory that most irked Mourinho and Madrid.

Mourinho's print-outs included one tackle by Cristian Romero on Bellingham, which looked particularly bad upon second viewing but only drew a yellow card.

Kang-In Lee's tackle on Fede Valverde went without punishment, while Huijsen got a straight red card for holding Giuliano Simeone inside the box.

In an official club statement, Real Madrid said: 'Real Madrid lose the derby at the Metropolitano in a match marked by Ortiz Arias' VERY TERRIBLE REFEREEING.

'He failed to send off Cuti Romero in the first half for stepping on Bellingham's knee (despite going to the monitor to review the incident), nor did he send off Kang-In Lee for stepping on Valverde's left ankle.

'Both decisions had an impact on the match, which was ultimately decided in Atlético's favor in the second half.'

🚨🫵🏽 Jude Bellingham against the referee at full time: “Two red cards! Two!”.@postunited — oscarolleroo on IG 📸 pic.twitter.com/1qkCTlsMUO — Fabrizio Romano (@FabrizioRomano) September 20, 2026

Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham was furious at officials after Cristian Romero was not sent off

Frustration in Real Madrid's ranks also extended to star man Jude Bellingham who was seen giving the referee a piece of his mind following the final whistle.

Footage showed the Englishman shouting 'oh my god' at Arias, before adding 'two red cards!'

Bellingham was particularly aggrieved that Romero's challenge on him did not see red when replays suggested that it was a sending off offence.

Sports.title: RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: It's all very well Howard Webb sending his VAR bunglers to the naughty step - but those that know him tell me 'back-stabbing' referee supremo must look in the mirror
Sports.content:
Matt Donohue and Blake Antrobus will have a sharper grasp of what it means to interfere with play this weekend. On account of their VAR blunders at the Manchester derby, Howard Webb has decreed they won’t have that option in the Premier League for the foreseeable future.

We know enough by now about their journey to the naughty step. But what about their boss? What about Webb?

How many of these malfunctions need occur before the guy in charge of refereeing takes a look closer to home?

He gave his opinion on Tuesday, which is to say he took a dim view of how his best official, Michael Oliver, saw a correct decision to disallow Erling Haaland’s winner overruled by his eyes in the sky. When Webb reviewed it all, he blamed Donohue’s ‘tunnel vision’ on Haaland and Antrobus was guilty of following Donohue down the same hole.

Neither of them factored for the obvious, that Enzo Fernandez was offside and interfering, and each of them will spend some time below ground as a consequence.

‘They'll not be officiating again until after the international break,’ said Webb.

Howard Webb may have a few questions of his own to answer if the Premier League refereeing standards keep slipping

Enzo Fernandez clearly interferes with play in the Manchester derby but it was missed by the VAR officials, who have now been stood down by Webb

I chatted over a few of these sentiments with a former Premier League referee on Friday and there was no disagreement about standing down the officials. Donohue, the VAR, and Antrobus, his assistant, had committed a cock-up in a high-profile game. Of course they should be benched for a while, we agreed.

But the issue was the man whose organisation put them there in the first place. That being the man who was also responsible for the training and refinement of Michael Salisbury, Lee Mason, John Brooks, Darren England and Dan Cook.

What do they have in common? They have all been in the VAR booth since Webb took over at what was then known as the PGMOL in late 2022 and they have all sat on that naughty step for human errors in their handling of the machine era. Salisbury has visited it more than once.

Errors will happen. That is fine. And it is also fine to view VAR as the worst encroachment in the recent history of the game; a joy-sucking, time-wasting, immensely flawed attempt to find a level of perfection that sport never needed and won’t be delivered. That’s my view and immediate abolition is my wish.

But so long as it exists, where is the accountability from Webb for its botched application in the Premier League? How many people have to be stood down for huge mistakes on his watch before Webb himself stands down?

To follow my conversations with those who have worked with him is to construct a complicated portrait. ‘He’s a clever man and he can be very charming,’ one former official tells me. ‘He can be very impressive, but he is also a master politician and will stab you in the back if it suits him.’

We can take those thoughts or leave them – refereeing is a competitive world. They can bitch and moan about a colleague as well as the best of us.

But other observations go deeper, namely around his key appointments, which include the import of Kevin Blom from the Dutch Eredivisie as performance coach and Hugh Dallas as manager of Pro Ref’s select group.

Erling Haaland celebrates the goal that should not have stood but that won the Manchester derby

Referee Michael Oliver takes his instructions from the VAR in Stockley Park

Dallas was fourth official in the 2002 World Cup final, so his credentials have merit; Blom is perhaps more famous in Scotland over a bad penalty decision that favoured Czech Republic in a Euro 2012 qualifier.

The latter is part of the tit-for-tat of football, but there is a perception in some quarters that they do not pose enough of a challenge to Webb’s leadership. In other words, who is keeping the boss in check?

As a former Premier League referee put it: ‘As ex-referees, we are asking: “Really, are you really surrounding yourself with these people?” It’s so Howard can be comfortable. I think he will always want people who he can be above.’

Only Webb will know if that’s true. But it is hard to deny that a vast amount of Premier League expertise has been lost to the migration of officials elsewhere once they leave the frontline.

Martin Atkinson refereed in the Premier League for more than 20 years, and then led the select group, but he is now the VAR manager for the Scottish FA. Jon Moss oversaw almost 300 top-flight games and left Webb’s PGMOL in 2024 – he is now head of refereeing at Football Australia. Mark Clattenburg presided over a Champions League final and today works on Gladiators.

All of them will have their reasons for being where they are and all of them dropped the occasional clanger. That’s football. That’s refereeing.

But it also looks a little like a drain of know-how that would doubtless help in the English game, where the quirks and rhythms are a unique challenge to officials.

I tend to doubt the idea that the VAR system is better implemented abroad, because statistics around the error rates across the major European leagues are fairly consistent.

Why is former referee Mark Clattenburg working on Gladiators and not helping out in the Premier League?

Martin Atkinson refereed in the Premier League for more than 20 years but he is now the VAR manager for the Scottish FA

I would also suggest that Webb is hardly the face of gross incompetence – one former colleague of his says that he is a better manager than his predecessor, Mike Riley, and worse at training referees.

Equally, some applaud the greater transparency he has pursued with video analysis on television; others say the referees ‘hate’ it.

It’s a tricky picture to study. It’s certainly far tougher to interpret than the one showing Enzo Fernandez interfering with play in front of the Manchester United goalkeeper. But one thing is clear – Webb cannot persist with the charade of blaming everyone except himself.

Sports.title: Pierre Sage appears to have saved his job at Crystal Palace for now after his well-drilled side played out a disciplined stalemate against Leeds, writes BOBBY MANZI
Sports.content:
Pierre Sage appears to have saved his job at Crystal Palace for now after his well-drilled side played out a disciplined stalemate against Leeds, writes BOBBY MANZI

Pierre Sage will be breathing a sigh of relief heading into the international break.

The pressure was on as Crystal Palace travelled to Leeds United with whispers suggesting Sage could become the first manager sacked if the performance was unpropitious.

In his post-match press conference, Sage admitted that he felt the pressure. ‘When I read social media, there is big pressure,’ Sage said. ‘I don’t care about it. I do my job honestly, I give my best with my skills and limits and at the end I have no regrets with what I do.’

At Leeds, they may not have won but their second positive Premier League result was a step in the right direction after conceding 11 goals in the first four league games.

Palace defended as a cohesive, disciplined unit - keeping a league clean sheet for the first time in the Sage era.

This was the second time this week Palace did not concede after beating Lech Poznan 4-0 in their maiden Europa League tie on Thursday. But the manner of those defensive performances were entirely different.

Palace were fragile defensively in Europe and offered chances a better attacking team would have taken. On Sunday, though, Palace were rejuvenated.

Leeds scarcely threatened as Palace nullified their frontline. Dominic Calvert-Lewin was denied from six yards after a fantastic stop from Walter Benitez, but aside from that, there were no real nervy moments.

Pierre Sage appears to have bought himself time as Crystal Palace manager

Chris Richards significantly improved against Leeds United after a slow start to the season

Takehiro Tomiyasu, who started at central centre-back and was a standout performer in the first half, was forced off at the break. Their control did not suffer, though, as Jefferson Lerma replaced him and Richards shifted into the middle.

That, in itself, is progress. Palace's back three has changed in every Premier League game this season and, as a result, they have lacked consistency and understanding.

But here, they won their duels and did not give the ball away as cheaply. Jaydee Canvot, who was dropped in the previous two games, improved drastically and made a vital interception in the dying minutes to prevent Calvert-Lewin from bombing through on goal.

Palace had planned to consider Sage's future at the beginning of the three-week-long international break. This performance, though, makes a managerial change implausible and unjustifiable.

The result should settle the nerves and fears. Offensively, Palace were laboured but a boring game with a solid defensive performance is exactly what they needed to restore confidence in the group.

In their five games this season, Palace have either matched or bettered their results from last term against the same opposition. Last term at Leeds, they could not handle the atmosphere and were thrashed 4-1. This time, they were fearless.

Even if Palace had lost at Leeds, sacking him would have been questionable. The offensive ideas are exciting, the defence has just struggled to click.

He has been trying to change the style of play, pressing higher and playing on the front foot and that has exposed the defensive weaknesses. Effective transformation cannot be achieved overnight, though. He requires time to integrate his ideas.

He came into a new job with two of his centre-backs signed in the final week of the window while the club did not purchase a replacement for Maxence Lacroix, relying on Axel Disasi on loan from Chelsea instead.

His other options were Richards, who struggled to settle without Lacroix's presence guiding him through games, and Canvot, a developing teenager who makes the occasional mistake.

For all the problems thrown Sage’s way, he has dealt with them calmly. He deserves time to implement his ideas. At Lens, he showed he can get a team competing above their perceived level, finishing second to PSG and winning the French Cup.

He is a talented, young and progressive manager. That was the right style of appointment in the summer and remains exactly what Palace need. Sacking him would have been premature and the response at Leeds, who are unbeaten this season, proved that.

Leeds should be aiming for Europe

Daniel Farke’s side, meanwhile, continued their impressive start to the season - remaining unbeaten after five games.

This was a far cry from the free-flowing Leeds played when they bossed Newcastle on Monday night. They were passive and crafted just one clear-cut chance against Palace’s resolute defence. But Farke admitted that it cannot be perfect every week.

‘It’s mixed emotions,’ Farke said. ‘We would have preferred to win but the reality is there are not 38 games with magic nights under the floodlights and champagne football where you overrun the opponent and score goals for fun.

‘Sometimes there are scrappy Sunday afternoons where we must dig in. I liked the clean sheet, extending the unbeaten run and the attitude to fight for every point where we tried to dig in.’

Daniel Farke admitted post-match that his side cannot play 'champagne football' every week after following up their 4-1 win against Newcastle with a goalless draw

His team did show defensive grit, too. Much like Palace, they were disciplined and made it tough for the opposition to break them down.

In goal, James Trafford made five saves and was key to securing a point.

Even though Leeds were heavily fancied, the result is overwhelmingly positive given they were not at their best but still managed to take something from the game. That is often the sign of a good team.

With nine English teams in Europe this season, Leeds should be contending for a European spot - taking advantage of their beneficial schedule while rivals slog through a 50-game-plus season.

The litmus test will come after the international break, though, with tough matches against Arsenal, Manchester United, Sunderland and Bournemouth in October.

Sports.title: Enzo Maresca's Man City prove they are the great entertainers in rout of Sunderland... but curious midfield make-up gives boss plenty to ponder, writes JACK GAUGHAN
Sports.content:
Manchester City's high wire act was back by popular demand and Enzo Maresca's sigh of relief when Robert Jones called time suggested the ringmaster was briefly worried they might fall off.

But what is not to like about this new City? The great entertainers, the daring pressers who give up plenty in behind their midfield, will throw up more afternoons like this – as long as the opposition are as strong as Sunderland, whose striker Brian Brobbey became the first man to net a top-flight hat-trick and end up on the losing team since Roque Santa Cruz for Blackburn in 2007.

This was not what followers of Chelsea and Leicester City had predicted when Maresca took the reins.

The talk of 'safe zones' and endless loops of sideways possession are so far removed from City's current reality that the detractors could well have been describing a different coach altogether.

Maresca has won five on the bounce at the start of his reign, capitalising on Arsenal's slip to go three clear, and if these sort of games continue, this team will become the country's hottest ticket.

Imagine it when they go to Anfield in three weeks' time, on the back of this eight-goal thriller. Potentially a fitting tribute to Klopp and Guardiola on its way. 'I prefer to win 1-0 than 5-3,' Maresca smiled. Those watching certainly do not.

Manchester City maintained their 100 per cent start to the league season against Sunderland

Brian Brobbey scored a hat-trick at the Etihad Stadium but still ended up on the losing side

MARESCA'S MIDFIELD MUSINGS

Maresca sounded philosophical late last week when discussing the likelihood of soon seeing the true best version of his City, claiming – perhaps somewhat cautiously – that they might be at around 40 per cent at the moment.

The Italian is barely three months into the job and given there are tweaks to the style with which City have been wedded for the past decade, the idea of requiring considerably more time to perfect the masterplan is understandable.

And when he pores over the first five league matches in his study over the international break, Maresca will doubtless pay particular attention to the make-up of the midfield.

Going forward they are scary, only Brighton scoring more goals so far, but it was noticeable how much joy became available to the likes of Enzo Le Fee in the great expanse of vacant central areas.

Elliot Anderson wants to be everything to everyone, charging into areas to halt the opposition at source, but if he is to be allowed that freedom then Enzo Fernandez might need to operate slightly deeper. Too often Sunderland picked pockets – Noah Sadiki firing two warnings either side of Brobbey's second goal coming from exactly this problem.

The idea appeared to be for Fernandez and Anderson to press higher from their starting positions in a bid to squeeze the Black Cats. Captain Ruben Dias was tasked with filling that hole, following Brobbey, to tuck City into a back three.

Dias lost the individual battle with Brobbey though, the Dutchman too strong, too wily, just too good. City were easily turned around and effectively ceded far too many inviting opportunities against a team who should have taken something against Arsenal last week, and who left the Etihad Stadium having created an expected goals tally of more than four.

Maresca's man-to-man defending, following markers across the pitch, has its benefits and gives City so much going in the other direction. It can throw up some oddities too.

Their second goal, Rayan Cherki's, came from tireless right winger Iliman Ndiaye turning over possession on the left of midfield, with Anderson pressing inside the box. The whole aesthetic of it just seemed a little askew but clearly this risk and reward style is paying serious dividends.

'The message is try to win the ball back as soon as possible,' Maresca said. 'To attack immediately. It was a nice goal because we won the ball and attacked immediately. Generally we can control things better, keeping the ball. We made mistakes.'

Enzo Fernandez opened the scoring for City en route to edging out this eight-goal thriller

Enzo Maresca has plenty to ponder, not least working out who should occupy which spaces

WING WIZARDS

There can be no argument about City's business in the wide areas across the calendar year - and the weekend's fixtures were the perfect case study for that.

Semenyo's brace took him to 13 goals in all competitions since arriving from Bournemouth in January, initially a summer target but who City accelerated interest in, while Ndiaye's start to life at the Etihad Stadium could not have gone much better.

At £65m, and £20m cheaper than Savinho, Ndiaye could become a steal if his last two league displays are anything to go by.

He manfully did a defensive job at Old Trafford last week while carrying that threat on the right to force Manchester United to think twice, with the remit against Sunderland slightly different and the way he glided past Dayann Methalie in the eighth minute – scythed down for a free kick that ultimately saw Fernandez cleverly open the scoring – showcased a more direct attitude than his predecessor in that spot.

Despite being heavily involved for Tottenham, Savinho – one league goal since 2024 - again struggled to impact proceedings in defeat by Aston Villa.

Ndiaye should overtake the Brazilian's overall output at City of two league goals within weeks and his first for the club is only a matter of time.

HAALAND'S FULL HOUSE

Erling Haaland completed the set of scoring against every Premier League team he's faced with the late goal awarded via VAR, who adjudged Josko Gvardiol was not offside in the build-up. The correct call, Sunderland boss Regis Le Bris was more vexed by Semenyo's strike moments before the break.

Le Bris felt Marc Guehi handled inside the box before Semenyo thundered underneath Robin Roefs.

'It looks like a handball,' Le Bris said. 'It's hard not to see it as handball. They don't explain, they just say yes or no.'

Sports.title: Andoni Iraola takes more positives than negatives into the international break as Alexander Isak finally shows his sharpness in hard-fought 1-0 victory... but there is still plenty to fix, writes LEWIS STEELE
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola toasted to a happy homecoming – and then prepared to jet off on his holidays knowing his work-in-progress Liverpool side are heading in the right direction, slowly but surely.

It would be wrong to say the Reds’ victory at Iraola’s old stomping ground Bournemouth was thoroughly deserved or even convincing but as the new boss takes stock over the international break, he will have more positives than negatives to evaluate.

Match-winner Alexander Isak is finally showing the sharpness and attacking efficiency the Anfield top brass thought they were paying £125million for a year or so ago, while other new signings are settling and previous sub-par performers look back to their best.

It was Isak’s second-half strike that helped Liverpool on their way to their second league victory of the new era and ensured the three-week break from Premier League can be enjoyed knowing they are still unbeaten.

This was not the perfect afternoon by any stretch and the result probably glosses over the fact that, like last Saturday’s goalless draw with Fulham, Iraola’s side did demonstrate several frailties and areas to improve.

But given the limited pre-season owing to the World Cup and late returns to camp, the new boss is needing to learn on the job and righting the wrongs of last season is akin to fixing a plane while it is airborne.

Match-winner Alexander Isak is finally showing the sharpness and attacking efficiency the Anfield top brass thought they were paying £125million for a year or so ago

It was Isak’s second-half strike that helped Liverpool on their way to their second league victory of the new era and ensured the three-week break from Premier League can be enjoyed

The win, therefore, makes the three-week break between this fixture and a home clash against league leaders Manchester City all the more relaxing for Iraola and Co.

This was a banana skin for Liverpool, who at times were sluggish and the front four – especially Florian Wirtz and new signing Bradley Barcola – flattered to deceive. But they came through unscathed and Bournemouth, perhaps in a European hangover, never severely threatened.

This game was not a pinch-me moment in the same way that midweek trip to San Sebastian – and win in Europe over Real Sociedad – was for the Cherries fans but it still was a day to remember as Iraola, the man who took them to the continental stage, returned.

Telling a Bournemouth supporter that their manager would one day be poached by Liverpool might have prompted the same disbelief as informing them they would be playing in European competition, and Iraola deserves acclaim for their journey as much as anyone.

The Basque boss created a monster down here on the south coast, one that had lost just two matches in 2026 – to Arsenal and Manchester City – before this match. And it was those energetic, resilient traits that plagued his new team in the first half.

Just like in Iraola’s three years here, Bournemouth strangled their opposition and allowed them barely a second of peace on the ball. They were dangerous going the other way and Liverpool looked vulnerable in the opening stages.

Iraola created a monster down here on the south coast, one that had lost just two matches in 2026 – to Arsenal and Manchester City – before this match

Iraola’s return to his old stomping ground was an apt opportunity to make a true evaluation of his new team and how much they had improved so far this season

Evanilson had the best chance when a zapping one-touch team move culminated in Marcus Tavernier squaring for his Brazilian striker, who unleashed an audacious flick only to be denied by a smart, reflex stop by compatriot Alisson.

Iraola’s return to his old digs was an apt opportunity to make a true evaluation of his new team and how much they had improved so far this season. In the early stages, however, they put in the sort of performance we became accustomed to last year.

MATCH FACTS BOURNEMOUTH (4-2-3-1): Petrovic 6; Smith 6 (Cook 75, 6), Hill 7, Silva 6, Truffert 6; Adams 6 (Gannon-Doak, 88), Scott 6; Rayan 6 (Toth 89), Christie 6 (Jebbison 75, 6), Tavernier 7 (Brooks 75, 6); Evanilson 6. Subs not used: Di Gregorio, Soler, Diakite, Sanchez. Booked: None. Scorers: None. Manager: Marco Rose 6. LIVERPOOL (4-1-4-1): Alisson 7; Araujo 6, JACQUET 8, Van Dijk 7, Kerkez 6; Mac Allister 6; Barcola 5 (Munoz 71, 6), Szoboszlai 5 (Gravenberch 81), Wirtz 4 (Nyoni 71, 6), Gakpo 7; Isak 7 (Koumas 81). Subs not used: Mamardashvili, Frimpong, Gomez, Ngumoha, Tsimikas Booked: Szoboszlai, Isak. Scorers: Isak 57. Manager: Andoni Iraola 6. Referee: Michael Oliver 5. Attendance: N/A.

Like Arne Slot’s second season, Liverpool were lacking in ideas going forward and appeared to be lethargic, lacking the verve and intensity Iraola craves. If not for some canny defending by the imperious new boy Jeremy Jacquet, they might have fallen behind.

Indeed, Bournemouth’s energy and impetus belied the fact they had played in the Basque country less than 72 hours earlier. All the excitement Liverpool showed in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday – with ten chances and a few academy kids starring – was gone.

Saying that, Alisson was never severely threatened other than Evanilson’s early chance. Ryan Christie had two chances at the start of the second half but fluffed his lines on both counts, unable to wrap his boot round one to find the correct angle, then pulling another wide.

Marco Rose might have felt the happier manager for the majority of the first hour but his team never capitalised on the lethargic mood of his predecessor’s team. Soon, Rose’s Cherries were punished as Isak opened the scoring after 57 minutes.

The goal came after fine work from Cody Gakpo on the left flank, the Dutchman eventually finding Isak who needed no second invitation to pull the trigger and put his side ahead, firing hard and low past Djordje Petrovic.

It was the sort of goal all forwards need. A quiet day at the office had preceded it but when the chance fell to Isak, he did not hesitate in taking it. The Swede could have had a couple more in the ten minutes that followed but was thwarted by strong defending.

Gakpo deserves praise, too, and has been Liverpool’s most-improved player year on year. The Dutchman has seven goal involvements in his first six games this season and is currently the first forward Iraola will sketch on to his team-sheets.

In the end, Liverpool held on for a well-fought victory and their fans could enjoy their day on the sunny south coast. The three-week break will feel all the sweeter for Iraola, too, who marked his return to Bournemouth with three points.

Sports.title: Inside Burnley's shocking decline under Alan Pace's ALK: The humiliating sponsor fiasco, why highly-respected CEO quit the Clarets, club staff aghast at changes behind the scenes and the 'ominous shadow' of debt leaving supporters terrified
Sports.content:
The threat of mutiny has long been simmering away at Turf Moor. And earlier this month, as Burnley threw away a lead against Bristol City, extending a barren run at a ground in which they have now not won a league game in nearly a year, the fury of a despairing fan base finally boiled over. Boos thundered around the stadium. Clarets striker Armando Broja got into an angry confrontation with a disgruntled fan in the car park. No one was immune to the ire, and certainly not owner and chairman Alan Pace who bore the brunt of the chanting. You expect he may well suffer it again if Burnley flounder against Derby on Saturday as they return to Turf Moor rooted to the foot of the Championship with one league win in the last 328 days and none since February. The last time they were in this division they won promotion with 100 points. How far away those days feel now. Not just because of the dismal football they are having to endure, and the precarious position that’s put them in, but for the ever-growing list of questions for which they are so rarely given answers. Why did the club wait until relegation before sacking Scott Parker? Why did they wait 71 days to appoint Nicky Hayen and start pre-season without a manager? Why did they sell top scorer Zian Flemming on deadline day with no replacement lined up, and why did they only receive £20million for a player with 11 top-flight goals in a summer when Premier League clubs spent £3.5billion? Why did they have to drop shirt sponsor Finotive One, a self-titled ‘trading ecosystem’, on the eve of the season? And why, after all that, has the club’s chief executive James Holroyd just left his position after little more than a year in charge? Pace promised an ‘exciting journey’ when he bought the club in December 2020. That’s certainly one way of putting it. And all of this against the backdrop of that leveraged buy-out, one akin to Manchester United under the Glazers, that used Burnley’s own money to turn a once debt-free organisation with £80m in the bank into one with £13m cash in the coffers, according to the last accounts, and £142m of debt casting an ominous shadow. No wonder it’s starting to turn toxic. Burnley owner Alan Pace (centre) has been the subject of fan ire at recent games amid worries about the Clarets' performance on and off the pitch Nicky Hayen's side slumped to a 2-1 defeat at home to Bristol City a fortnight ago. They have not won a league game at Turf Moor in 2026 Holroyd’s arrival was seen as a huge coup for the club, a man steeped in experience having spent 14 years at Manchester United following another 14 years at adidas. One former colleague described him to Daily Mail Sport as ‘incredibly serious and incredibly methodical about his work’. A man who spent the best part of three decades working for just two companies was out of his third one after just over a year. Burnley confirmed his departure to Daily Mail Sport and said that Holroyd had ‘decided to step down to pursue a new challenge’. He will continue to work at the club as part of their Burnley In The Community department but is no longer involved on the commercial side of the business. ‘It's been an honour and a privilege to serve this great club,’ said Holroyd. ‘There's a pride and a resilience that runs through Burnley that you feel from the moment you arrive. That's what makes this such a difficult decision, but it's why I'll keep supporting the incredible work being done by BFC in the Community. 'I want to thank Alan and the board for the opportunity to serve this club, and the staff and supporters for making me feel truly part of the Claret family.' Daily Mail Sport understands the embarrassing and expensive Finotive One fiasco, where the club dropped their shirt sponsor after just 42 days despite a star-studded launch that featured investor and former NFL star JJ Watt, England cricket legend Jimmy Anderson and Arnold Schwarzenegger, and replaced all purchased shirts free of charge, played a part. Burnley refused to confirm the reason why the sponsorship ended but it’s understood Finotive One failed to meet its payments. Sources also told Daily Mail Sport that difficulties had arisen in Holroyd and Pace’s working relationship and the Finotive One debacle did nothing to ease matters. A parting of the ways was decided to be best for all concerned.

Your browser does not support iframes.

The club dropped their shirt sponsor after just 42 days despite a star-studded launch that featured investor and former NFL star JJ Watt (right) Holroyd has been replaced on an interim basis by Amy Wells, who was head of HR, and director of strategy and transformation Nathan Kavanagh. Sources suggested Holroyd found the chairman too hands-on, a complaint echoed to Daily Mail Sport by other former members of staff, with one saying employees often felt they were not trusted to get on with their job. Most of the staff who were in place when Pace's ALK took over are no longer there, many leaving within a year, leading to a sense among those close to the club that they cannot recognise the one they once knew. ‘These were local people, where the club meant everything to them, and one by one you saw them leave,’ said one former member of staff. There’s a feeling that the sense of community and togetherness that forged a spirit able to take Burnley into Europe has been eroded. Pace has spent money, and appointed two good managers in Vincent Kompany and Parker, but fans struggle to connect to an ever-revolving door of players they see as mercenaries as the club bounces between the Premier League and the Championship. None of them they see as personifying the famous ‘Legs, Hearts, Minds’ motto emblazoned on Sean Dyche’s request on a wall at the training ground. The overwhelming sense among the fanbase now is that the last two promotions have papered over the cracks and the fissures are growing too wide to fix. Manager Hayen is already under pressure and facing questions about his future and whether he’s been told defeat by Derby could spell the end. ‘Not at the moment,’ he said. ‘They didn't tell me this can be my last game. It can be, I don't know.’ Kyle Walker addressed staff this week to tell them that the players were doing everything they could to fix things. Manager Nicky Hayen is already under pressure and facing questions about his future and whether he’s been told defeat by Derby today could spell the end Midfielder Reo Hatate looks pained during Burnley's draw at Wrexham last week So much of it, though, comes back to the money. The £142m debt from the most recent accounts for the 2024-25 promotion season, the interest on bank loans of up to 12 per cent, the £36m of net interest payments over the last five seasons when there was none before the takeover. The £9.5m taken in ‘management fees’ under the current ownership, ones that jumped from £1.5m to £4m after relegation. The transfer debt of £95m that was just £3m four years ago and takes the club’s total gross debt to nearly a quarter of a billion. The near £40m sale of incoming transfer fees to London-based firm Fasanara Capital. And why Velocity Capital, ALK’s investment arm, still owes the football club around £81m. Under the previous ownership, made up of local businessmen, Burnley were famously debt-free, cash rich, and one of the most profitable clubs in Premier League history. Dyche worked miracles on a budget as he established the Clarets in the Premier League and took them into Europe. Now, according to respected finance blog Swiss Ramble, Burnley’s external debt of £142m last year was the fourth highest in England behind only Tottenham and Everton, who have built new stadiums, and the Glazers’ United. ‘There’s a few of us who have been querying the leveraged buyout model of Alan Pace for a few years,’ football finance expert Kieran Maguire tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘It’s reliant on Burnley regularly being in the Premier League for the broadcast cash flows, when its matchday income is only seven per cent of total revenue. ‘The concerns are that the club has £75m of short-terms loans, £30m of long-term loans, has sold players but has sold the transfer instalments from the sales and owes £94m in unpaid transfer fees. Under those circumstances they will struggle to borrow more and, if they do, will have to pay punitive interest rates. ‘It therefore could come down to whether or not Alan Pace has (a) the cash and (b) the desire to provide funding himself.’ Kyle Walker addressed staff this week to tell them that the players were doing everything they could to fix things Sources suggested outgoing CEO James Holroyd found Pace too hands-on, a complaint echoed to Daily Mail Sport by other former members of staff In response to questions about Burnley’s financial position, the club told Daily Mail Sport that the latest set of accounts, due to be submitted to the Premier League by October 31, ‘will give a more accurate picture of the current position’. Those accounts are expected to show a fall in both debt and how much is still owed by Velocity to the club. The management fees, meanwhile, are understood to be payments to non-full-time Burnley employees, such as consultants, for their services. The increase is thought to be due to performance-related bonuses. The worry for Burnley, especially after such a torrid start to the campaign, is what happens if they don’t go up again this time. They are only getting two years of parachute payments instead of three as they came straight back down last season. The £35m settlement Everton were forced to pay for breaking financial rules in the season Burnley were first relegated was a lifeline, but it remains uncertain whether the Clarets will ultimately receive it after the Toffees appealed against the decision. Concerns have been raised, too, about whether Burnley will become a side dish as Pace and ALK expand their multi-club model. They have already purchased Spanish side Espanyol and are believed to be eyeing up Club Leon in Mexico. In the most recent meeting between the club and its independent supporters association, the group was told, according to the latest newsletter, that ‘while EPL TV money is still available to the club, we will remain the priority’. ‘The question does remain what happens in the circumstances where the club is not quickly re-promoted to the EPL and the parachute money comes to an end,’ the newsletter continued. There’s a feeling that the sense of community and togetherness that forged a spirit able to take Burnley into Europe under Sean Dyche has been eroded Burnley have not been outside the top two divisions in more than a quarter of a century. They may well no longer exist had they not beat Leyton Orient on the final day in 1987 to stay in the Football League. Supporters worry that their status as a modest town club, surrounded by big cities, will make it even harder to fight their way back up. ‘There’s a feeling that we could be the next Leicester,’ said one source. The deeper fear, of course, is whether they could also become another Bury and be the first Premier League team to go bust. The club, for now, are not in immediate danger of that and plans are said to be in place should the worst happen. But the longer Burnley remain outside the top flight and, heaven forbid, fall through the divisions, the more difficult it will be to keep on paying the piper.

Sports.title: Premier League propose big Carabao Cup change in £1.8bn 'new deal for football'
Sports.content:
Premier League propose big Carabao Cup change in £1.8bn 'new deal for football'

The Premier League are offering the English Football League a 'new deal for football' worth £1.8billion, but they now want one massive change to the Carabao Cup

View 2 Images Premier League clubs wants changes to the Carabao Cup semi-finals (Image: Liverpool FC via Getty Images)

The Premier League reportedly want Carabao Cup semi-final ties to be decided over one match rather than two as part of a 'new deal for football'. A proposed agreement with the English Football League is said to effectively double the existing solidarity payment, which is divided among clubs across all three EFL divisions, to £1.8billion.

‌



It would be spread across 10 seasons, and both leagues are reportedly around £27million apart in negotiations. However, there is growing confidence of an agreement.

‌



Premier League clubs have unanimously approved the proposal. EFL sides doing likewise would avoid any involvement by the Independent Football Regulator (IFR).

‌



Andros Townsend delivers perfect response after being run over by pitch roller in freak accident READ MORE :

Richarlison takes to social media with clear message after Tottenham lose again READ MORE :

The Daily Mail reports that another condition of their additional funding would be to progress talks with the National League over new clubs earning League Two promotion every season. They cite sources that claim the Premier League wants to reduce its reliance on ownership funding for EFL clubs.

Controls on how these funds are spent are proposed, including a stop on any increases in player wages. The proposition also requires 15% of the funds to go towards infrastructure.

It also features a 'lifeboat fund' for clubs entering administration in future. They would be loaned £20million to continue paying essential creditors and operating.

‌



View 2 Images The Carabao Cup semi-finals could stopping being two-legged ties (Image: Paul Currie/Shutterstock)

The EFL want a tweak to their current divisional split of 80:12:8 between the Championship, League One and League Two. Despite the Premier League seeking no change, a change to 75:15:10 is being sought.

Under the new split, based on a mid-table finish, Championship clubs would receive £8.5million more, rising from £12.1million to £20.6million. That translates to a £1.3million uplift in League One, up from £2.5million to £3.8million, whereas League Two payments would grow by £700k, from £1.8million to £2.5million. A 2% increase in the Premier League transfer levy is to cover the increase, which would go from 4% to 6%.

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

The deal is around 17.5% of what all top-flight clubs earn from their collective broadcast rights. That is 6.5% more than the current level, but half of what the EFL initially sought.

EFL clubs were told about the proposal last week. They will make the final decision once it is ready for the league's board to recommend.

Article continues below

The deal has already been under discussion for six weeks now. It is said that the EFL prefers to wait until the IFR's State of the Game report, which is due to be published by them on 12 October.

Sports.title: Eddie Hearn reveals Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury 'drug testing' delay before announcement
Sports.content:
Eddie Hearn reveals Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury 'drug testing' delay before announcement

Eddie Hearn has provided an update on Anthony Joshua's expected bout against Tyson Fury later this year suggesting a date is 'locked in' but another issue has cropped up

View Image Eddie Hearn has provided an update on Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury (Image: Ben Roberts Photo/Getty Images)

Eddie Hearn has revealed another problem ahead of Anthony Joshua's anticipated bout with Tyson Fury. The British boxing giants finally looked to be on a collision course later this year, before a dispute over the destination of the fight.

‌



Plans appeared to be being put in place for a monumental clash at Madison Square Garden in New York on November 20, AJ's contract for the fight includes a clause insisting it takes place in the United Kingdom. His determination to see that honoured has seen Cardiff's Principality Stadium come into the running, though the bout could be pushed back until December.

‌



But the location of the fight is not the only area causing some contract confusion, according to Hearn. The boxing promoter has suggested there is a discrepancy in expectations between Joshua and Fury.

‌



Olympic champion Joshua has already been required to undergo drug testing since the outset of the bout agreement, while Hearn isn't convinced the same stipulation is within Fury's agreement.

Conor Benn has world title shot shut down just days after Ryan Garcia loss READ MORE :

"The drug testing protocol was the same as what has always been in there," said Hearn, following Pat Brown's win over John Hedges on Saturday. "It wasn't adhered to in its form.

"I don't actually necessarily blame Tyson Fury for that. As we've found out on many occasions, what's in AJ's contract is not necessarily in Tyson Fury's contract.

‌



"Testing was supposed to start when the original contracts were signed, and it didn't for them. And I don't think [Fury] had in his contract that it had to start then.

FOLLOW OUR FIGHTING FB PAGE! Latest boxing and MMA news, analysis and much more via our dedicated Facebook page

"So this is not me saying, 'He didn't enrol'. I don't think he was obligated to enrol [in his contract]. But in our contract, he was obligated to enrol. There have been many issues along the way with the contract that we have let slip and ride because we want to stay in the fight and make sure it happens."

‌



Despite that, Hearn believes that a date for the fight is now locked and that announcement is imminent. Regular conversations have taken place with Netflix.

He said: "Over the last week or two, obviously we made our decision, and AJ was the guy leading that decision that we weren’t interested in accepting any extra money or changing the terms of the agreement to change the location.

"He decided that he wanted to make sure that the fight was in the UK, and since then they've accepted that. We've worked together and we've been speaking to Netflix on regular occasions to basically lock in the date.

Article continues below

"I think the date is locked in, and I'll let them give you the official announcement. It was supposed to be this week, but I think it's going to be very, very soon."

Sports.title: Ronald Koeman Jr breaks down in tears on pitch during emotional tribute after his mum's death
Sports.content:
Ronald Koeman Jr breaks down in tears on pitch during emotional tribute after his mum's death

Ronald Koeman Jr, the son of ex-Everton manager Ronald Koeman, cut an emotional figure after a tribute was made to his late mother while playing for Telstar

View 3 Images Ronald Koeman Jr in tears after his mum died earlier this week (Image: ANP/Shutterstock)

Ronald Koeman Jr broke down in tears following an emotional tribute to his mother after she died earlier this week.

‌



Koeman Jr's father, Ronald Koeman, announced in an Instagram post on Tuesday that his wife, Bartina Koeman-Boddeveld, passed away at the age of 65 after a long battle with cancer.

‌



Koeman said: "With intense sadness, but also with great pride and love, we say goodbye to my beautiful wife, our dearest mom and grandma. Bartina Koeman-Boddeveld. January 30 - September 15 2026. Familie Koeman."

‌



The couple had been married for 41 years and have three children together. Koeman Jr is one of his three children, with Tim Koeman his eldest and Debbie Koeman the only daughter.

Premier League star's partner sends message to Thomas Tuchel after England snub READ MORE :

Koeman Jr, who is a professional goalkeeper for Dutch side Telstar, played his first game since his mum died on Sunday afternoon, as his team went up against AZ Alkmaar.

In tribute to Koeman-Boddeveld, AZ stopped the game in the 12th minute for a minutes applause and during that they put a photo up of the 65-year-old on the big screen.

‌



Unsurprisingly, that drew an emotional reaction from Koeman Jr, who had to wipe the tears away as the whole stadium stood up and clapped in tribute of his mum.

3 View 3 Images (Image: ESPN) 3 View 3 Images (Image: ESPN)

‌



Footage from ESPN also showed Telstar head coach Henk Brugge in tears following what has been a difficult week for the Koeman family, including his goalkeeper.

AZ ended up going on to win the match 1-0 with Mexx Meerdink striking the decisive blow in the first-half, leaving Koeman Jr's side down in 13th with just one league win all season.

Koeman Jr has spent the last five years at Telstar, after moving to the club from Oss in 2021. The 31-year-old has since made 165 appearances for the IJmuiden side, who won promotion to Eredivisie in 2024/25.

‌



His father, Koeman Sr, meanwhile, had his wife alongside him throughout his legendary football career. The defender was one of the best players of his generation and scored the winning goal in the 1992 European Cup final, which saw Barcelona beat Sampdoria.

After hanging up his boots, the Dutchman went into management and recently had been in charge of his national side, but stepped down this summer after their World Cup exit, making it clear that his wife's circumstances had given him a new perspective.

He said: "The past years have made me realise again that there are more important things than football. Football has been my life, but health is priceless.

Article continues below

"When someone you love is fighting a tough battle, your perspective changes. My wife Bartina has supported and encouraged me every day to finish my work as a national coach, despite her own illness process. That is a testimony to incredible strength. I appreciate her more than I’ll ever be able to put into words."

Sports.title: Rugby star knocked out one minute into his debut in worrying collision as medics rush to aid
Sports.content:
Rugby star knocked out one minute into his debut in worrying collision as medics rush to aid

Medics rushed to provide treatment for a rugby union player who was reportedly knocked out after colliding with a stray knee during the first carry of his debut

View 3 Images George Furbank endured a nightmare debut for Harlequins (Image: CameraSport via Getty Images)

George Furbank was reportedly knocked out by a stray knee while making his first carry for Harlequins in their pre-season win over Edinburgh. The England full-back left Northampton Saints this summer after 11 years, having captained them to their third PREM Rugby title last season.

‌



Furbank, 29, was one of several internationals who played at Twickenham Stoop a week before the new season starts. However, he did not get back up from his first carry, staying down after 46 seconds.

‌



Extensive medical treatment soon followed for the debutant. Furbank was eventually able to walk off the pitch before being substituted.

‌



The Gallagher Prem is back and is better than ever! READ MORE :

Rugby event that unearthed Noah Caluori backed to continue producing stars of the future READ MORE :

Rodrigo Isgro initially came on for him, and the Argentina international scored Quins' second try of the game. He was also withdrawn after an hour, with Isgro's replacement Edward Sigauke making an immediate impact by scoring with his first touch of the ball.

The Zimbabwe international added another with three minutes to go. Connor Slevin converted to cap a 33-19 pre-season win.

Furbank is now due to be stood down and miss Quins' opening match of the new PREM season against Bath at The Stoop on Friday night because of World Rugby's concussion protocols that forced him off against Edinburgh.

‌



View 3 Images George Furbank did not get back up after his first carry for Harlequins (Image: CameraSport via Getty Images)

One of the reasons a player is immediately and permanently removed from matches is loss of consciousness. There is then a graduated return-to-play process for them to go through before being cleared to feature competitively again.

The expected delay to his PREM debut for Quins is just the latest setback for Furbank this summer. Appendicitis prevented him from playing at all for England during their Nations Championship games against Argentina, Fiji and South Africa.

‌



Furbank was selected to make his first Test appearance since November 2024 before being withdrawn after ending up in a Johannesburg hospital after experiencing painful symptoms.

View 3 Images George Furbank was able to walk off the pitch after receiving medical treatment (Image: CameraSport via Getty Images)

He played just 25 times for his former club over the past two seasons because of various injuries. A broken arm kept him on the sidelines for four months after re-fracturing it.

Article continues below

Furbank returned in last year's Champions Cup quarter-final against Castres. Calf and knee issues had also prevented him from playing more for the Saints before he decided to leave in April.

They have also limited him to just 14 international caps, six-and-a-half years on from his first call-up. That was for the Six Nations in 2020, which England won while Eddie Jones was still coach of the team.

Sports.title: Man City beat Sunderland in eight-goal thriller to move three points clear at top
Sports.content:
Man City beat Sunderland in eight-goal thriller to move three points clear at top

MANCHESTER CITY 5-3 SUNDERLAND: Brian Brobbey scored a hat-trick for the Black Cats but it wasn't enough as City maintained their 100% start to the season

View 3 Images Man City have moved three points clear at the top of the Premier League (Image: Getty Images)

Manchester City retained their 100% start to the season and moved three points clear of Arsenal at the top of the Premier League with victory over Sunderland in an eight-goal thriller at the Etihad.

‌



Brian Brobbey struck a hat-trick for the Black Cats but it wasn't enough for Regi Le Bris' side to even earn a share of the spoils on a crazy afternoon in East Manchester.

‌



Enzo Fernandez scored his first City goal while Antoine Semenyo struck twice and Rayan Cherki was also on target. Erling Haaland notched the fifth meaning he has now scored against all 25 teams he has faced in the Premier League.

‌



Fernandez opened his City account with a cheeky free-kick from an unlikely angle. As the entire stadium expected him to cross, the Argentine noticed Sunderland keeper Robin Roefs offering too much room at his near post and clipped into the corner.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



The Black Cats hit straight back with Brobbey's first of the game. He latched on to a stupendous through ball from Enzo Le Fee and finished confidently past Gianluigi Donnarumma.

City began to exert some control and re-took the advantage through Cherki. Semenyo unselfishly laid it off for his teammate when he could have shot himself, and Cherki showed brilliant close control before lashing past Roefs.

But Sunderland were undeterred and once again drew level. Le Fee again provided the key pass, playing in Thomas Meuiner who just about held his run to stay onside. He then squared to Brobbey who couldn't miss with the goal at his mercy.

‌



There was a long VAR check with the officials being extra careful to get this one right after the Haaland debacle last week, but the goal was allowed to stand.

View 3 Images Brian Brobbey scored a hat-trick in vain for Sunderland (Image: Getty Images)

Semenyo scored the fifth of a pulsating first half after Marc Guehi's persistence paid off. The England defender brought down a cross and battled to keep possession before it fell to Semenyo who hammered into the back of the net.

‌



City should have been two clear going into the break but the Etihad was left in disbelief as Haaland inexplicably put the ball wide from Iliman Ndiaye's cute lay-off.

Semenyo doubled his tally 11 minutes into the second half. Cherki's through ball deflected into the path of the Ghanaian and he struck sweetly with his left foot to give City some breathing space.

But only a couple of minutes later Brobbey had his hat-trick. Nilson Angulo's effort looked like it had enough to cross the line but Brobbey made sure from close range and thumped into the roof of the net.

‌



View 3 Images Antoine Semenyo scored twice for City (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Ruben Dias almost put through his own net after some unconvincing goalkeeping from Donnarumma but managed to hook off the line to prevent Sunderland from drawing level again.

And Haaland allowed the home support to breathe a sigh of relief as he made the game safe at the back post from Josko Gvardiol's centre. The goal was initially ruled out for offside against Gvardiol, but VAR showed the Croatian had timed his run to perfection.

Article continues below

City head into the international break with five wins from five and a three-point buffer over Arsenal at the top, while Sunderland sit 14th with just one win to their name.

Sports.title: Arsenal sent JJ Gabriel transfer warning after Man Utd exit demand
Sports.content:
Arsenal sent JJ Gabriel transfer warning after Man Utd exit demand

JJ Gabriel is looking to quit Manchester United as a host of Europe's top sides circle - but Arsenal have been urged to look deeply at the teenager before they consider any move

View 2 Images JJ Gabriel is looking to leave Man Utd (Image: Getty Images)

Arsenal have been urged to do their "due diligence" should they consider signing JJ Gabriel, who has made it clear he wants to quit Manchester United.

‌



The teenage prodigy shocked the Red Devils recently when he expressed a desire to leave the club. The 15-year-old has been fast-tracked through United’s academy ranks and is thought of as one the brightest young talents in world football.

‌



Last year he was named the Under-18 Premier League Player of the Season last term despite his tender age, but is poised to move on without ever making a senior appearance. It is thought that Michael Carrick's decision to play Shea Lacey and Harry Amass in the Champions League last week was the final straw, claims The Sun.

‌



But with Europe's top clubs circling, PSG are keen whilst Gabriel has also been seen in Barcelona, Darren Bent believes the Gunners would want to know more about the player's character before they made any move.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



He told talkSport: "So say he was going to go to Arsenal, JJ Gabriel, Arsenal straightaway would go, 'hold on a second here', because they would have played against Manchester United and seen how special he is. First thing they’d do is go, 'Hold on a second, why is he going to be leaving?', so they would call up Manchester United straightaway and go: 'Alright, what’s the problem?'

"If Arsenal are thinking about taking him then Arsenal would call up Manchester United straightaway and ask what’s the problem. That happens all over the globe. It goes on even at first-team level: what’s he like as a character? Why is he leaving?"

Young players moving between top clubs has become increasingly common. United defender Ayden Heaven has become a first-team regular since leaving Arsenal to join the Red Devils.

‌



View 2 Images Arsenal have been told to look deeply at JJ Gabriel before they consider a move (Image: Getty Images)

Bent insists United cannot be held to ransom by the teenager, no matter how talented, as the former Premier League striker insists not every young star who is tipped for big things goes on to deliver.

He has also raised concerns over Gabriel's conduct given he's yet to accomplish anything as a professional.

Article continues below

Bent claimed: "I just don’t understand that at 15, when you’ve barely scratched the surface, why you would try and throw demands out like that. There are more senior players out there who are more accomplished than you who have conducted themselves better than this."

Sports.title: Arsenal given new Declan Rice red card verdict after Brighton VAR decision
Sports.content:
Arsenal given new Declan Rice red card verdict after Brighton VAR decision

Declan Rice kicked out at Brighton's Malick Yalcouye during Arsenal's 3-0 loss away on Saturday, and he was shown a yellow card by on-field referee Darren England

View 2 Images Declan Rice was booked for his challenge (Image: BBC Sport)

Alan Shearer believes that VAR was right not to intervene as Declan Rice avoided a red card against Brighton. Arsenal star Rice kicked out at Malick Yalcouye in stoppage time during the Gunners' stunning 3-0 defeat at the Amex Stadium.

‌



Rice was driving with the ball in the sixth minute of additional time when the Brighton midfielder gave him a nudge. The 27-year-old responded by kicking Yalcouye, who went tumbling to the ground.

‌



On-field referee Darren England blew his whistle for a foul, as the crowd chanted 'off, off, off'. But England decided to give Rice a yellow card rather than send him off.

‌



Video assistant referee Tim Wood is understood to have looked at the incident but didn't recommend an on-field review. That sparked a debate over whether Rice was fortunate but Shearer reckons that the officials were correct.

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



On Match of the Day, Shearer concluded: "This was frustration from Declan Rice. Yalcouye gives him a little nudge there and I do think the referee gets that right.

"He gives him the yellow card, I don't think it was too aggressive; he didn't lash out at him. Therefore, I think the referee got that right, but it sort of summed Arsenal's day up."

Rice is now set be available when Arsenal host Leeds on October 10 following the international break. The Gunners will find themselves second in the table by then if Manchester City draw or win at home to Sunderland on Sunday.

‌



"They've been beaten, they've been well beaten. It could have been six or seven," Shearer went on to say. "I would say there's no panic because after five games last season, Arsenal had 10 points. After five games this season, they've got 12 points. But that performance can't happen too many times, if again."

Do you agree with Alan Shearer? Have your say in the comments section.

View 2 Images Arsenal suffered their first defeat of the season (Image: Clive Rose/Getty Images)

‌



Mikel Arteta couldn't hide his disappointment and described the loss as a 'big lesson'. "First I think we have to congratulate Brighton for the victory. I think they deserve it, I think they were the better team," the Arsenal boss began in his post-match press conference.

"From our side, there were certain basics you need to accomplish in football, especially in the Premier League that we were very far from. Winning the first duel, the second ball, that put to the game, especially how direct they were in a really difficult place for us.

"On top of that, especially in our own half, we didn't respect any of the principles of play to get out of that man-to-man situation. That puts us on the back foot, so it was very difficult to control the game.

Article continues below

"When we had moments of dominance and control, we did open them up, but we didn’t finish those actions with the quality that is required to compensate for the things we did wrong. So overall, they deserved to win the game, and it’s a big lesson for us."

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
