Following an incident which occurred while she was under her aunt’s supervision on February 1, 2026, the aunt refused to accept [the teen] back into her care, and as such she was placed in institutional care at the Maxfield Park Children’s Home,” said the agency.

According to the CPFSA, while there is no law mandating the agency to update family members who are not legal guardians of wards within a given time frame, it is the practice of the agency to keep primary family members as up to date as possible with the movements and activities of their child and important life updates.

“Depending on the type or importance of the update, our officers may contact family members immediately or may wait for scheduled appointments or meetings with the family members to share, such as at a CPFSA case conference.

“The [teen’s] aunt had not yet been updated by the agency of her transfer to the facility in St James when the police notified her directly of [the teen’s] arrest, which was done before they contacted the agency regarding the same, as the teen’s aunt had not expressed interest in assisting with her care when she was informed that [the 16-year-old] could not stay at the facility in Kingston because of her pregnancy. The update on her transfer to the maternal facility was slated to be shared at her next CPFSA case conference,” the CPFSA sought to explain.

The agency added that attempts were made to inform the aunt of the outcome of the matter before the court regarding the teen being transferred into the care of DCS, but they were unsuccessful.

World.title: FINAL FLIGHT
World.content:
Keemo Paul of Jamaica Kingsmen attempts to catch Shimron Hetmyer of Guyana Amazon Warriors (out of picture) during their Men’s 2026 Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League Qualifier-2 at Kensington Oval in Bridgetown, Barbados, on Friday night.(Photo: CPL T20)

JAMAICA Kingsmen Captain Rovman Powell says his side will need special plans to stop Antigua and Barbuda Falcons, after booking their place this evening in the Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League (CPL) Final with a five-wicket win over Guyana Amazon Warriors.

Powell’s debutant Kingsmen chased down 207 runs to win Qualifier 2 by five wickets at Kensington Oval, Bridgetown, Barbados on Friday, but the skipper has quickly turned his attention to the final. The grand finale is set for Kensington Oval at 6:00 pm (Jamaica time).

“I think if you look at it, Antigua is one of those teams that have played the best cricket throughout the entire competition. They have been really successful, especially as a spin group, and even as a fast bowling core. They have been a very successful team,” Powell said in a televised interview.

“We’ll take the next 24 hours to sit down, revise some plans, and see if we can come up with some good plans against their match-winning players.”

The Kingsmen reached the final the hard way. After losing their first three games they roared back to squeeze into the play-offs, beat Barbados Tridents in the Eliminator, and then knocked out Guyana who posted 206-4, thanks to Shimron Hetmyer’s unbeaten 102 off 45 balls.

Hetmyer smashed eight sixes and four fours; shared in a 96-run, third-wicket partnership with Shai Hope, 40 from 33 balls; and a further 65-run fourth-wicket stand with Quentin Sampson, 29 from 17 balls.

For the Kingsmen, Hassan Khan, Andre Russell and Hunain Shah took one wicket apiece.

In reply, the Kingsmen reached 207-5 from 19.4 overs. Maaz Sadaqat gave them a blistering start, smashing 41 from 17 balls with three sixes and five fours to take them to 42-1 from three overs. Kirk McKenzie, 34, and Keacy Carty pushed the score to 90-2 in 8.2 overs. Saim Ayub chipped in with a fiery 23 off 17 balls to leave the Kingsmen at 152-3 in 15.1 overs. Carty was run out for 56 off 40 balls at 172-4 in 16.5 overs, before Powell’s 40 runs not out from 17 balls sealed it with Russell, two, and Hassan Khan, four not out.

Powell said reaching the final is a proud moment for the new Jamaica franchise.

“It’s a proud journey, to be honest,” he said. “It started out with us losing three games early in the competition. In the middle of the competition we found some form, some confidence, and realised that we can play cricket as a bunch.

“Coming in, we just wanted to squeeze into the play-offs because, you know, once you get a Jamaica team into the play-offs, they’re dangerous.”

Powell defended his bowlers after conceding 206, saying the wicket was excellent for batting.

“Nah, I think we bowled well in patches, to be honest,” he said. “Andre Russell and a few of the other guys kind of struggled, but when he came off the field the energy that he came back with was exceptional. I told the guys at the halfway mark that they got 15 extra runs. After Saim Ayub bowled the first few balls to Hetmyer, he says, ‘Skipper, it’s a very good wicket.’ ”

Powell also credited the Kingsmen owners and coaching staff for giving him full control to lead the team back to Jamaica.

“They have given me the control to actually run the franchise, to actually lead,” he said. “And that is something that I’ve always wanted — especially with a team coming back to Jamaica and needing to know the local players.

“So this is one year that I tried to get involved as a captain, and it’s good to see that bearing fruit. So a lot of credit has to be given to the boys. I think they fought really hard.”

On winning Player of the Match ahead of centurion Hetmyer, Powell was gracious in sharing the spotlight with his fellow West Indies teammate.

“It’s special,” he said. “[He’s] a really, really special player to come off in a play-off game like this with his entire country on his back. You know the pressure you get from Guyana when you don’t score, and to turn that around from a few nights ago and come and score a hundred is fantastic. He’s a world-class player, and it’s just unfortunate that he came out on the losing end.”

Powell had a final message for the Jamaican fans ahead of Sunday.

“Just keep on supporting us,” he said. “It’s been a tough start but we have fought a good battle. We have one more last push. Keep supporting us from home, or if you can come to the stadium in your Jamaica colours, please come down. Come down; it’s a CPL final.”

World.title: Respect: ARC, 30 years
World.content:
[ESTABLISHING SHOT]Garfield Robinson

“Big, big respect, ARC.”

That was NCB Financial Group Chairman Michael Lee-Chin’s sentiment as ARC Group of Companies celebrated three decades in business — a milestone he described as no small feat.

After all, 30 years in business has meant navigating recessions, high interest rates, currency depreciation, earthquakes, hurricanes, and financial hardships. Yet, as Lee-Chin noted, ARC, under the leadership of Chairman Norman Horne, has not simply survived — it has prospered, becoming a role model for entrepreneurs and businesses across Jamaica.

The story began in 1996, when Horne returned home from New York with neither a large company nor deep pockets.

“I did not come home with great resources. I came home with an idea and a conviction,” Horne told a ballroom filled with approximately 400 family members, employees, stakeholders, and partners inside the M Style-designed Jamaica Pegasus ballroom on Wednesday, September 16. The evening’s formalities were handled with aplomb by Dr Terri-Karelle Johnson.

ARC rolled out with five employees, a handful of machines and, as Horne recalled, a very large ambition. His brothers and sisters were part of those early days, when job descriptions were fluid and everyone simply did whatever needed to be done.

“You could operate a machine in the morning, drive a forklift in the afternoon, clear goods at the wharf, load a truck, or go out and sell. That was our management training,” he said.

And sell they did.

“We were not sitting in a boardroom developing sophisticated five-year strategies. We were trying to sell zinc!” Horne continued.

Thirty years later, that inauspicious beginning has transformed into a group of companies marking its longevity with a black-tie, 30th anniversary banquet attended by a veritable roll call of Jamaica’s movers and shakers, including mayor of Kingston Andrew Swaby, Commissioner of Police Dr Kevin Blake, Minister of Tourism Edmund Bartlett, and NCB Financial Group Chairman Michael Lee-Chin.

World.title: NEPA urges caution as sharks feed on whale carcass in Salt Marsh
World.content:
The whale carcass which washed ashore on Friday in Salt Marsh, Trelawny.

TRELAWNY, Jamaica — The National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA) is advising members of the public to exercise caution and avoid entering the water in the Salt Marsh area of Trelawny after sharks were seen feeding on a whale carcass that washed ashore on Friday.

NEPA said the presence of sharks and marine mammals in Jamaican waters is a natural occurrence and that the feeding activity is also part of the marine ecosystem’s natural process and does not, by itself, suggest an unusual environmental event.

Sharks play an important role in maintaining healthy marine ecosystems as both predators and scavengers. By consuming dead or weakened animals, they help remove organic matter, recycle nutrients and support the balance of ocean environments.

NEPA noted that the reddish colouration observed in the water is likely linked to blood and tissue released during feeding and should not automatically be considered a sign of pollution.

Members of the public are being urged to stay out of the water, keep children and pets away from the shoreline, and avoid touching, disturbing or attempting to remove the carcass. Individuals should also refrain from feeding, capturing, provoking or attempting to move the sharks, and should observe the animals only from a safe distance.

NEPA also advised against approaching the area with boats or surrounding the animals, as the carcass may continue to attract sharks and other scavengers even after visible feeding activity has ended.

Swimming, fishing and other recreational activities in the immediate area should be avoided until authorities advise that it is safe to return.

NEPA said encounters like this provide an opportunity to better understand the role of marine wildlife and how ocean ecosystems function.

World.title: Anger in Cooper’s Pen
World.content:
Tents on the site of demolished houses in Cooper’s Pen, Trelawny (Horace Hines)

COOPER’S PEN, Trelawny — Residents here whose homes were demolished on August 11 say they are being forced to choose between accepting relocation grants they have not yet received and moving their tents and belongings temporarily to a site in New Town, Salt Marsh, for two weeks, with no clear indication of what will happen afterwards.

The residents, who have lived in tents since their homes were demolished, say they had been told by government officials to leave by today, Saturday, September 19. They have opted for the grants but insist they will not move until the money is deposited into their accounts.

The Government’s response to the demolition initially included humanitarian assistance for approximately 44 affected families, with the Ministry of Labour and Social Security, the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management, and other agencies providing emergency support.

Among those affected are Shane Ricketts, Moesha Richardson, and a woman who identified herself only as Tia.

Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer that he had signed for a $500,000 grant but would not leave before receiving it.

Richardson explained that residents were given the choice of accepting the grant or moving to the temporary location for two weeks. She questioned the practicality of relocating families for such a short period without a plan for their accommodation afterwards.

“Two weeks from now I still cannot find somewhere to live,” Richardson said. She said although she would accept the grant, she would have preferred a more permanent housing solution from the Government.

Richardson said Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness had previously given residents the impression that they would receive assistance with housing and eventually have an opportunity to acquire land.

Following Holness’s August 28 visit to Cooper’s Pen, the Government announced that land had been identified for eligible residents and that the intervention would include serviced lots and relocation grants. Holness said the lots would form part of a properly planned subdivision with roads, water, and electricity, while beneficiaries would contribute to the cost of the land and utilities according to their circumstances. He said he intended to oversee the process and hoped relocation could begin by December.

Meanwhile, Tia said her name was not on the grant list, leaving her uncertain about what assistance she would receive.

“I am feeling bad because I don’t know what’s happening for me because my name didn’t come down on the list,” she said, adding that she has lived in the community for a very long time.

Her house was demolished, and she said she and her baby had been separated, with the child staying with someone else while she remained in a tent. She said she would prefer a house or parcel of land.

“If I get a house option or a land option I’ll definitely choose the land or the house,” she said.

Tia said residents were unwilling to move to Salt Marsh for two weeks without knowing where they would go afterwards.

“No one is willing to go to Salt Marsh for two weeks and then we’re going to get kicked off,” she said.

Richardson, who has three family members in her household, including a three-year-old child and a 14-year-old nephew, said residents were particularly concerned about being required to move before receiving the grants.

“They are saying we have to move before we get the grant. So we have to take up our stuff before we get the grant,” she alleged.

She also questioned what she described as unequal treatment between residents whose homes were destroyed and those whose houses remain standing. Richardson said residents whose homes were not flattened were being considered for relocation to land, while those who lost their homes were being offered money to relocate.

“Our houses are demolished, and our businesses are demolished. So I don’t know why they’re not giving us back land as well,” she said.

Richardson said officials were expected to return earlier in the week to collect copies of documents residents had signed and provide arrangements for the grants, but no one had done so at the time of the

Observer interview on Friday.

Tova Hamilton, the Member of Parliament for Trelawny Northern, told the

Observer that the affected residents had opted for the grants and that the Government was proceeding with the relocation process.

“The Government is working with them to provide them with grants,” Hamilton confirmed.

She said development of land for the original Cooper’s Pen residents was also under way, including site clearing and preparations for roads, lot preparation, and other infrastructure. The Government said land was being surveyed for the first group of displaced families, with civil works expected to follow.

World.title: Merz vows to stay on as chancellor despite ‘disaster’ in another German regional vote
World.content:
BERLIN — Germany’s embattled Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his conservatives suffered a second major defeat to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in a regional vote Sunday — a result Merz conceded was a “disaster.”



But the chancellor moved to quickly quell a rising storm of speculation that he would move to step aside following the loss, which comes only two weeks after another historic defeat to the AfD in a regional contest. He appeared before cameras just minutes after the polls closed Sunday to say he would continue to push through his reform agenda and act as an anchor of stability in turbulent times.



“These reforms are the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism,” he said. “What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness, and patience. I will demonstrate these qualities as chairman of the CDU and, above all, as chancellor of our country.”



The AfD won 37.9% of the vote in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — the second-best result in its history, just ahead of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) on 35.7%, according to preliminary results.

Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) suffered its worst election result in a state or national election since the end of World War II, coming in with just 5%, just winning enough votes to make it over the threshold needed to win seats in the state parliament.

AfD leaders hailed their victory — party national co-leader Tino Chrupalla called the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result a “sensation” — while also putting the pressure on a profoundly weakened Merz to step aside and abandon his party’s policy of maintaining a “firewall” around the far right.



“Friedrich Merz is the wrong chancellor for the CDU and is dragging the CDU down with him,” national co-leader Alice Weidel told German public television. “So the CDU must ask itself, above all else, does it want to continue with this chancellor and with these left-wing policies?”

World.title: Meloni promises to ban veils in Italian schools and limit foreign students
World.content:
Giorgia Meloni is pictured at Palazzo Chigi in Rome on Sept. 15, 2026. | Alberto Pizzoli/AFP via Getty Images

“Italian children cannot feel like a minority in the classroom,” the country’s PM said Sunday.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said her government is preparing two legislative proposals that would ban face coverings in Italian schools and restrict the number of foreign students allowed in classrooms.

“Italian children cannot feel like a minority in the classroom,” she said Sunday in a speech at Fenix, an annual event organized by the youth division of her right-wing Brothers of Italy party.

“If the number of children who do not understand the language of instruction becomes large, or even forms the majority, that is no longer integration; that is neglect,” Meloni added.

World.title: Massive Ukrainian drone attack hits Moscow on last day of Russian elections
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed attacks had been carried out against infrastructure facilities in and around Moscow. “Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night. One of Russia’s key oil industry facilities and the aggressor’s logistics facility were hit,” he said on X.

Russian voters have been heading to the polls this weekend in the first parliamentary elections since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Russian President Vladimir Putin’s ruling United Russia party is expected to retain its dominance in the parliament and present the win as proof of public support for the war in Ukraine.

“Your choice, and your will, will once ​again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory, and love for our homeland, and that no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us,” Putin said in a televised address before the vote.

On Saturday, Ukrainian officials said three children and a woman had died in Russian attacks on the Vyshgorod district of Kyiv. Regional Governor Tymur Tkachenko said Sunday a child who was injured in Saturday’s attack had died in hospital.

World.title: France’s National Rally criticizes Russia in rare rebuke
World.content:
But the statement also came after French President Emmanuel Macron chaired a rare crisis meeting Friday at which the country's political leaders, including Bardella, were briefed on the threats posed by Russia’s war in Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East.



Le Pen and Bardella also cited the August drone attack at Leipzig airport, which German authorities attributed to Russia. "No provocation, clandestine operation, or destabilization effort could lead France to facilitate Russia’s achievement of its war aims in Ukraine," the far-right leaders write.

The statement marks a rare show of unity within a party that has been divided over whether to treat the Kremlin as the enemy. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 exposed fault lines within the movement.

Le Pen has historically taken a warmer stance toward Russia; she has met Russian President Vladimir Putin in the past and her party took a €9.4 million loan from a Czech-Russian bank with links to the Kremlin, which has been repaid since. Bardella, a member of the European Parliament, has been more eager to portray Russia as a threat to France and Europe.

Le Pen, who hopes to succeed Macron as president next year, is open to supplying military equipment to Ukraine but has ruled out providing additional financial assistance as Kyiv continues to fend off Russia's ongoing assault.

"Firmness in the face of hostile actions and the pursuit of a diplomatic resolution to the war are not contradictory," reads the statement.

The National Rally is expected to release its campaign platform before the end of the year, potentially clarifying its positions on Ukraine and Russia.

World.title: Germany’s top general to lead NATO’s highest military authority
World.content:
Breuer will take over from Dragone next July and will serve a three-year term.

The rest of the votes were kept secret to avoid the risk of breeding disloyalty and divisions over the result, said one NATO official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely.

The German four-star general beat Canada's chief of defense Jennie Carignan for the role. He was seen as the favorite given Berlin's status as Europe’s top defense spender and implicit backing from Washington. Breuer had campaigned on Germany's leading role in defense spending as European allies come under U.S. pressure to take control of their own defense.

Carignan, Ottawa’s top general since 2024, made her pitch about reinvigorating the role of the military committee and signaling enduring transatlantic unity inside NATO. Strained bilateral ties between Canada and the U.S. were seen by NATO officials as making Carignan’s case more difficult.

The result underscores Berlin's growing role in the alliance, as it takes over senior military roles and assumes greater operational responsibility for protecting frontline states with a regional army command focused on Estonia and Latvia and a permanent deployment in Lithuania.

The chair of NATO’s military committee is expected to give honest military advice to allies — helping assess the feasibility, financing and capabilities of operations. They oversee dozens of working groups of NATO military staff, and broker consensus on formulating military advice.

World.title: NATO ‘ready’ for potential Russian false flag attack, alliance’s top general says
World.content:
NATO is ready to respond to a potential Russian escalation on Europe’s eastern flank, the alliance's top general Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone said Saturday, amid growing warnings of a possible staged attack by Moscow.

“The alliance is ready, the structure is ready, the soldiers … the weapons are ready,” Dragone told reporters during a regular meeting of the alliance’s 32 top generals in Copenhagen, adding that NATO was continuing its work in “increasing” these forces “in number … and also in sophistication.”

The remarks follow growing warnings by European leaders about a possible Russian escalation in Europe. On Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Moscow could send drones or missiles into a frontline NATO country in “the next few months” in a staged provocation to test the alliance — a risk that was later echoed by France and the Netherlands.

World.title: Smoke and flight delays at Riyadh airport after air raid alert
World.content:
Residents said they heard explosions during the first air raid alert issued for the Saudi capital.

A large plume of black smoke was seen near Riyadh’s main airport on Saturday after an overnight air raid alert, amid an escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

Reuters footage showed black smoke rising and flames near Riyadh’s King Khalid airport, while residents told AFP they heard explosions before Saudi’s civil defense issued an all-clear on Saturday morning.



Flight-tracking website FlightRadar24 rated the airport at Level 5 on its disruption index, indicating a very high likelihood of delays or cancellations.

Saudi authorities have not commented on the reported incident. The Saudi ministry of defense and Riyadh’s airport authorities did not immediately reply to requests for comment.

The first air raid alert for the Saudi capital came amid escalating attacks between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed rebel group. The Houthis tightened their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb strait last week by seizing the Red Sea port of Mokha and Mayyun Island, also known as Perim.

On Monday, Yemeni and Houthi officials said they captured the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands, though those claims have not been independently verified. The roughly 30-kilometer-wide strait carries about 8.7% of global seaborne trade, according to UN figures.



Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called U.S. President Donald Trump twice last week to seek U.S. strikes on Houthi targets, but Washington has so far resisted direct military intervention.

World.title: Germany cuts fuel tax as Middle East conflicts send prices soaring
World.content:
Germany will lower tax on petrol and diesel by 17 cents per liter in a relief package worth €2.5 billion, the German government announced Friday.

"Those who rely on their cars every day are reaching their financial limits. ... The relief package of €2.5 billion is no small sum in times of strained budgets," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said. The tax discount is to be implemented next month.

The measure, brokered between Germany's federal and state governments, is part of the package promised by Merz as fuel prices continue to climb in response to the war in Iran and the escalating conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

Two weeks ago, a key oil benchmark reached $100 a barrel for the first time since July following the latest escalations in the Middle East, sending pump prices soaring all over Europe.

The Merz government also plans to introduce a temporary fuel price cap on petrol and diesel modeled on similar policies in Luxembourg and Belgium. The price cap would take into account price moves on the oil markets, transportation and distribution costs, and retailers’ profit margins. Berlin aims to introduce the measure by Jan. 1, 2027.



Germany, through the voice of its Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, is among the EU member countries calling for a bloc-wide windfall tax on oil companies that have reaped billions of euros in excess profits since the start of the war. The topic is high on the agenda at an informal meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday and Saturday.



Ahead of the meeting on Friday, Klingbeil has called on the European Commission to present a proposal by the end of October.



“Several member states have been calling for models for a long time,” Klingbeil, from Germany's Social Democratic Party, told reporters. “People can see how oil companies are exploiting the situation, overcharging and significantly increasing their profits.”



But Merz's conservatives have pushed back on the proposal. Germany's Economic Affairs and Energy Minister Katherina Reiche said a windfall tax would only make sense in case of abusive price increases, she told Handelsblatt.



“The fact that eleven refineries are producing in Germany makes us less dependent on foreign countries; that must not be put at risk,” Reiche said.

World.title: Macron and Carney vow closer France-Canada ties amid strained US relations
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron declared that France and Canada are "two great independent nations who want to stay that way" during a joint news conference with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sunday.

 

The bilateral summit—held in the French territory of Saint Pierre and Miquelon, located just off Canada's Atlantic coast—comes against the backdrop of increasingly strained relations between the two nations and the United States.

Carney stated that the time had come to significantly strengthen ties with France and the European Union. His comments follow a high-profile visit to Brussels and Strasbourg, where the European Commission formally proposed granting Canada "associate member" status within the bloc.

Macron confirmed that Paris and Ottawa would work together to deepen cooperation across key sectors, including fisheries, regional security, and energy infrastructure.

Looking beyond bilateral ties, Carney proposed establishing a four-way collaborative framework involving France, Canada, the US, and China to oversee the development and governance of artificial intelligence.

The leaders delivered their remarks following a working lunch and a series of high-level meetings on the island earlier in the day.

Foundations of new Atlantic ties amid Trump's unpredictability

US President Donald Trump’s tariffs, demands for economic concessions, and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st US state have pushed Ottawa to reduce its dependence on its southern neighbour and pursue deeper economic, security, and political ties with Europe.

“This is an important moment,” Macron said on Saturday upon his arrival. He noted that the bilateral discussions "will allow us… to strengthen our bilateral economic ties and defence relationship."

Macron added that Sunday’s talks form part of broader European efforts to secure stable energy supplies as the war in Iran continues to disrupt global energy markets, stoking fears of sustained price increases for fuel and other essential commodities.

“Canada is a country with significant resources of critical minerals and rare earths. It is also a major oil and natural gas producer,” Macron said. “What we want to do is conclude agreements to secure more liquefied natural gas that can be shipped to Europe’s Atlantic coast.”

Carney’s office confirmed in a statement that the leaders discussed deepening the Canada-France partnership across strategic sectors, including aerospace, energy, critical minerals, and advanced technologies such as quantum computing, satellites, and supercomputing.

The meeting also comes in the wake of Trump’s announcement regarding a deal on Greenland that will expand the US military presence on the island while maintaining Danish sovereignty, ending months of threats by the US president to seize the semi-autonomous territory of a fellow NATO ally.

Macron publicly welcomed the resolution on Saturday.

“Danish sovereignty is being respected; international law is being respected,” Macron stated. “Anything that helps ease tensions is a good thing.”

World.title: Meloni announces ban on burqa and niqab in Italian schools, cap on foreign students
World.content:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has announced that the government is preparing a bill that would ban burqas and niqabs in schools and introduce a limit on the number of foreign pupils in each class.

 

Several European countries, including France and Belgium, already ban face coverings in public places. Austria has also introduced restrictions in schools. Elsewhere, including Spain and Poland, freedom of conscience and religion is protected by the constitution.

Meloni said a package of measures will soon go before the Italian cabinet, including a ban on burqas and niqabs in schools, a requirement for parents of pupils facing “serious difficulties integrating” into the national school system to learn Italian, and a limit on places for foreign pupils.

Italy heads to the polls next year, with competition intensifying to the right of Meloni’s party following the entry of retired general Roberto Vannacci, who has called for even tougher measures. Migration is a highly political and divisive issue in Italy.

“It is unacceptable that in an Italian classroom the children who end up feeling pushed into a corner are Italian children because they have become the minority. That cannot be allowed,” she said during a rally organised by Gioventù Nazionale, the youth wing of her Brothers of Italy party.

“Calling all this integration is yet another lie, a convenient lie for those who live off ideology, for those who preach to us from their living rooms and then send their own children to schools where this problem does not exist.”

Previous initiatives and legislative proposals

Meloni’s announcement comes after several related initiatives in recent months.

In early August, Education and Merit Minister Giuseppe Valditara proposed action on the full-face veil through an amendment to the security bill.

At the end of July, Futuro Nazionale — the party founded by far-right MEP Roberto Vannacci, who has backed Meloni’s proposal — tabled a resolution against the full-face veil in the Chamber of Deputies’ Culture Committee. It was approved with centre-right votes after being redrafted at the government’s request.

In March, the League introduced a bill in the Senate to amend Article 5 of the 1975 Reale law, which was introduced by then-Justice Minister Oronzo Reale during the Years of Lead to ban face coverings in public places.

The proposed amendment would create a new offence of forcing someone to conceal their face, punishable by one to two years in prison and fines of between €10,000 and €30,000. It would also bar those convicted from obtaining Italian citizenship.

Full-face veils in Europe

Meloni referred specifically to a ban on burqas and niqabs. A burqa traditionally covers the entire body and includes a mesh over the eyes, while a niqab covers the face, leaving only the eyes visible. A hijab, by contrast, covers the hair and neck but leaves the face uncovered.

Several European countries have introduced restrictions on face coverings in public spaces.

France imposed a nationwide ban on concealing the face in public places in April 2011, a measure later upheld by the European Court of Human Rights.

Belgium approved a nationwide ban in July 2011, with fines and prison sentences for violations. Bulgaria has prohibited full-face veils in state, administrative and educational institutions since September 2016.

Austria passed an anti-mask law in October 2017 requiring faces to remain visible in public spaces. From September 2026, girls up to the age of 14 will also be prohibited from wearing at school any veil that “covers the head according to Islamic traditions”.

Denmark introduced a nationwide ban in August 2018, with financial penalties increasing for repeat offences. The Netherlands introduced a partial ban in August 2019 covering schools, hospitals, government offices and public transport.

Switzerland introduced a federal ban on face coverings in public spaces following a national referendum, with the implementing legislation coming into force in 2023. Portugal completed its legislative process in August 2026 with a law banning face coverings in public spaces and imposing financial penalties.

Germany has no nationwide ban, but federal legislation prohibits public employees, judges, members of the armed forces and motorists from covering their faces while driving. Several Länder also restrict full-face veils in schools and universities for students and teachers.

Foreign pupils in the classroom

If Italy introduces a statutory maximum for foreign pupils in each class, it would become the first European country to adopt such a rule, according to the proposal.

Italy already has a 30% limit on non-Italian pupils, set out in a 2010 ministerial circular issued by then-Education Minister Mariastella Gelmini. The limit has often gone unenforced because of local demographic conditions and a lack of flexibility, particularly in urban outskirts.

Other European countries use different approaches.

Denmark has some of the most restrictive policies. The government has allowed upper secondary schools to introduce caps of up to 50% for pupils of “non-Western origin” or from disadvantaged neighbourhoods. Schools can also organise classes based on parents’ income, with the aim of encouraging social and ethnic mixing — a model the Italian government is watching with interest.

In France, quotas based on origin would be unconstitutional because the state does not collect statistics based on ethnic or religious identity. Instead, authorities use “zoning” to redesign school catchment areas, linking working-class and wealthier neighbourhoods. In areas with high concentrations of migrants, the state also reduces the number of pupils per class.

Criticism of Meloni’s proposal

Meloni’s announcement has received support from members of the governing coalition but has also drawn criticism from the opposition and legal experts.

Speaking to ANSA, Salvatore Curreri, a professor of constitutional law at the University of Enna, pointed to Article 34 of the Constitution, which states that “school is open to everyone”, including foreign children.

“If the measure were so restrictive as to uproot minors and their families to other areas, far from where they live, it could prove excessive precisely because it conflicts with the overriding functional aim of integration, with the risk of infringing a right recognised by the constitution,” Curreri said.

Angelo Bonelli, an MP for the Green and Left Alliance (AVS) and co-spokesperson for Green Europe, also criticised the proposal.

“Yet again, instead of dealing with schools, she is chasing the neo-fascist right of AfD and Vannacci, who has proposed separate classes for students with disabilities,” he said. “The truth is that the prime minister is not at all interested in how schools work. Our teachers’ salaries are among the lowest in Europe.”

World.title: Climate Week warns of challenges in delivering the energy transition
World.content:
A Climate Week (source in Portuguese) began in New York this Sunday, with a series of events across the city, and runs until the 27th. Over the coming days, business and political leaders from around the world will discuss solutions for a more sustainable society with lower carbon emissions.

 

The event is an initiative of the non-governmental organisation Climate Group (source in Portuguese), organised in coordination with the United Nations General Assembly, which takes place at the same time in the same city.

The first day, Monday, features contributions from the Prime Minister of Australia, Anthony Albanese, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Milliband, and the Icelandic prime minister Kristún Frostadóttir.

This is the largest event in the world dedicated to climate change. It includes more than a thousand events at various locations in New York, bringing together on average more than one hundred thousand people.

This year's debates will focus on three aspects:

Energy and the changes taking place in this field,

The impact those changes are having,

The joint action that is needed.

This series of debates comes at a time when the impact of climate change is highly visible, with tragedies such as the one that recently hit Nepal and the heatwaves that have been battering many parts of the world in recent weeks.

Heatwaves have been recurring in recent weeks Ahn Young-joon/AP

Climate Group has been in existence for around 20 years and aims to help create a world with zero carbon emissions by 2050.

According to the description Climate Group gives on the event website, "the context is changing rapidly. Energy systems are being redesigned, supply chains are under pressure and demand for electricity is rising, driven by electrification, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital infrastructure. At the same time, the transition is opening up new sources of long-term growth, investment and competitiveness."

The organisers also say that "the current challenge is not ambition but implementation". "Progress is being held back by outdated regulation, infrastructure constraints and misaligned markets. The priority is to remove these barriers and deliver change quickly and at scale. Climate Week exists to accelerate that progress," they add.

This year's conference is taking place against a backdrop of the rapid expansion of AI and the revolution that implies, but also of the strongly climate-sceptic actions and policies pursued by the Trump administration.

The last global climate summit, COP30, held in Belém do Pará, Brazil, ultimately delivered results that fell short of expectations. While a plan was agreed to help the countries most affected by the climate crisis, no precise timetable was set for the phase-out of fossil fuels.

World.title: Russians vote in final day of parliamentary elections
World.content:
Russians are casting their ballots on Sunday in the final day of voting in parliamentary elections, with the pro-Putin United Russia party widely expected to emerge victorious.

 

United Russia has won every parliamentary election in the country since 2003.

The 2026 vote marks the first since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, meaning it could offer a slight hint at public sentiment towards the conflict, which has been increasingly impacting Russians at home.

However, in August, Russia's Supreme Court ordered the only party opposing the war - the Yabloko party - to be struck from the ballot. Its candidates are reportedly still able to run for individual seats in some districts.

In a statement at the time, Yabloko cofounder Grigory Yavlinsky hit out at the decision and said they would appeal.

"Barring Yabloko from the elections means refusing to engage in dialogue with people who ask questions that are uncomfortable for the authorities," he said. "We stand for a ceasefire, diplomacy and peace, for the prevention of nuclear war".

On Saturday, the party reported that one of its election observers had "lost consciousness" while being "subjected to force" by police in St. Petersburg. It also complained that party observers were being "denied access to polling stations" and that their movement was being "restricted."

Russia reports cyberattacks

Ella Pamfilova, the chair of Russia's Central Election Commission, said on Sunday that Russia had recorded more than 1,000 waves of distributed denial-of-service attacks (DDoS) on election infrastructure over the last few days, per the Interfax news agency.

"The level of impact is assessed as very high," she said, adding that the attacks appeared to have been "carried out by highly professional, well-coordinated groups using artificial intelligence tools."

A DDoS attack involves hackers attempting to disrupt a targeted network, server, or service by attempting to overwhelm the system with a large volume of traffic.

Moscow hit by 'largest-scale attack'

The vote comes as the Russian capital was hit by what its governor described as the "largest-scale attack" on the city since the war in Ukraine began.

Sergey Sobyanin reported that Russian air defences had shot down more than 1,600 drones across the country since Saturday, 450 of which he said had been heading towards the capital.

"Several drones reached the territory of the Moscow refinery, and one struck a residential building. There were no fatalities," he wrote. Moscow Oblast governor Andrey Vorobyov said two people had been killed in attacks across the wider region.

Sobyanin also accused Ukraine of attempting to "disrupt" Russia's elections - which will determine the makeup of the 450-seat state Duma - with the attacks.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine had targeted the Moscow region overnight, saying a "key" oil industry facility as well as a logistics facility were hit.

"Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night," he wrote in a post on X, adding that Russia had launched over 2,000 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 19 missiles against Ukraine this week.

World.title: Germans head to the polls in state elections as pressure mounts on Merz
World.content:
Germans are heading to the polls on Sunday in two state elections that could prove decisive for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's future.

 

In Berlin, Merz's ruling Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is facing a close fight against Die Linke, which has strong support among young people and has pledged measures to tackle the housing crisis.

In the coastal state of Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania in northeastern Germany, the main race is between the Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the hard-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD).

The AfD comes into Sunday's vote fresh off the back of its election success in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month and will be hoping for further gains.

However, the party faces a sterner test in "MeckPomm," where it will come up against the SPD's Manuela Schwesig, who has served as minister-president of the state since 2017.

The latest polling figures show Die Linke edging ahead of the CDU in the city-state of Berlin, while the AfD leads the SPD in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania - with the CDU flirting with the 5% hurdle required to remain in state parliament.

Gains for the far-right or far-left would heap pressure on Merz, who became chancellor in May 2025 and has seen his popularity continue to decline.

Moritz Lembke-Oezer, 43, summed up that feeling while speaking to the AFP news agency outside a polling station to the south of Berlin, saying that while he feared the vote could benefit the AfD, he hoped it would see the CDU "punished."

"Maybe then Friedrich Merz will be gone," he said, adding that he planned to vote for Die Linke because of the far-left party's vows to address the housing issue.

Speaking to AFP outside a polling station in Schwerin, the state capital of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, pensioner Peter Sommer added: "I'd be in favour of the AfD winning, because then they'll have to prove themselves: either something will happen, or it'll be the last time they get any votes."

World.title: Moscow hit by 'largest-scale attack' on capital so far, mayor says
World.content:
Ukrainian forces launched their "largest-scale attack" on Moscow since the war in Ukraine began, the city's mayor said on Sunday.

 

In a post on Telegram, Sergey Sobyanin reported that Russian air defences had shot down more than 1,600 drones across the country since Saturday, 450 of which he said had been heading towards the capital.

"Several drones reached the territory of the Moscow refinery, and one struck a residential building. There were no fatalities," he wrote. Moscow Oblast governor Andrey Vorobyov said two people had been killed in attacks across the wider region.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine had targeted the Moscow region overnight, saying a "key" oil industry facility as well as a logistics facility were hit.

"Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night," he wrote in a post on X, adding that the attacks had involved FP-1 attack drones and Palianytsia missiles, among other munitions.

"Moscow must end its brutal war and choose peace instead of building layered rings of air defense at the expense of other regions," Zelenskyy continued, while also sharing video footage appearing to show the aftermath of the strikes.

Russian attacks on Ukraine

It comes as Ukrainian authorities reported that a child had died following a Russian strike on the Kyiv region, bringing the death toll from the attack to four.

Timur Tkachenko, the head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration, said on Sunday that the child died in hospital after having been injured in an attack on the Vyshhorod district.

"The Kyiv region has endured more than a day of enemy attacks," Tkachenko said in an update, adding that 31 structures had been damaged across five districts.

In the southern Kherson region, a 71-year-old priest was also killed in a drone attack on a monastery in the village of Chervonyi Mayak on Saturday, per local authorities. Four others were reportedly injured in the incident.

According to Zelenskyy, who has been calling for further sanctions against Moscow, Russia launched over 2,000 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 19 missiles against Ukraine this week.

World.title: Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next
World.content:
Turkey has jailed dozens of people pending trial as a sweeping crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups widens, prompting international condemnation and protests outside Turkish embassies on Friday.

Advertising

By Thursday, courts in several provinces had jailed at least 82 people following raids on LGBTQI+ organisations, clubs, cafes and homes.

The cases include LGBTQI+ activists and members of rights groups as well as people accused of prostitution, drug offences and other crimes. Not everyone jailed is accused of gay rights advocacy.

The United Nations human rights office has called on Turkey to uphold human rights without discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity and to immediately release anyone arbitrarily detained.

Protests were held outside Turkish embassies in cities including Paris, Brussels, London, Oslo and Washington on Friday.

The crackdown began on Saturday, when police carried out coordinated raids targeting nine LGBTQI+ organisations. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said legal action was being taken against 162 people, nine associations and 13 businesses in 15 provinces.

Turkey arrests dozens in ongoing crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups

Mass detentions

The raids prompted protests across Turkey, including outside Istanbul’s main courthouse on Tuesday. Police broke up the demonstration and detained more than 100 people, including journalists. They were later released.

“I am here because I want to say that LGBTQ+ friends are not alone in this country,” said Ayse, a protester who asked to be identified only by her first name.

“I want to support them and to stay in solidarity with them, which is not easy these days in Turkey, but they are not alone, and we are not alone, and we will be here until the end.”

Opposition DEM Party parliamentarian Ozgul Saki remained at the protest, protected from arrest by parliamentary immunity.

“This oppression against LGBTQ+ people is an attempt to compress society into a single type; to build an Islamist, Turkish, racist society,” Saki said. “Those who are here say, 'No! Society will live equally, freely and honourably with all its diversity,' and that's why they were all detained.”

The operations have been defended by Gurlek, from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s conservative Justice and Development Party (AKP).

“No criminal organisation, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated,” Gurlek posted on social media.

Among the organisations affected was Istanbul-based SPoD, which provides psychological support to LGBTQI+ people.

“As a community, we were expecting that such an operation would come one day. But we didn't imagine it as that violent, that much unlawful,” said a SPoD representative who asked to remain anonymous.

“They raided our office; I think four or five have been detained, and they are still in custody. What will happen to the LGBTQ+ community after this day? Like they can implement a kind of informal criminalisation upon our community, so my personal feeling is an immense feeling of uncertainty.”

Surge in anti-LGBTQ disinformation targets Pride in Europe

Obscenity allegations

Homosexuality has been legal since the foundation of the Turkish republic in 1923, but authorities are using an obscenity law as part of the crackdown.

“All of our board members are detained due to the allegations of obscenity,” said Yildiz Tar of Ankara-based KAOS GL, Turkey’s leading LGBTQI+ news portal.

“They look into our social media account, and our news articles are seen as obscene because, for example, there is one picture of two women kissing, and they see that it's obscene. So that is why they have been detained.”

The measures resemble actions taken against LGBTQI+ communities in Russia and Egypt, Tar said.

“It's very similar to Russia and Egypt, like the things they want to do is very similar to anti-gay propaganda laws, and there were huge operations, and people got detained,” Tar said.

“So it's very similar to both countries. And actually, like the Turkish government is very fond of Putin's way of dealing things.”

The crackdown has also drawn condemnation from the European Union and international human rights groups.

“It's an attempt to show LGBTQ+ people as immoral and against the family. But in fact, none of this does anything to protect the family at all,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, who leads Human Rights Watch’s Turkey office.

“It's all about discrediting and stigmatizing people for their sexual orientation or gender identity.”

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Wider crackdown

The arrests form part of a broader crackdown on people regarded as opposing the government, Sinclair-Webb said.

“This operation should be set in the context of a very wide crackdown on anybody who is regarded as oppositional to the government, whether in terms of being politically or in terms of their lifestyle or their outlook… there is a general attempt by the government to impose as well as, you know, ideological conformity on people, lifestyle,” Sinclair-Webb said.

President Erdogan routinely refers to LGBTQI+ people as perverts and has stepped up his rhetoric ahead of much-rumoured early elections. Gurlek has called on prosecutors to increase investigations into the LGBTQI+ community, fuelling fears of further arrests.

The crackdown has also prompted condemnation across Turkish civil society, with trade unions, doctors’ associations and opposition parties voicing their opposition.

For Tar, that support offers some hope amid fears over what could follow for Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community.

“If this attack won't be stopped, it would mean a lot of maltreatment and torture; it can also cause hate crimes; it incites hatred inside the country too,” Tar said. “And it will mean that you cannot be openly queer; if they succeed in their operation, that is a really, really hellish scenario.”

World.title: A doubleheader feast!
World.content:
This week on The Sound Kitchen it’s a doubleheader: you’ll hear the answers to TWO quiz questions, as well as TWO “Listener's Corner" with Paul Myers, and of course, Erwan Rome’s “Music from Erwan”. So sit down, relax, and join the banquet! Just click the “play” button above to join the feast.

Advertising

Hello everyone!

As noted on the show, I am retiring on 1 October. Unfortunately, The Sound Kitchen is retiring too – I will not be replaced.

We’ve had a great time together all these years, haven’t we?

Click here to listen to past Sound Kitchen podcasts.

I know you will all stay loyal to RFI English – our service has so much to offer. We’re small, but my colleagues are firebrands!

For example, we have wonderful podcasts: Spotlight on France, with journalists Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas; Melissa Chemam’s insightful Spotlight on Africa, and our International Report, usually sent to us by one of our foreign correspondents. We also have an award-winning bilingual series – an old-time radio show, with actors (!) – to help you learn French, called Les voisins du 12 bis.

Remember, podcasts are radio, too! As you see, sound is still quite present in the RFI English service. Please keep checking our website for updates on the latest from our team of journalists. You never know what we’ll surprise you with!

To listen to our podcasts from your PC, go to our website; you’ll see “Podcasts” at the top of the page. You can either listen directly or subscribe and receive them directly on your mobile phone.

And don’t forget, in addition to our audio bilingual series, you can also learn French through our website “Le Français facile avec rfi”. In addition to online lessons, there are news broadcasts in slow, simple French, with exercises to practice what you’ve heard.

Go to their website and get started! At the top of the page, click on “Test level”, and you’ll be advised on the best-suited activities for your level, according to your score.

Do not give up! As Lidwien van Dixhoorn, the head of the “Le Français facile” service, told me: “Bathe your ears in the sound of the language, and eventually, you’ll get it”. She should know – Lidwien is Dutch and came to France hardly able to say “bonjour,” and now she heads this key international award-winning RFI department – so stick with it!

For the quiz on 24 January: I asked you a question about the Africa Cup of Nations, and an article sent to us by Paul Myers, who was there. You were to re-read his article “Senegal outwit Morocco to claim 2025 Africa Cup of Nations”, and send in the answer to this question: At the 2026 World Cup, which took place in the United States, Mexico, and Canada in June, in which group did Morocco play, and in which group did Senegal play?

The answer is, to quote Paul’s article: “Morocco will play in Group C against Brazil, Scotland and Haiti.

Senegal will feature in Group I with France, Norway, and the team that emerges from the intercontinental play-off in March.”

In addition to the quiz question, there was the bonus question: “What is your favorite day of the year? Why? What is it about that day that makes it your favorite?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Dipita Chakrabarty from New Delhi, India. Dipita is also the bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners this week are Muhammed Naved, a member of the International DX Radio Listeners Club in West Bengal, India; Muhammad Abdullah, a member of the RFI Online Visitors Club in Sahiwal, Pakistan; RFI Listeners Club member Rodrigo Hunrichse from Bio-Bio, Chile, and last but not least, RFI English listener Sakila Musarrt from Chapainawabganj in Bangladesh.

Congratulations winners!

For the quiz on 31 January: You were to listen to our podcast “Spotlight on France”, the brainchild of my colleagues Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas. I hope you listen to it regularly, it’s really quite good.

On their programme number 138, Alison reported on La Ménardière, an alternative living arrangement for seniors in the village of Bérat, close to the southern French town of Toulouse. The aim of the project is for seniors to live and grow old together, contributing to society for as long as possible, and to delay – or avoid – the moment when people are forced into institutional care.

The answers you were to send in were: How many residents can live at La Ménardière, and what is the selection process?

The answer is, to quote Alison: “La Ménardière can house up to 20 residents. The selection process to become one is rigorous. Candidates stay for trial weekends and, if they decide to join, they must then complete a six-month probation period.”

The bonus question you answered that week – suggested by Murshida Parvin Lata, the co-chairman of the Sonali Badhan Female Listeners Club in Bogura, Bangladesh – was: “Which daytime temperature do you prefer: cold or hot? Why?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Father Steven Wara, who lives and serves in the Cistercian Abbey in Bamenda, Cameroon. Father Steve is also the winner of this week’s bonus question.

There’s long-standing RFI Listeners Club member Zenon Teles, who is also the president of the Christian – Marxist – Leninist – Maoist Association of Listening DX-ERs in Goa, India, as well as another faithful Sound Kitchen listener – and club member – Radhakrishna Pillai from Kerala State, also in India.

Moving over to Bangladesh, Anjana Parvin – she’s the secretary of the very active Shetu RFI Listeners Club in Naogaon. And last but not the least, club member and my fellow dinosaur, Alan Holder, from England’s Isle of Wight.

Congratulations winners!

Here’s the music you heard on this week’s programme: “Take the A Train” by Billy Strayhorn and Duke Ellington, performed by Duke Ellington and his orchestra; the “AFCON 2025 Official Intro Theme – Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025” by Othmane Laaouina; “What a Wonderful World” by Bob Thiele and George David Weiss, sung by Louis Armstrong; “The Cakewalk” from Children’s Corner by Claude Debussy, performed by the composer, and “Étincelles”, Op. 36, No. 6 by Moritz Moszkowski, played by Alexander Zhou.

I’ll talk to you next week, 26 September, for our final Sound Kitchen together. You’ll hear the answers to the questions about the Grammy Awards Lifetime Achievement Awards and the Benin Bronzes, as well as your responses to the bonus questions on "The Listener’s Corner" with Paul Myers, so be sure and tune in.

Until then, fare thee well!

World.title: A city at the crossroads of history: Unearthing Gaza's ancient heritage
World.content:
Before Gaza became synonymous with conflict, it was a place where merchants sold wine from local vineyards, pilgrims crossed continents, fishermen set out before dawn, and generations of families lived between sea and desert. RFI explores its deep history.

Advertising

Sitting on the coastal corridor linking Egypt, the Levant, the Arabian Peninsula and the Mediterranean, the port city has always been a strategic crossroads.

Like many places around the Mediterranean, Gaza's identity wasn't built by a single people or culture. It was shaped by generations of arrivals, departures and exchanges.

As the Mid-East Junction podcast returns from a six-year hiatus, we'll trace the city's history from the age of the Philistines until the creation of Israel in 1948.

In this first episode of season 3, a Gazan archaeologist, a historian, and a professor of contemporary Arab people shed light on Gaza’s little-known yet fascinating ancient history.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora.

World.title: Germany faces energy tax losses as EV sales rise
World.content:
The rapid shift to electric vehicles in Germany is cutting fuel tax revenue for the government. As EV sales surge, policymakers face growing pressure to find new ways to fund roads and transportation infrastructure.

"People are moving away from gasoline and diesel," Jens Boysen-Hogrefe, a tax and transportation expert at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW), told DW bluntly. "The boom in electric cars triggered by high fuel prices is accelerating the transition in drive technologies that was already planned anyway."

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), sales of electric vehicles in Europe rose by nearly 30% in the first quarter of 2025 compared with the same period last year.

Norway is leading the way, with electric cars accounting for as many as 95% of all newly registered cars in the country.

The agency's "Global EV Outlook 2026" reveals that EV growth rates in Asia-Pacific countries, excluding China, were even more remarkable, with sales in some regions rising by up to 80%. In Latin America, that figure was about 75%.

Fossil fuels remain a tax windfall

The boom in electric mobility has not been met with universal enthusiasm in the German government, as charging an electric car does not incur energy taxes, but only minimal electricity taxes.

Currently, a liter of diesel in Germany is taxed at 47.04 euro-cents (54 US cents per gallon), and a liter of gasoline at 65.45 euro-cents. On top of that, there is a carbon levy and a 19% value-added tax.

With gasoline priced at €2.10 per liter, taxes account for €1.14 of the total, meaning that more than half of the pump price goes to the government, according to the ADAC motoring club.

The current fossil-fuel-based system, with its energy taxes, truck tolls and CO2 tax, is very lucrative for the government, Boysen-Hogrefe said. "The finance minister doesn't benefit much when people drive electric cars," he noted. "Quite the opposite."

Energy tax revenue in decline

"If the shift to electric cars takes place and nothing changes in the tax system, the road system will become a money-losing venture for the federal government," Boysen-Hogrefe said, predicting billions of euros in losses.

EU overturns combustion engine ban amid industry pressure To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, revenue from the energy tax on diesel and gasoline fell from €37 billion in 2016 to €33 billion last year.

In 2022, a report by the scientific advisory committee to the German Transport Ministry projected that revenue from the energy tax would drop to as low as €5 billion by 2050.

Pressure to reform road funding

"The transition to electric vehicles has fiscal implications that have hardly been discussed so far," the report stated. The expected tax shortfalls add to the costly subsidies for electric vehicles that are currently still necessary to drive the transition forward, the report added.

In Germany, government incentives to purchase electric cars — amounting to several thousand euros per vehicle — were scrapped at the end of 2023.

Electric cars are still exempt from vehicle tax through 2035. And companies that invest in electric cars continue to enjoy tax benefits.

In their report, the transportation experts advised the government not to wait until the tax deficit becomes so large that it is forced to act.

That's because "the lead time for such measures spans several legislative terms," they argued.

Boysen-Hogrefe said fiscal pressure could now increase. If people continue to buy electric cars in droves, "the government can't just shrug it off," he said.

How other countries are responding

Countries such as the United Kingdom and Norway have already come up with measures to deal with the new situation.

In the UK, a levy on electric cars is set to take effect in April 2028. The so-called "Electric Vehicle Excise Duty" charges 3 pence (3.5 euro-cents) per mile (1.6 kilometers) on fully electric cars and 1.5 pence on plug-in hybrids.

Since 2024, New Zealand and Iceland have required annual odometer checks for electric vehicles to calculate mileage-based fees.

In Switzerland, meanwhile, electric vehicle owners will be required to pay a road-use charge from 2030, either through a weight-based fee per kilometer or a tax on electricity purchased at charging stations.

Meanwhile, Norway, a trailblazer for electric vehicles, has restricted the VAT exemption for electric cars starting this year. It has also introduced a weight-based purchase or registration tax and tolls.

Why big automakers are losing China To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Are road tolls the answer?

In Germany, many experts are advocating for a passenger car toll to compensate for the shortfall in energy tax revenue while also taking road use more fully into account.

"The recommended policy option is a distance- and traffic-based toll," according to a recently published study by the University of Münster .

"If we realistically assume that policymakers will shy away from this step, the vignette solution is recommended," according to the report.

Under a vignette system, drivers pay a flat fee for road use over a defined period.

"If this, too, encounters insurmountable political resistance, the only solution left is to raise the motor vehicle tax," they concluded.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Peter Thiel: Power, Palantir, and the antichrist
World.content:
He was early to back Facebook, early to back Donald Trump, and is one of the world’s richest people. But from his theories on the antichrist and AI to his distinctive politics, Peter Thiel is hard to pin down.

He may not hog the limelight in the same way as Donald Trump, Elon Musk, or many of his other friends and associates, but Peter Thiel has a fair claim to be one of the world's most influential figures — as well as one of its richest.

Born in 1967 in Frankfurt am Main in what was then West Germany, the Thiel family moved to the US when Peter was just a year old. The family also spent six years in South-African occupied Namibia from 1971 to 1977.

Thiel's later rise to prominence came on the back of his tech firms and investments. His first major success was Paypal, a digital payments provider with which Musk was initially involved. Thiel then became the first outside investor in Facebook.

Today he also owns part of Musk's SpaceX, as well as OpenAI, and multiple other companies. Forbes puts his personal wealth at $35.7 billion (€31.1 billion).

But perhaps his most noteworthy company is Palantir. The surveillance, AI, and data-analytics company has won government contracts worth billions to create software for the Pentagon as well as US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The company released a 22-point manifesto in April that critics said bore the imprint of "techno-fascism."

But Thiel could be considered as influential in politics as he is in business, and not just in the US.

Palantir’s AI manifesto sparkes global debate on weapons To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Though several European countries, including the UK, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Spain are starting to reevaluate or end their governmental and military links with Palantir due to security concerns, the company is deeply embedded in security systems across the globe.

Thiel himself has recently moved to Argentina, where he has reportedly held talks with the country's right-wing president, Javier Milei, as the government proposes a series of regulations that include incentives for foreign companies and targets investments in AI data centers.

Early Trump support paid off

Thiel was an early backer, and later advisor, of Donald Trump, donating $1.25 million to Trump's 2016 election campaign and speaking at the Republican National Convention in the same year, at a time when Silicon Valley was broadly considered to be Democrat-leaning. Bar a hiatus between 2023 and 2025, he has been a generous donor to Republican campaigns and figures, including Vice President JD Vance.

Thiel's own political beliefs are not easy to pin down. He's been described as a libertarian nationalist and consistently expressed the belief that "technology is the alternative to politics."

He also shows a distrust of authorities, regulation, and liberal elites. This is partly born of a frustration with what Thiel considers inefficient decision-making by elected officials and voters.

"It's bordering on fascism," Max Chafkin, who wrote a 2021 biography of Thiel, told Time magazine. "He talks about how companies are better run than governments because they have a single decision-maker — a dictator, basically. He is hostile to the idea of democracy. That's pretty scary when you consider the role the companies that he's been involved in play."

Thiel backed Donald Trump's first run for president. The two are seen here in December 2016, shortly after Trump won the election Image: Albin Lohr-Jones/dpa/picture alliance

These beliefs seemed to start to rise to the surface during his time at Stanford University in California. Thiel railed against the prevailing liberal campus ideology and founded the Stanford Review, a publication to express those contrary beliefs, something that would echo his current disdain for beliefs labeled as "woke."

Christianity, the antichrist, and AI

Thiel was raised in a strongly Christian household, and there is little doubt that his religion has colored his life and career. Thiel recently described himself as a "small 'o' orthodox Christian," something which seems to influence his conservative politics. His homosexuality, and marriage to American financier Matt Danzeisen, seem to many go against that grain. But paradox is not unusual for Thiel.

More recently, he has become preoccupied with the concept of the antichrist, touring with a series of lectures all over the world during the last few years. Rather than the figure depicted in the Bible, Thiel sees this as someone, or some group, who will deliver the apocalypse "by playing on our fears of technology and seducing us into decadence with the antichrist's slogan: Peace and safety."

Among those who have been, somewhat vaguely, cast in the role of soldiers of the antichrist have been environmental activist Greta Thunberg, whom he sees as a "Luddite who wants to stop all science," or governments that seek to regulate AI. He accused Pope Leo XIV of "working for the Chinese communists" in July after the pontiff warned about the "risk of dehumanization" by AI.

Despite his deep association with tech, Thiel also benefits from his relationships with powerful people, Musk, Trump, and Vance among them.

"I've built some great friendships over the years with people I've worked with," Thiel told the Washington Post in 2014. "And I think that's a really important part of what enables one to be successful in the long run in our society."

Inside Peter Thiel's secretive elite Dialog club To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Using Vance to future-proof his interests?

Many observers think that Thiel may be using his relationship with Vance to help protect himself and his business interests in the future, with the vice presidentconsidered the most likely Republican to succeed Trump.

The pair met back in 2011 when Thiel gave a talk at Yale Law School. Vance, whose religious beliefs and politics have since shifted, wrote in Christian magazine The Lamp that Thiel "defied the social template I had constructed — that dumb people were Christians and smart ones atheists."

Thiel then reportedly became a mentor figure for Vance, before smoothing the relationship between Vance and Trump as Vance U-turned from previous opposition to the president to join his 2024 ticket. Most notably though, Thiel donated $15 million to Vance's Senate campaign in 2022, the largest amount ever donated to a single US Senate candidate.

The recent calls to slow the pace of AI, made in part by CEOs in similar positions to Thiel, may end up having an impact on Thiel's business interests. But his distinct character and connections have so far kept him a step ahead.

Edited by Carla Bleiker

World.title: Russia: Ukrainian drone strike on Moscow kills 2
World.content:
An oil refinery was hit in one of the largest attacks so far on the Russian capital, as the country holds a parliamentary election. Meanwhile, at least four people were killed in Russian strikes in Ukraine's Kyiv region.

Two people were killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, local authorities said Sunday, with an oil refinery in the region also being hit.

Energy infrastructure has been repeatedly targeted by both Ukraine and Russia, despite US President Donald Trump saying both sides had agreed to stop.

Ukraine's repeated targeting of oil refineries has led to oil product shortages and fuel price increases in Russia.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strike had "a very significant impact," saying the oil in the hit refinery funds "billions of dollars to sustain the war machine."

"Moscow must end its brutal war and choose peace instead of building layered rings of air defense at the expense of other regions," Zelenskyy posted on X.

According to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, more than 1,600 drones have been intercepted by Russia since Saturday, including 450 aimed at the Russian capital, making it one the largest Ukrainian drone attacks on the city since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Moscow mayor accuses Ukraine of trying to disrupt parliamentary election

Sobyanin said that numerous drones had made it to the oil refinery, and another one hit an apartment. The scale of the damage done to the refinery has not been confirmed.

This comes as Russia is entering the last day of its three-day parliamentary election.

Sobyanin said the "unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections."

Meanwhile, in the eastern Ukrainian, Russian-occupied region of Kherson, a drone attack on a bus had killed two people, including an election official, Russian state news agency RIA reported.



War anxiety casts shadow over Russia's election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Three children killed in Kyiv region

In Ukraine, four people were killed in a Russian drone attack in the Kyiv region, local authorities said.

Among the casualties are a mother and her two 3-year-old children, as well as a girl who was taken to hospital in another district and later died.

The southwestern Fastiv district suffered damage to homes and industrial buildings.

Russia's Defense Ministry said a warehouse of drone and missile maker Fire Point was struck in the Kyiv region. It also hit a cargo vessel and a postal logistics center in the Odesa region, saying both were used for military shipments.

Russia has been repeatedly carrying out drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent weeks.

Edited by: Karl Sexton
