World.title: Azerbaijani gymnasts win medals at world acrobatics competitions (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 20. A world competition in acrobatic gymnastics among pre-juniors was held in the Italian city of Pesaro from September 17 to 20.

This was reported by the Azerbaijan Gymnastics Federation.

Azerbaijan was represented at the competition by a men’s group consisting of Yusif Huseynzade, Rasul Amiraslanov, Timur Khamidulin and Sarkhan Aghayev; a women’s pair comprising Hokuma Aliyeva and Fidan Rashidova; and a women’s group consisting of Aylin Mammadova, Ayan Hajily and Firuza Gasimzade.

The men’s and women’s groups, which successfully performed in the qualification round, advanced to the final.

In the decisive stage, the women’s group consisting of Aylin Mammadova, Ayan Hajily and Firuza Gasimzade scored 27.650 points to win the silver medal.

The men’s group of Yusif Huseynzade, Rasul Amiraslanov, Timur Khamidulin and Sarkhan Aghayev finished the competition with a bronze medal after scoring 27.200 points.

It should be noted that this was the first participation of Azerbaijan’s pre-junior men’s gymnasts in a competition of such a high level and their first medal.

World.title: Construction work continues in Azerbaijan's Aghdam, Fuzuli, and Khojavend
World.content:
KHOJAVEND, Azerbaijan, September 20. Reconstruction and construction work in the territories liberated from occupation, including the Agdam, Fuzuli and Khojavend districts, is continuing according to schedule within the framework of the First State Program on the Great Return, Special Representative of the President of Azerbaijan in the Aghdam, Fuzuli and Khojavend districts Emin Huseynov told journalists, Trend’s Karabakh bureau reports.

According to him, construction work is currently underway in the city of Aghdam and two villages in the Aghdam district.

“Currently, the reconstruction of the fourth and fifth residential complexes in Aghdam city, as well as the villages of Eyvazkhanbeyli and Bash Garvand, is continuing. These four settlements are expected to be commissioned by the end of this year. This means the return of a total of 8,000 people to Aghdam city. At the initial stage, 427 and 851 families, respectively, are planned to be resettled in the villages of Eyvazkhanbeyli and Bash Garvand,” Emin Huseynov said.

The special representative noted that reconstruction work is also underway in two villages in the Fuzuli district.

“In Fuzuli, the reconstruction of the second ‘smart village’, Dovletyarly, designed to accommodate 450 families, is continuing. At the same time, construction and reconstruction work in the village of Pirahmadli is progressing at an accelerated pace to facilitate the resettlement of 146 families at the initial stage. Our goal is to complete the construction and reconstruction work in both villages,” he added.

World.title: Meet the teens training to play for the Tasmania Devils
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The Tasmania Devils AFL team has secured a coach, is on track to build a stadium and is training its up-and-coming players as the state prepares to join the national football league in 2028.

Some of the Devils' first official players are likely to be sourced from interstate, but the Tasmanian club is looking to its homegrown talent as the foundation to field a strong side for the future.

Through its pathways program, about 420 young people from areas around Launceston, the North West and Hobart already train regularly to develop their potential as AFL and AFLW players.

Prince trains with the Tasmania Devils' Launceston hub, which supports young talented footballers to develop their AFL potential. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

Fifteen-year-old Launceston local, Prince, is part of the program and trains four times a week, splitting his sessions between the Devils and his local football club.

He said being considered for a future AFL career was a "dream come true", and that he was motivated by his family's refugee journey from Sierra Leone before he was born.

Prince's family migrated from West Africa to Tasmania before he was born. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

"[My family] went to a refugee camp in Ghana … where my brother and sister were born … and then [to] Australia," he said.

"It requires a lot of resilience to migrate and raise multiple kids in a different country.

" That work ethic has been passed on through my upbringing and I just really want to work hard at my sport to give back to [my family]. "

Loading...

Coby, 15, is a fellow Tasmania Devils pathways player who almost left football behind after a loss in his family.

Playing in the AFL had been his dream since watching a football game at the MCG when he was six years old.

He said getting the call to say he had made the pathways team was "one of the happiest days" of his life.

Coby says his Nan's passing has inspired him to push on with chasing his AFL dreams because she was his biggest supporter. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

"But when my Nan passed away, I thought, 'How am I going to overcome this and do what I usually do without my biggest supporter?'" he said.

"Then I realised, if I quit I would never know how good I could be.

"Now I want to be the best that I can be [for her] … hopefully that's going as far as the AFL."

Devils set sights on AFLW

The Tasmania Devils pathways program also focuses on creating a competitive AFLW side for the state.

Lilanni plays in the Tasmania U18 Talent League side. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

Lilanni, 17, plays in the Tasmania under-18 talent league side and is draft eligible this year.

She hopes to join her sister, Fremantle Dockers' player Tunisha Kikoak, in the AFLW ranks.

"When I first touched the ball I [knew I] wanted to be in the draft and be an AFLW player like my sister," she said.

Lilanni said the increased focus on women's football across the country had led to better development for young female players.

"There's more opportunities for the girls that I play alongside [than before] and there's more chances to grow as a player," she said.

Brad Cox-Goodyer is AFL Tasmania talent pathways skills acquisition coach and says the Devils are building a strong side ahead of their debut in 2028. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

AFL Tasmania talent pathways skills acquisition coach Brad Cox-Goodyer said the Devils had already been working to develop individual talent.

"We're in our third year now and it's exciting … [we] get better every year and [are] hoping to get more kids playing for the Tassie Devils," he said.

World.title: Germany's right-wing party AfD returns strong election results
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The right-wing Alternative for Deutschland (AfD) party has made strong gains in more state elections, according to exit polls, leaving Chancellor Friedrich Merz's future balanced on a knife's edge after 16 months in office.

The AfD emerged with 37 per cent of votes in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, according to polls conducted by public broadcasters ARD and ZDF.

However the anti-immigration party is set to remain iced out of power in both states due a "firewall" of non-cooperation, agreed by other major parties.

Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla are the co-leaders of the Alternative for Germany party. (Reuters: Annegret Hilse)

The firewall was formally established in 2018, acting as an agreement between mainstream parties to suppress the growing influence of extreme politics, by ruling out any coalition with far-right-aligned parties.

Worst results since 1949

If confirmed, the results from Sunday's election would be the worst in any state election for Mr Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) since 1949.

A 'serious moment in Europe' The weekend win by Alternative for Germany in the state of Saxony-Anhalt has sent shivers across the continent, and could embolden the right across Europe.

It would also be another first-place finish at state level for the AfD party, which is topping national opinion polls despite being shunned by mainstream parties.

"It's a disaster," Mr Merz said in televised remarks after the exit polls were published, but signalled that he would fight on as chancellor after speculation that a bad result could prompt him to resign.

Friedrich Merz has been shaken by increasing support for the far-right and far-left. (Reuters: Christian Mang)

Another state election in the capital Berlin also took place on Sunday, with the far-left Die Linke party polling 24.5 per cent, while Mr Merz’s conservatives stood at 20 per cent.

The AfD also gained in strength, polling 16 per cent of votes in Berlin.

The future of Friedrich Merz

Sunday's results may not prove a knock-out blow for Mr Merz, who last week received backing from eight conservative state premiers.

Low approval ratings, unpopular reforms and the triumph of AfD in the earlier Saxony-Anhalt state election have left the chancellor's future in question.

The elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin follow the early September election in Saxony-Anhalt, a pivotal moment where the AfD came close to winning an absolute majority.

The support for AfD is expected to drain backing for Mr Merz's CDU party, which has since called for a party meeting to discuss the way forward.

Alice Weidel's party is coming off a strong result in the Saxony-Anhalt state election. (Reuters: Lisi Niesner)

The AfD pitted the two state elections as their first stride in winning the federal election due in 2029.

The party's poster policies have included leaving the European Union, restoring relations with Russia, significant reductions in immigration and tightening asylum laws.

In just over a decade, AfD transformed itself from a fringe movement to the country's most popular party.

ABC/wires

World.title: Murder accused former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon trial begins
World.content:
Two-and-a-half years after the deaths of Sydney couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, the trial of a former police officer accused of their murder will begin today in the NSW Supreme Court.

Beau Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two counts of domestic violence-related murder and one of aggravated break and enter.

It is alleged he shot the pair with his service firearm inside Mr Baird's shared terrace at Paddington, in Sydney's east, in February 2024.

The break and enter offence is alleged to have occurred at the Paddington property in August the previous year.

Mr Lamarre-Condon, now 31, was charged days after NSW Police issued a public appeal for information to locate the young couple, who had last been seen at a pre-Mardi Gras party.

Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird who were allegedly killed by Mr Lamarre-Condon. (Supplied: Instagram)

It was not until the following week that their bodies were found at a rural area in Bungonia, nearly 200 kilometres south-west of Sydney's CBD, in surf bags.

Mr Baird was a television presenter for Channel Ten, while Mr Davies worked for Qantas as a flight attendant.

The case deeply impacted families and wider friendship circles, and sent shock waves through the LGBT community.

When police appealed for information about the pair's disappearance, items including personal possessions had been found in a bin at Cronulla, in the Sutherland Shire.

The trial, being heard at Sydney's King Street Courts before Justice Natalie Adams, has an estimated duration of three months.

Jurors are likely to hear from dozens of witnesses.

Today, the court is expected to complete the process of empanelling a jury from a wider jury pool, before Crown Prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC makes an opening address.

World.title: Hacking this BYD was too easy. It didn't even have a password
World.content:
On a narrow country road outside Canberra, I'm driving a BYD Shark 6, the hybrid ute loved by tradies and even a cabinet minister.

But while I'm at the wheel, I'm not the only one in control — a hacker has access to the car.

As the 2.6 tonne ute rounds a bend, he gets to work.

Loading...

With the stroke of a key, he kills the headlights, plunging me into darkness.

The attack is not a total surprise. The Shark has spent the last two weeks with Dan Hreszczuk, a cybersecurity expert, who specialises in cars.

His task was to hack the vehicle and find out what could be seen and done remotely by the Shark's Chinese manufacturer.

"It was easier than we were expecting," Hreszczuk says.

The Shark 6 is a plug-in hybrid ute. ( )

Modern connected cars — particularly EVs and hybrids — are increasingly run by software, giving manufacturers the power to change, update and control vehicles, like never before.

In the case of BYD and others, that software is controlled from China.

With fuel prices on the rise, EVs and plug-in hybrids like the Shark have gone mainstream this year, making up almost a third of new cars sales to date. More than half of these are from Chinese brands.

EVs, with all their sensors, cameras and microphones, hoover up and spit out vast amounts of data. Experts say that data poses a greater risk in the hands of Chinese EV makers, as they can be compelled by the country's national security laws to co-operate with authorities.

To put this potential access to the test, it made sense to pick a model from China's top EV brand, BYD.

There's been a rapid uptake of hybrids and fully electric cars in Australia. ( )

Dan Hreszczuk takes a look at the Shark. ( )

Hreszczuk, the co-founder of Fortify Labs in Canberra, was stunned by the BYD Shark's lack of cybersecurity.

"The access we took advantage of didn't even have a password," he says.

" It's a little bit scary how open … the BYD Shark is to a hacker. "

This lack of a password allowed Dan to access the car's digital arteries.

From there it was a matter of unpicking the software programs which control different functions in the car.

After two weeks, Dan was ready.

I meet Dan on a country road so he can show me what his remote access can do. ( )

Sitting by the side of the country road, he demonstrates what could be done with remote access to a vehicle.

First, he locks the doors while I'm inside, blasts music over the speakers and plays images on the BYD's giant infotainment screen.

Then, as I drive, he remotely switches the wipers on at top speed, sprays the windscreen with water and turns the lights on and off.

Dan accesses the BYD from his laptop. ( )

Loading...

The combination is unsettling and highly distracting.

Adding to the distraction: Dan has the speaker telling me repeatedly; "For safety use low beam".

Fortunately, I was only travelling 30km/h and the road was pretty straight.

Then, Dan kills the lights altogether.

Dan says he wasn't able to access more critical functions like brakes and cameras as these were well protected.

But it doesn't take much imagination to understand how dangerous, even this kind of access could be in the hands of a malicious actor, with a vehicle travelling at high speed on a winding road.

Surveillance

While sabotage is one worry, the concern most-often cited is surveillance, due to the array of cameras and microphones on an EV.

Last year, the UK military banned Chinese EVs — even those made with Chinese components — from parking within 3 kilometres of some of its most sensitive locations.

China itself has previously banned foreign EVs from military sites and political enclaves, aware of their surveillance potential.

BYD is China's top EV brand. ( )

In Australia, there's no blanket ban on Chinese marques by Defence, but ASIO has warned ministers and public servants not to have sensitive conversations in their cars or connect work devices.

But there's nothing to stop them owning a Chinese EV.

Trade Minister Don Farrell has a BYD Shark 6, the same vehicle that Dan hacked.

Farrell recently told a newspaper it's the "best ute I've ever owned".

ASIO's surveillance fears appear well founded, based on what else Dan is able to do to with the Shark even at a low level of access.

We devise a demonstration: I'll take the BYD for a drive around Canberra, and give my mum a call to talk her through some internet banking.

As I drive past the war memorial and down Anzac Parade, Dan has already remotely accessed the vehicle and is tracking my progress.

I drive through the heart of Canberra in the BYD Shark. ( )

Dan is following in real time. ( )

Dan watches the Shark's journey. ( )

Then he gets to work.

"How about we turn on the microphone?" he suggests to the crew back at his lab.

At that point Dan can hear everything.

"Hey Siri," I say to my iPhone.

"Call 'mum mobile'."

When she picks up, I'm straight into the details of how I had set up her internet banking.

"I'm going to use as a temporary password, my initials, the number of my house, and then my full date of birth. And then you can go in later and change it if you want," I tell her.

Back at the lab Dan records the whole conversation.

The key is he's now got a recording of me saying, "Hey Siri".

When I pull into a service station and leave my phone unlocked in the car, Dan seizes his opportunity.

He's done a simple audio edit, stitching together me saying "Hey Siri" and his voice asking a few questions to get the personal details he needs.

Dan records my "Hey Siri" to make his own audio file. ( )

He has access to the car's speakers. ( )

Using the car's speaker system, Dan plays the voice command from his computer into the car.

"Hey, Siri, what is my home address?" the edited audio asks.

Siri replies, without questioning why I don't know where I live.

Dan repeats this process and quickly extracts my date of birth and age.

Within minutes, he's obtained the internet banking password.

Dan keeps fishing.

"Let's try and grab a few of his contacts. Let's see if he knows a prime minister.

"Hey Siri, tell me the phone number from my contacts for Malcolm Turnbull."

Once again, Siri dutifully delivers.

Dan's hacking challenge was made easier as Australia has no minimum cybersecurity standards for cars. That means BYD is not compelled to keep its software up to date or have a system for managing cybersecurity risks to its vehicles.

"I didn't need to pick the lock as BYD left the front door open," he says.

"I think people overlook a lot of these concerns for the convenience. It is a beautiful car to drive. It looks beautiful inside, but there are real security concerns."

BYD has gone from a virtual unknown four years ago to challenging Toyota as the country's top-selling brand. ( )

Surprisingly, Australia has more cybersecurity regulation around connected washing machines or vacuum cleaners than cars.

Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke defends this, saying the government has started by putting regulations around connected devices in the household.

"You want to first regulate where you will get the fastest uplift and … you also want to focus first on where the cyber attacks have principally been," he says.

The government has just started consultations with industry to introduce new cybersecurity and software rules for cars in Australia, but they likely won't be in force for years.

Alastair MacGibbon, Australia's former national cyber security adviser, says there needs to be greater protections for the data collected by all connected cars, and clearer rules about what data can be sent overseas.

MacGibbon says a cabinet minister should not be able to own a Chinese EV.

"China has always shown its strong desire to steal things, to surveil," he says.

"No one should be in any doubt that [Chinese EVs] are used in the same manner.

"The real question would come down [to]: could they cause harm with these vehicles? The capability is definitely there.

"Is the intent? I don't know."

Opposition Defence spokesman James Paterson says Australians' data needs to be better protected.

"A connected EV vehicle from China is the highest risk product in the marketplace. And right now, there's nothing that says to that brand what data you can collect on Australians, how it can be stored, when it can be transmitted."

BYD says the data it collects is stored in Australia. It says it has not and would not hand over the data of Australians to Chinese authorities.

Watch Four Corners' full investigation, Asleep at the Wheel, tonight from 8:30 on ABC TV and ABC iview.

Credits

Reporting:Angus Grigg, Jonathan Miller and Maddy King

Photography and video: Ron Foley

Animation: Alistair Kroie

Editing:Nick Wiggins

World.title: SCG madness and Plugger's point: The Swans-Bombers prelim, 30 years on
World.content:
When Dale Lewis recalls being at the Sydney Swans in the 1990s, it certainly was not all about big games and big crowds.

"We're training, doing preseason out of the showgrounds next door [to the SCG] and one of the days, the Big Day Out was on at these showgrounds. We had to walk the oval, arms linked like we're in a search party checking for needles and shit in the grass before we trained," he says.

"The Swans weren't popular. We were having crowds of 5,000 people. I jumped the fence one day to get the footy for a boundary umpire.

"I've got a great mate … his brother used to come, and he used to love it because he could sit anywhere, and he cracked the shits when we started getting good because he had to go buy a ticket and couldn't get a decent seat and sit where he wanted to."

It all changed in the mid 1990s, when the Swans went from the basement to the penthouse.

With three straight wooden spoons between 1992 and 1994, they went from winning one game in 1993 to four wins in 1994 and eight wins in 1995, then a surge to 16 wins and top of the ladder in '96.

A finals win over Hawthorn put them in a home preliminary final against Essendon at a heaving SCG, 30 years ago today.

Swans utility Troy Luff had gotten his opportunity that season. Originally from Traralgon in Victoria, he grew up attached to a footy like most kids, then he and his family moved to Nelson Bay near Newcastle.

He was spotted while kicking goals for fun in the Hunter, but struggled to make a mark with the Swans under Ron Barassi.

Then new coach Rodney Eade changed everything as Luff became a permanent fixture in the side.

Troy Luff got his big opportunity for the Sydney Swans in 1996, and he rode the momentum to the prelim. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"It was more excitement rather than pressure," Luff says.

"If we lose, we lose. We got this far, but everyone just went out there and enjoyed themselves, and the results came our way."

Lewis agrees.

"None of us saw it coming, but by Christ it was addictive once you started to win, especially at home," he says.

"Because I think that was the year we started. We ended up winning 22 or three in a row at the SCG as the run got going. You started to get a feeling about it.

"And once we'd beaten Hawthorn in that first qualifying [final], the expectation was why not?"

In 1992-93, the Swans lost 26 games in a row.

Lewis, who was drafted against his preferences in 1990 by Sydney, was out the week they broke the run against Melbourne, and ended up playing in 33 consecutive losses. He had tried to get out of Sydney in 1994, but ended up staying.

In 1995, there were a series of important arrivals, none bigger than the famous bookends, Paul Roos and Tony "Plugger" Lockett.

The former St Kilda superstar Lockett had won his third Coleman Medal (and first in Sydney) in 1996, booting 114 goals in the home-and-away season.

Former Fitzroy key position player Roos brought skill, leadership and experience.

Now they and the Swans were a win away from a grand final.

The game

It was fierce, frantic footy early doors. Not a heap of composure was shown, with lots of scrubby kicks under pressure, aiming for territory, not accuracy.

Early in the game, Essendon was looking for James Hird, who - along with Michael Voss of the Brisbane Bears - would win the Brownlow Medal two days later. Hird kicked long from 60, and Steven Alessio marked before converting from 20 out.

Soon after, Lewis marked, then tripped over Hird and was crunched in a tackle. Hird grabbed the ball and scored. Swans fans were livid, but Essendon led by two goals.

The Swans tried kicking to Lockett, but Essendon cleared – their movement was better, and Hird earned a free on 50. He went long, Justin Blumfield came down with it and ran around to kick Essendon's third.

Sydney could not take a trick. Lewis grabbed the ball in the centre square and quickly went long again in Lockett's direction; in the end, Jason Mooney kicked a point to make it 3.1 to 0.1.

Hird came off the ground with blood streaming from his left cheek after he and Andrew Dunkley contested a ball, the Swans defender roughing the Bombers star as he lay on the ground with Dunkley on top of him.

A Barry Young point extended the lead, then Gary O'Donnell took possession and went long to Che Cockatoo-Collins, who marked and drilled it from inside 50. Seven minutes left, Bombers by 25.

The Bombers were dominating clearances, and Damien Hardwick set up Mick Symons for a contested mark, but his kicking radar was off. The Swans' forward forays were like chaos balls compared to the Dons.

Dale Lewis's long-kicking, strong marking style made him an important player for the Swans against the Bombers. (Getty Images: Mandatory Credit: Allsport Australia/ALLSPORT)

Another series of points, then Wade Chapman marked a Stuart Maxfield kick near horizontal at half-forward. His kick came, and Lewis drifted in from the side for a great mark. He kicked it, and the Swans trailed by 19 at quarter time.

"Part of your job is to kick goals and everything else, but to take a big mark," Lewis says.

"That was in front of the Ladies Stand too, I think. A mad, mad Swans house there. Always nice to do that."

Luff says the Swans had built up confidence during the season.

"There was never an attitude of, 'Oh geez, they've got three goals on us, we're going to lose this.' We were like, 'No, no, we'll get that back'."

Tough night for Essendon's Lloyd

On the Essendon side of things, forward Matthew Lloyd was playing a prelim in game 16 of his career, at just 18 years old.

Drafted at 16, thanks to a one-off change of the rules due to draft concessions for the new Fremantle side, Lloyd was highly touted.

He kicked three on debut against the Crows in 1995 before playing a couple of finals as a schoolboy.

In 1996 he kicked another seven against Adelaide, and then just before finals he booted three against the Swans at the MCG.

"I was playing local footy in 1993, Western Jets in '94, and then suddenly I'm playing as a 17-year-old in '95. So yeah, it all happened so fast, but I was very driven," Lloyd says.

"[The focus] was all footy, footy, footy. I was 78 kilos, and I actually ended my career at 92 to 94 kilos.

"So I was out of my depth physically. I did kick three on debut, and I kicked three in the first [1995] final, so I had some good moments."

Matthew Lloyd kicked three against the Swans in August 1996, but he struggled in the cauldron of an SCG prelim a month later. (Getty Images, file photo)

Fast-forward to the prelim in 1996; it was a different story.

"I just felt like the SCG, where I hadn't played before, the crowd was on top of you, it was loud, and it was physical," Lloyd says.

"I was a very nervous type. I had a big fear of failure. I wasn't able to get my hands on the footy; it was more the atmosphere in that stadium and some big Sydney players too that I was playing on [that was intimidating]."

In the second quarter, Sydney was trying to hit back, and narrowed the gap through goals to skipper Paul Kelly and Daryn Cresswell. The lead was four points.

Lloyd was scrambling to make an impact. Nearly halfway through the quarter, a big Mark Harvey kick was bouncing towards the boundary at half-forward.

Mark Bayes and Hird were running one way, and Lloyd was racing out of forward 50. As Lloyd recalls, what happened next was "quite innocuous" as he tried to bump Bayes.

"You bump someone, and instead my elbow came back into my side. It took my breath away, and I felt winded. I played out the rest of the second quarter, but I felt like I was deteriorating health-wise," he says.

A review of the video does not suggest there was a huge problem – Lloyd kept launching himself into packs, although if you were keeping your eye on him rather than the ball, he was taking longer to get up each time.

"It's all a bit of a blur for me because I remember I couldn't concentrate; I couldn't really take in the half-time address [from Kevin Sheedy]," he says.

"I was losing colour in my face and body. I said to the club doctor, I'm not feeling very well, and they decided to have me start the third quarter and see how I was feeling after five minutes.

"I'm not sure how long I was in the third quarter where I eventually came off … but they knew to get me to hospital at that point."

Lloyd went to emergency at a Kings Cross hospital.

"I just remember lying there still in my full Essendon kit of the football jumper, the shorts, socks, and boots I presume, and just pain, just in so much pain," he says.

He was given morphine, and the pain subsided a little.

"They asked me to hop, and I hopped, and I said, 'I actually feel a bit better,'" he says.

"I can't remember what they thought it could have been, but they said, 'He's right to go back to the hotel.'"

Swans making a run

Back at the SCG, things were improving for Sydney.

After those two early goals, the Swans sensed an opportunity. Derek Kickett kicked from the right pocket to the square for Lockett to mark and goal. The crowd erupted and Sydney led by two with 9:26 left in the half.

Another scrambled ball was toed toward goal by Lockett, only for Sean Denham to palm it away like a goalkeeper.

Somehow Lockett got it out to Luff, who kicked the goal and Sydney led by eight. It was pandemonium at the SCG.

"From memory, he burst through and pushed someone out of the way, then handballed it to me at the top of the square and I snapped the goal," Luff recalls.

"And you just get pumped; it helps you keep building from moments, whether it's a good tackle or a good spoil [or a goal]."

Misses by Barry Young and Hird brought the margin back to six.

The play was getting faster and more chaotic, and the ball pinged in and out of 50 for Sydney. A kung-fu style kick from Luff found Greg Stafford, who ignored a furious Plugger before Cresswell snapped his second. Swans led by 12 at half-time.

Early in the third, a Lewis kick found Lockett near the point post – he marked then stumbled and fell over. His kick hit the post.

On the ABC Radio broadcast, commentator Peter Longman said: "He's done some good things, Lockett, but if he was a racehorse they'd be checking him out behind the barriers and declaring him a non-starter, I feel sure."

Teammates knew Lockett was in pain.

"An 80 per cent Plugger is better than not having him in the side at all, even 70 per cent Plugger. He was just that good," Luff says.

The back and forth continued, with a kind of stalemate.

Luff snapped over his shoulder, but it bounced out 15 metres wide of the posts. Luff then got the tap to Kelly, who took two steps and snapped for a Sydney goal. Cue huge chants from the red and white faithful.

Utility Troy Luff contributed to the Swans' historic prelim challenge, setting up a goal and kicking one of his own. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"I started in defence when Paul Roos was injured. I'd play centre-half-back. Andrew Dunkley was injured, I'd play full-back. Plugger was out, I'd play full-forward. So I just played any role the team needed [including ruck]," Luff says.

There were 41,731 at the SCG that night – and they were totally fired up, making the noise of a much bigger crowd.

"David Murphy used to tell me prior to that year, 50,000 people, you can just hear your teammate. [With a] 75,000 crowd, you can barely hear your teammate," Lewis says.

"Anything over 85, 95,000, you can't hear your teammate, and you can't even feel yourself get hit. Such is the noise and the adrenaline; you don't even know what's happening.

"The messaging was always, [finals are] going to be quicker, it's going to be faster, it's going to be harder. And none of it's bullshit."

Just when Swans fans might have been feeling a little confident, the Bombers had a forward 50 stoppage; the tap went to Harvey, and then O'Donnell, who kicked from 35 and the lead was 13 points.

But Sydney went down the corridor, and Lewis marked. A huge roar greeted his goal, and a fan leapt the fence and ran next to the umpire to do a tandem goal signal. He then got out of there quick-smart.

At 19 points down, the Bombers were not done. Dean Wallis marked in the pocket, then Sydney gave away 50. Dunkley was in the umpire's face – Wallis goaled, then confronted the Sydney full-back.

The Bombers won the next clearance, and Alessio found Hird in the square to score. With 3:00 left in the term, it was a seven-point game.

In the final minute, Alessio marked around 50 – and converted. A quarter to go, Sydney led by a solitary point, 8.7 to 8.6.

Troy Luff recalls Swans coach Rodney Eade urging players to keep things tight to start the final quarter at the SCG. (Getty Images, file photo)

"I remember Rocket (Rodney Eade) just saying that we needed to shut that down at the start of the last quarter, not go out and try and kick a goal," Luff says.

"If they got the first goal, they've kicked four in a row, and they may have gone on with it. But if we just shut that momentum down, play a bit defensive to start with, then once the game settles, then we [can] go out and attack."

Only three of the 16 goals kicked had been to the left-hand end. The Bombers would be kicking to that end in the final quarter.

Early on, O'Donnell fed Che Cockatoo-Collins, who burst down the right. His kick found Hird, and the Essendon champion slowed, then raced forward and snapped. The umpire scampered around. The Bombers had their early goal.

With 18:27 left, Essendon led by five. Everyone was tiring, and play was largely stuck between the arcs. Time ticked slowly; after a series of misses it was 9.9 to 8.9.

The tension was rising. Essendon's Denham might have cracked a rib; Sydney's Michael O'Loughlin hurt his knee. He came off and returned, still limping.

From a boundary throw 40m out, Harvey handballed to a running Symons.

ABC's Peter Longman was left incredulous:

"He's put it through! The Bombers lead by 12 points! Symons, a duffer from a standing start, has a checkside kick from 35m out and he's put it through – and he might have put the Bombers into the grand final next week!"

The Bombers led by 12, 4:09 on the clock.

The final minutes

Lewis had a sick feeling, wondering if this was how it was going to finish.

"Something you've wanted so bad as a kid, as a senior footballer, as an AFL player, it's within your grasp, but you can't touch it … It hits you in the gut real hard. I'm not going to lie to you, that was a shit feeling when he kicked that one," he says.

The runner told Lewis to drag Hird to full-forward because Sydney needed goals.

"So I hightailed it out of there," Lewis recalls.

Essendon hacked it forward; Adam Heuskes cleared to Kelly. He found Maxfield, who was chased through the middle, taking two bounces as the roar built. A kick from 60 to Hird and Lewis – and Lewis grabbed it and kicked the goal. Six points, 2:48 left.

It got even more frantic, the ball stuck in the middle. The Swans cleared, and it went to Simon Garlick, then Chapman, then Maxfield to Lockett, who played on but didn't go for goal, opting to kick inside to Cresswell. Cresswell marked then lay down, cramping.

He got up and kicked it, and with 89 seconds left, the scores were level.

Cresswell raised his arms skywards. The Sydney Airport curfew was still half an hour from kicking in, but the roar erupting would have matched a take-off from Mascot.

The clock ticked down, a ball-up with 1:02 left, no real progress.

The play was ferocious as players collided. The ball went inside 50; Swans couldn't mark. Blumfield cleared it desperately, and Chapman marked to the right of the centre square. He back-pedalled, then kicked high to the left side of 50.

From stage right came Tony Lockett to pluck it from the sky and draw every single decibel from surrounding suburbs with 17 seconds left.

He was 52 metres from goal, with an injured groin, and no other options. The clock ran down.

"The video shows me walking past him as he's about to line up to take the shot. I've just turned around to him and said, 'All you have to do is get it over the line. Doesn't matter what it is, just get it over the line,'" Luff recalls.

The siren's gone, the crowd's collective blood pressure had spiked into the stratosphere, but Plugger had it.

Loading...

Everyone watched the ball fly towards goal. Was it there? A point was enough; out on the full or short meant extra time.

The roar gathered. The umpire fired out one finger to signal a behind, and absolute bedlam ensued at the SCG. The Bombers were distraught. The Swans were ecstatic.

Sydney vs Essendon AFL preliminary final Sept 21, 1996 (SCG) SYDNEY: 10.10 (70) def ESSENDON 10.9 (69) Goals: Sydney: D Lewis 3, D Cresswell 3, P Kelly 2, T Lockett, T Luff Essendon: J Hird 3, S Alessio 2, J Blumfield, C Cockatoo-Collins, G O'Donnell, M Symons, D Wallis Crowd: 41,731

It was over. Two seasons removed from the wooden spoon, the Swans were in their first grand final since South Melbourne's infamous "Bloodbath" decider against Carlton in 1945.

Lewis recalls the feeling when Lockett took the grab.

"Call it presumptuous, but the moment he marked it, I knew we were going to play in a grand final," he says.

What about Plugger's groin, the distance, the pain, the effort required?

"None of it became relevant because he's Tony Lockett," Lewis says.

"We would pick him from anywhere, any angle, any distance. Because that's what he does. Not only was it his job, but the belief we had in him when he had the ball in hand, kick a goal or convert and finish was just amazing."

The aftermath

Sydney's Tony Lockett pushed himself to the limit for the most important behind of his career that put the Swans in the grand final. (Supplied: AFL Photos)

Luff was quick to the party.

"We're like, 'That's going to score.' And then the excitement hit us. And I was one of the first ones to jump on Plugger, and then everyone else just piled on top," Luff says.

"And what I do remember is Plugger on the bottom going, 'Get off me, get off me.' He was so sore from his groin that everyone jumping on didn't help his cause.

"Then [we] got up and we're like, 'We're in the grand final. We're in the grand final.' It was ecstatic. It was fantastic."

Lewis turned to Stafford in the square to find he was already off running.

"I get in a bit late on the pile on, and all I can do is pat a few blokes … because I was too busy celebrating down the goal square looking for a bit of love from teammates who'd already done the bolt," he says.

Dale Lewis says the surge of euphoric Swans fans onto the SCG after the 1996 prelim was the precursor of the "Buddy moment" in 2022. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

The euphoric crowd of Swans fans surged onto the ground.

"That's the precursor to the Buddy moment [Lance Franklin's 1,000 goals] in terms of the crowd getting on the ground at the SCG," Lewis says.

"You didn't want to get off [the ground], but you wanted to get off because you wanted to get into that little room downstairs and soak it all in with each other and just go, 'F***, how good is this. We're in one.'"

Lloyd's dream turns 'nightmare'

Back at the Bombers team hotel, Matthew Lloyd was in his room with his parents. Players were coming in, but the morphine was wearing off.

Once people had gone, Lloyd asked his parents to help him to the bathroom, where he passed blood.

Essendon's Dr Bruce Reid came, and Lloyd says he was "rolling around in bed, just the worst pain of my life." Reid asked him if he had shoulder pain.

"I stopped for a second, and I said, 'Yeah, really strong shoulder pain.' I just remember him saying, 'Get him an ambulance. He's got a ruptured spleen'," Lloyd recalls.

Scans showed a large tear in his spleen, and a litre and a half of blood. It could have been fatal if left longer. As scary as this was, Lloyd had to come to terms with what it meant for his footy career.

"I knew going into this game, the reserves had qualified for the grand final," he says.

"I thought, 'Well, I'm going to play in that because I qualify for that or I'm going to play in the AFL grand final,' and then it turned into my nightmare."

Lloyd lost eight kilos, was bedridden for a time and could not do anything physical for three months. But in 1997 he burst out with a 63-goal season.

"I lived and breathed footy, no interest in going to parties," Lloyd says.

"My dad played 29 games for Carlton, and from the moment I was three or four, I had a footy in my hand, and it's all I ever wanted to do … and I was no different with my rehab; I was willing to do anything to play AFL footy."

That determination saw Lloyd finish as Essendon's top goal-kicker and eighth in VFL/AFL history, with 926 majors.

While Lloyd was suffering through a ruptured spleen, the other Bombers were dealing with a season cut short.

He says the players filing through his hotel room that night let him know coach Kevin Sheedy had exploded like never before after the game.

Lloyd was told Sheedy was pointed in his criticism of the team and of individuals, not just for the loss but for the way they lost and a perceived lack of toughness.

Three years later, a dominant Bombers team came up against Carlton and lost in the prelim. Lloyd says it still hurts today.

"In 1999, [Sheedy] was very different. He [went], 'OK, how I'm going to go to sell to these boys the hurt and what we're going to do in 2000 and this should steel us for 2000.' But in '96, he wasn't like that."

Essendon, including Lloyd, had to wait until 2000 for the flag, as they tore through the AFL going 24-1, including three finals by a ridiculous combined margin of 230 points.

For Sydney's Dale Lewis (centre), the ultimate grand final success eluded him, but the prelim win remains unforgettable. (Getty Images)

For the Swans, the euphoria became a magic grand final week and a dream first quarter and a half – but then the Kangaroos put their foot down, and North ran away with it to win by 43 points. Lockett kicked six, but it wasn't enough. Sydney had to wait until 2005 for the drought to break.

Luff, Lewis and Lockett never won a flag, although Plugger made history with an untouchable 1,360 goals.

It is now 30 years, but Dale Lewis, for one, has not forgotten that night.

"I can see it now. I get a little bit emotional about it," he says with a slight crack in his voice.

"I can see that [night]. I can see the looks in a couple of guys' eyes. I know who I turned to. You look at it, and you go, 'Unbelievable'."

World.title: Labor's dilemma is that Australia needs two things voters fear
World.content:
The two things holding up the economy are fast becoming the two most potent and dangerous political issues confronting the federal government.

Data centres and migration are the twin issues the government needs to keep pumping to keep the country in positive economic territory, but they are also the two issues voters have the most complex and hostile relationship with.

It presents a dilemma for the government: it can't live with it, but it also can't live without it.

Migration has long been a key contributor to the economy, with international students, workers and their spending helping tip dollars into treasury coffers.

One Nation and the Coalition want to drastically cut immigration and are smashing the government on the idea that they have allowed a "mass migration" program. Labor, stung by months of relentless campaigning on this issue, finally unveiled a plan to try to cut it back too.

But figures out from today's Intergenerational Report (IGR) show just how much we need migrants for the economy to keep growing, albeit slowly.

Australia's population growth is projected to slow from an average of 1.4 per cent a year over the past 40 years to 0.9 per cent a year over the next 40 years. This is 0.2 percentage points lower growth compared with the projection period of the 2023 IGR.

The population is projected to reach 39.3 million by 2065–66. In 2062–63, the projected population is 1.8 million lower than projected in the 2023 IGR (Chart 8.2).

So while politicians from all the major, minor and yet-to-be-determined sides launch into a debate around migration, the projections are blunt — we are failing to build our own population from our own numbers.

Migrants are the ones renewing us whether we like it or not.

The data centre conundrum

And while migration is the government's perennial political headache, data centres present the same bargain: an economic boost at an unknown political cost.

Touted as the next boom, with some figures indicating they could deliver around $150 billion by 2030. For a country that has relied on revenue from selling the things we dig up, data centres have looked like the next pot of gold.

With inflation still high and economists predicting the Reserve Bank will deliver another rate rise this month, the government will be desperately relying on investment returns from both.

That both issues are the subject of furious debate not just in Canberra but across the country is inconvenient, to put it lightly.

Huawei, the Chinese-owned tech giant banned in 2018 from being involved in Australia's 5G rollout, released a report a few days ago predicting data centres could consume up to 10 per cent of the world's electricity by 2035.

The figure is staggering.

Australia is trying to thread the needle: the government's proposed standards would force new centres to generate their own renewable energy and minimise water use to offset their demand. But those standards are not yet law.

New data centres set to escape rules Dozens of approved but yet-to-be-built AI data centre projects are expected to escape the federal government's proposed restrictions around energy and water use.

Meanwhile, increasingly dystopian stories about the toll the centres are taking on power, water and the grid are emerging from the United States.

While migration is well-traversed political ground, the emergence of data centres and the community hostility is new territory.

The PM wants to build public consensus through national standards, but it is fanciful to think laws will contain voters' anger if people feel they are competing with global big tech firms for water and power.

Anthropic has signed an agreement to use part of a $32 billion data centre proposed for a site on Queensland's Western Downs. It will be the largest facility in Australia and would draw as much power as about 1.5 million average households.

AI questions won't disappear

Not afraid of calling a spade a spade, Labor MP Ed Husic says the government has so far had a "patronising" approach to people's concerns about artificial intelligence implementation.

"I'm still concerned that we don't have a uniform approach to dealing with the risks of AI," Husic told Afternoon Briefing.

"I've seen AI firms, in fact, some operating right here out of Canberra that are developing generative AI products that are way cheaper than what you're seeing out of US tech [companies]," he said.

But Husic said he did not think Australia would back itself to go local, pointing to leaked Treasury advice "that says we should just be the quickest at adapting someone else's technology".

"That massively undermines our ambition and capability and ability to scale up our own local solutions, and I've got to say, if you want to build confidence in AI, people knowing homegrown AI is available for them that can meet the job and give them a lot more confidence.

"I am concerned that we are dragging the chain. The best thing, if we want to have AI sorted out, is to get a national approach and get it done once, get it done right."

This is a wicked problem for Labor.

Political analysis that matters The ABC's politics podcast, Politics Now, dives into the biggest stories, giving you a balanced look inside the strategies and decisions behind the headlines.

Anthony Albanese has urged the United States and China, the two leading powers in the AI race, to strike a deal that ensures "humans remain in control". He has also left the door open to changing copyright laws to attract AI investment in Australia.

Albanese will speak with like-minded leaders at the United Nations General Assembly about global rules to regulate AI development, and while significant, those discussions won't fix domestic concerns over AI.

The government needs to show voters it won't leave them footing the bill for these new futuristic centres and the cash that comes with them; otherwise, the public will keep getting angrier.

Without a reckoning not just on data centres, but also on migration, the two streams the government is banking on to sustain the economy will become two of the government's biggest liabilities.

Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4 pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

World.title: From career crossroad to grand final, Erasmus 'stoked' he stayed with Dockers
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Nine rounds into the 2025 AFL season, Neil Erasmus was at a career crossroad.

The midfielder had played just 25 games since being drafted ahead of the 2022 season, and struggled to force his way into a stacked Fremantle midfield.

He was behind Caleb Serong, Andrew Brayshaw, Jaeger O'Meara and Nat Fyfe in the pecking order, and was playing a lot for Peel Thunder.

"There was [a chance of me leaving] and a little bit around just wanting a fresh start," Erasmus said.

"There's only so many times you can play sub and come in and out of the team and I was just looking for a bit more continuity.

"The potential for that elsewhere was probably luring me a little bit."

Neil Erasmus played just 39 games in his first four years in the AFL, before becoming a central part of the Dockers side this season. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

The 22-year old found form, and a spot in the Dockers side in the second half of the 2025 season, playing 13 more games including the elimination final loss to Gold Coast.

He ultimately signed a three-year deal with the club though until the end of 2028.

"Having some deep thoughts and conversations towards the back end of last year and playing the last couple of games and finding my feet a little bit, and really just enjoying my time made the decision pretty easy," Erasmus said.

"The club's been amazing and obviously stoked that I did stay in the end."

Grand final bound with mates

The decision to stay couldn't have worked out any better for Erasmus, who has played every game this year for the Dockers, and will run out on the MCG in the club's second-ever grand final.

A childhood West Coast Eagles fan, Erasmus is now all purple.

"To be honest, in my draft year, I probably went to being a bit indifferent," he said.

"A few of my favourite players stopped playing for the West Coast, obviously retired and when you get to be interviewed by so many different clubs you kind of see how they go about it and I really respected the way Freo went about it."

Jye Amiss was selected in the same draft as Neil Erasmus, along with Matthew Johnson. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Along with Erasmus, the Dockers selected Jye Amiss and Matthew Johnson in the 2021 national draft, and then took Karl Worner at the rookie draft.

All four have become key parts of Fremantle's charge to the grand final, though playing alongside Johnson holds a special place.

"I played cricket and footy with him and against him from a really young age. It's pretty cool to be lining up with him," Erasmus said.

The Dockers progressed to the decider with a stirring come-from-behind win over Sydney at the SCG, and the scenes in the rooms after the game drove home the scope of the achievement.

"There was a lot of emotion post-game and almost more around the staff, you just feel so happy for them," Erasmus said.

"They've been working here for a lot longer than me personally and it's just great that they can get a bit of that success."

Erasmus said he was particularly happy for two club stalwarts in Paul Salis and Gary Ingraham.

"They talk about the 2013 flag and that team never used to miss a kick at training, like, all the time," he said.

"They just absolutely love it and it's just so cool to be able to give them the opportunity to get back there."

World.title: The politics of migration hides Australia's real problem
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Everyone now understands that growing the economy only by increasing the number of people, while individuals feel worse off, is a recipe for unhappiness and dissent.

Aggregate growth is a statistic, but individual decline is a vote. The political solution? Fewer people.

That's because those in focus groups and answering polling questions complain about the number of people, who they can see, rather than the reason they are worse off: weak productivity, which they can't see.

As a result, we now have three significant political parties instead of the usual two.

The third newcomer, One Nation, is an anti-immigration party harvesting unhappiness and dissent. The other two have put on some anti-immigration clothes and have got on the grievance catwalk as well.

The starting number for the fashion parade is 300,000, roughly the current level of net overseas migration (NOM). We learnt on Thursday that population growth in the year to March was 392,700, of which 292,100 were migrants.

That is 100,000 a year more than it was between the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) and the COVID pandemic and 200,000 more than in the decades before that. ABS data shows that over the past four years population growth has averaged 400,000 a year or 1,100 a day. The result is a noticeable crowding of the cities and a 23.5 per cent increase the national median house price.

Population growth has produced average annual GDP growth since 2010 of 2.4 per cent, while GDP per capita has grown 0.5 per cent and real disposable income just 0.1 per cent and has often been negative, according to the ABC data.

Three offers to ease migration grievance

Here are the three competing bids for the migration grievance vote:

One Nation : Negative NOM for three years followed by a cap of 130,000 a year.

: Negative NOM for three years followed by a cap of 130,000 a year. The Coalition : 170,000 a year, or roughly the number of houses being built (based on the idea that each migrant needs a house to themselves).

: 170,000 a year, or roughly the number of houses being built (based on the idea that each migrant needs a house to themselves). Labor: 245,000 this financial year and 225,000 in 2027/28.

All agree that we need as much, if not more, skilled migration, preferably from those who can handle a nail gun or a trowel.

That means all three plans impact farmers and universities because the only flexibility available to reduce NOM lies in the unskilled visitors who pick fruit and vegetables. These workers are needed because Australians don't want to do this work. Students who pay higher tertiary education fees are needed because governments have cut university funding.

None of them is what you would call a promise.

One Nation is closest, offering a pledge and a commitment. The Coalition has an elastic target tied to housing. Labor has converted a forecast into a target.

Tony Burke laid out the government's plan to cap migration at the National Press Club last week. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

In a media release to go with his National Press Club speech on Thursday, delayed six weeks while he presumably negotiated with agriculture and education ministers over the impact the changes would have on their constituents, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the plans were "designed to deliver the Net Overseas Migration forecasts in the budget of 245,000 in this financial year and 225,000 in 2027/28".

Treasury must do migration forecasts for the budget every year and they are always wildly wrong because this is the first time the minister in charge of migration has taken any notice of them.

Does Canada have the answer?

Meanwhile two days earlier, in an exquisitely uncomfortable coincidence, the Canada announced a stunning set of policies designed to lift productivity.

It is a year since Canada announced a 23 per cent cut in temporary migration, that is, foreign students and temporary workers from 6.5 to 5 per cent of the population.

Australia's current stock of temporary residents is 10.5 per cent. Cutting that to 5 per cent would involve deporting 1.5 million people.

Maybe in a year's time the Australian government will also address productivity. If so, they could do worse than draw inspiration from Canada.

Should Australia consider the approach of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's government? (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

It's true that Canada is responding to an emergency: the collapse in its relationship with the United States and the imposition of 50 per cent tariff on its exports to the US. Drastic reform is neither optional, nor politically unpopular.

Australia is dealing with an emergency, of a different kind: a rut of low growth and low productivity, with high inflation likely to prompt more interest rate increases starting next week.

This will make life harder for people already in such hardship that they're prepared to try Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce.

Canada has introduced what it calls a "Productivity Mega Deduction" (PM Mark Carney says they already used "super" last year) that expands the number of investments that businesses can fully write off for tax purposes in year one from 15 per cent to 65 per cent.

The qualifying investments include fibre-optic cable and data-network infrastructure, mining property, oil and gas pipelines and production-related capital, software, computer equipment and R&D-related assets, aircraft and vehicles, patents, rail track, bridges and roads and Canadian development expenses.

The Canadian government says this will reduce the overall effective business tax rate on new investment from 13 per cent to 6.4 per cent.

At the same Canada's Carney announced a broader plan to streamline approvals for major projects and supply chains, framed as: "One project. One review. One year."

ABC Business Daily podcast The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news. Analysing the stories moving share markets, shaping industries and affecting the Australian economy.

The government's stated standard is that a project should face one coordinated assessment rather than overlapping federal processes and receive a decision within one year.

It sits alongside the new Build Canada Strong Act and extends the expedited approach beyond the projects already handled through the Major Projects Office.

So the tax package lowers the cost of investing and "one project, one review, one year" is designed to lower the regulatory time and burden and reduce the uncertainty.

The key reason for Australia's low productivity is declining business investment.

Not only could the Albanese government copy Mark Carney's approach, there are many benefits to doing so.

Alan Kohler is a finance presenter and columnist on ABC News. He hosts the podcast That’s Business with Alan Kohler in the ABC Business Daily feed on Friday. He also writes for Intelligent Investor.

World.title: Forget the grand final, this is the hardest week in rugby league
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion Forget the grand final, this is the hardest week in rugby league Roy Masters Sports Columnist September 21, 2026 — 5:22am

September 21, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Preliminary finals are to a grand final what a nervy, fumbling first date is to a comfy, content wedding anniversary. It’s edgy expectation versus partial fulfilment. The penultimate weekend of a season, where four teams fight for the right to advance to the Big Dance, often has players and coaches nervous and uptight. They are aware that a tiny slip-up could end their season days short of what could have been a premiership. Loading Grand final teams tend to be more relaxed, some clubs simply secure at having already achieved their place in history. “Players can lose their edge going from a prelim to the grand final,” says Storm coach Craig Bellamy. Even the most vigilant coach can’t counter the doorman whispering to grand final players before kick-off, “No matter what happens today boys, you have done the club proud.”



It follows that a defeat in the preliminary final can be more devastating than losing a grand final. Bellamy, coach of more preliminary and grand final teams than anyone over the past quarter-century, has been more gutted after losing preliminary finals than I have seen him after narrow defeats in deciders. In 2011, after the Warriors won in Melbourne, he isolated himself from everyone, desperately desolate. His team had been expelled from the previous year’s competition as punishment for salary cap cheating, stripped of all honours and a galaxy of star players. A grand final win would have been redemption for all the world to see. “That was the worst,” admits Bellamy. Melbourne captain Christian Welch with coach Craig Bellamy in 2023 after losing the preliminary final to Penrith. NRL Images Ten years later, a Storm winger dropped the ball with the line wide open, and it was the Panthers who advanced to the grand final against the Rabbitohs. The Panthers were still a little fragile, relying on a Stephen Crichton intercept to launch their dynasty. It denied Bellamy the one prize which eluded him – successive premierships – and he fumed at the front of the bus during the silent journey to the team’s Queensland COVID base where they had been isolated almost all season. As coach of St George in 1984, I felt a one-point loss in the preliminary final more than a one-point loss in the grand final the following year. Lose a grand final, and you can console yourself with having had the experience. Also, the disappointment is ameliorated if your two lower-grade teams win, as the Dragons did in 1985. Lose a preliminary final, and you walk away with nothing. Many a player has declared after losing a preliminary final, “I won’t watch the grand final.”



Yet, paradoxically, the culture both in the NRL and the AFL says there is only one winner in a season. Every team that failed to stand on the dais on grand final day is a loser. So how can losing a prelim be more devastating? It’s the opportunity missed factor, the nagging feeling that if you reached the big day, you would have won. It hurts more when, throughout the season, your team has dominated the team it could have met in the decider. Perhaps coaches feel the loss of preliminary finals more than players. Young players at the top clubs believe they will be back the following year. Many never are. After four straight premierships, Nathan Cleary and the Panthers were hit with preliminary final pain in 2025. Getty Images Melbourne’s Christian Welch won a grand final in 2020; lost grand finals in 2016, 2018 and 2024 and lost preliminary finals in 2021 and 2023. He counts losing grand finals as far more devastating. “Having to stand on the field watching the premiership rings being handed out, you picture yourself in their position on the stage singing the team song,” he says.



“You are so physically close to your lifelong dream but in reality, closer to the boys who won the spoon a month earlier. You can feel the euphoria of the winners; they are 10 metres away from you. A grand final loss is just so much more confronting and visceral, whereas a prelim loss you can justify in your head that you weren’t that close to premiership glory.” One thought I can’t reconcile in my head is how today’s NRL champions don’t display the prime trait of their generation. The social scientists insist the Gen Z population is the most risk-averse generation in history. They fear failure, yet today’s dressing shed disappointment is like non-stick cookware. The Dolphins will ride the emotions of preliminary finals week for the first time. Getty Images Maybe it’s the attack-focused nature of today’s rules that promotes the rocks-and-diamonds players, such as Reece Walsh and Scott Drinkwater. It follows that these preliminary finals may not be the nervous, mistake-dreading encounters they were in the past. Still, the bunker plays to the textbook Gen Z fear. The lottery luck of some of the decisions sees players concede “12-point tries”. That is when a try is denied and the opposition scores immediately afterwards. An NRL official, not authorised to speak publicly, says an incorrect bunker ruling followed by an opposition try occurs far more than is reported.



The psychiatrist’s riddle is relevant to this weekend’s finals in terms of the focus on the Sydney crowd turnout and the number of teams that progressed from week one with zero or minimal recent experience in the play-offs. Is the stadium half full or half empty? Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 The secret to DCE’s 424-game career? A ‘goldfish memory’, Ted Lasso and Dolphin days Will the newcomers be contenders or pretenders? To continue the analogy at the top of this column, will the teams like the Dolphins be nervous first daters or relaxed anniversary celebrants? By contrast, Penrith’s nucleus of playmakers are now in their seventh successive preliminary final. Maybe they will reach the altar a fifth time, but the bunker has a habit of being the disruptive, uninvited guest at a wedding. World.title: ASX eyes losses as oil prices, bond yields weigh on Wall Street
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX eyes losses as oil prices, bond yields weigh on Wall Street Stan Choe September 21, 2026 — 5:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street capped an up -and- down week with a mixed finish for US stock indexes, as elevated bond yields and oil prices weighed on the market. The S&P 500 inched 0.2 per cent higher after drifting between modest gains and losses for much of the day. The benchmark index also posted its second straight weekly loss. Wall Street drifted higher to close an uneven week. AP The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite added 0.4 per cent. The Australian sharemarket is set to slump, with futures on Saturday pointing to a loss of 57 points or 0.7 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.11¢. The majority of stocks on Wall Street fell, and helping to weaken them was rising pressure from the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 5 per cent from 4.94 per cent late Thursday after it topped the 5 per cent level early this week for the first time since 2023.



Higher yields slow the overall economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money, from the US government to people looking to buy houses to businesses wanting to build AI data centres. They also tend to undercut prices for stocks and other investments. Related Article Superannuation Super contributions surge more than a third after budget tax changes Yields have been climbing in a long march since the COVID pandemic knocked them nearly to zero in 2020. The ascent has accelerated recently because inflation has remained stubbornly high for years. Inflation is well above 3 per cent by several measures. It worsened due to higher oil prices caused by the war with Iran. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, got to nearly $US110 early this week, up from a little over $US70 in July. It has been seesawing since.



It briefly dropped below $US102 in overnight trading before erasing much of the loss and settling at $US103.87, down 0.9 per cent from the day before. Rising oil prices have pushed gasoline prices to $US4.47 per gallon, up from $US3.20 per gallon a year ago, according to AAA. That is tightening the squeeze on household budgets. Diesel prices are at a record $US6.45 per gallon and that has a more direct impact on shipping costs for everything from groceries to clothing. High inflation has been raising expenses for everyone, and more companies are giving details about how much. Steel maker Nucor said late Thursday that it expects to report an increase in profit from its steel mills business in the third quarter from the second because it’s able to charge higher prices. But it’s also having to absorb higher costs. It gave a forecast for overall profit in the third quarter that fell short of analysts’ expectations, and its stock sank 6.3 per cent. Berkshire Hathaway edged up 0.1 per cent after famed investor Warren Buffett said he’s giving up his role as chairman of the company. Buffett already gave up his role as CEO of the company, where he built a reputation for buying stocks at relatively cheap prices and being patient with his investments.



Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Why higher interest rates are the new normal Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor Elsewhere on Wall Street, General Motors fell 5.1 per cent and Qualcomm dropped 5.8 per cent. Among stocks that gained ground were Coinbase Global, which climbed 11.7 per cent for the biggest gain among S&P 500 stocks, and Robinhood Markets, which climbed 9.1 per cent. In stock markets abroad, indexes slumped across Europe, including drops of 1.5 per cent for the CAC 40 in Paris and 1.5 per cent for London’s FTSE 100. Wall Street will get a key update this week on the US housing market, along with a regular weekly unemployment update.

World.title: Why higher interest rates are the new normal
World.content:
BusinessBanking & financeInterest rates Opinion Why higher interest rates are the new normal Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor September 21, 2026 — 5:15am

September 21, 2026 — 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Trying to guess where interest rates might move from month to month is a favourite pastime for many people in the financial markets (not to mention finance journalists). And lately, we’ve all had plenty to speculate about. The surging oil price is making our inflation problem worse, prompting markets last week to price in up to three more Reserve Bank interest rate rises, which would push the cash rate above 5 per cent. Mortgage holders hoping for some interest rate relief are going to be disappointed. Peter Rae As dramatic as that would be, however, this column isn’t about what the RBA might do to interest rates this month or at the meeting after that. Rather, it’s about where rates are likely to gravitate in years ahead, and I’m afraid the recent news on that front is not what borrowers want to hear. Economists and market experts lately have predicted rising global interest rates in the long term, and that’s likely to mean we end up with higher rates in Australia.



Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Why the RBA won’t be coming to save the property market Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor The causes are not only increasing inflation but also global “megatrends” as the rise of artificial intelligence, growing geopolitical conflict and decarbonisation. What do these huge societal shifts mean for interest rates? Quite a bit, according to the “neutral interest rate,” an economic concept that’s big in the world of central banking. Raising interest rates is akin to hitting the economic brakes and cutting rates is like stepping on the accelerator, while the neutral rate is just that – one that neither stimulates nor slows the economy.



The dismal science of economics is known for being theoretical, but even here the concept of a neutral rate is fuzzy. It can’t be measured or observed, as with the unemployment rate can, and it changes over time. As fuel costs drive inflation higher, markets are betting on more RBA rate rises. Sitthixay Ditthavong Instead of measuring it, economists attempt to estimate where the neutral rate might be, and then use that in their analysis of whether interest rates should be more expansionary or contractionary. It can get highly technical, but the key point is this: market economists believe the neutral rate has been steadily rising in recent years. Commonwealth Bank’s senior economist Trent Saunders last week said CBA had lifted its estimate of the current neutral rate to 3.85 per cent, up from 3.7 per cent in July and 3.25 per cent last October.



These estimates have risen partly because our economy has been surprisingly resilient – it’s held up better than expected against three rate rises this year, for example. Related Article Federal budget What six failed predictions taught Australia about its future There is a much bigger global story, as estimates of “neutral” interest rates have also risen around the world since the pandemic. This is where the huge trends of our era – such as AI, increased military spending and decarbonisation – come in. Economists say that what ultimately sets global interest rates in the long term is the balance between savings and investment. If you’ve got too much saving for the amount of investment, the returns savers can expect for lending their money will be lower (that is, they’ll have to accept a lower interest rate), and the converse if you have more investment than savings.



From the late 1990s to the early 2020s, there was a long-term decline in global interest rates, and a popular explanation for this was the “savings glut”. This basically said there was too much saving compared to investment opportunities, which drove down global rates. Since the early 2020s, that trend appears to have stopped. There’s now huge demand for savings to finance the massive flows of money into artificial intelligence and data centres, the green energy transition and the lift in defence spending by governments. RBA governor Michele Bullock is desperate to rein in inflation. Louie Douvis “We expect investment demand to remain strong relative to global saving, placing continued upward pressure on neutral rates,” CBA’s Saunders says. Westpac’s chief economist Luci Ellis, who has been talking about a higher “neutral rate” for two years, lists various reasons why we’re not going back to the low-rate world of the 2010s.



There’s been a societal shift toward greater expectation of government intervention in the economy – a trend that was solidified in the pandemic – which has meant higher spending by governments. Raising interest rates is akin to hitting the economic brakes and cutting rates is like stepping on the accelerator, while the neutral rate is just that – one that neither stimulates nor slows the economy. The growing rivalry between the US and China has prompted governments to spend more on defence and on supporting “strategic” industries, such as certain types of manufacturing. The likes of AI and the energy transition are soaking up more private sector investment. Ellis’ view is that we’re not going back to the 2010s world of cheap money because it was an “aberration”. So, that is why economists are convinced that the “neutral interest rate” will be higher than in the past.



What does all this mean for borrowers? Put simply, it means the average level of interest rates in years to come is likely to be higher than it was in the low-interest rate world that preceded the COVID-19 pandemic. There will still be cycles of interest rate moves, meaning the RBA will raise and cut rates in response to shorter-term “cyclical” changes in the economy. The global surge in spending on AI and data centres is hoovering up more savings. iStock But the “structural” or deep-seated trend will be towards higher interest rates than we’ve had in the past.



And when the RBA does eventually cut interest rates in this cycle - a move some expect next year - it won’t need to cut them by very much to take its foot off the brake and move into “neutral territory.” Related Article Analysis

Finance The private credit cockroaches eating our rich-listers In short, even when the RBA is satisfied it has inflation under control, we should not expect rates to come down by much. And unless there’s a crisis, they won’t return to the rock-bottom levels of last decade. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion.
