World.title: Albanese names Murdoch’s former top lieutenant as consul-general in New York
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Albanese names Murdoch’s former top lieutenant as consul-general in New York Rob Harris September 21, 2026 — 5:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has named Siobhan McKenna - the former top lieutenant to Lachlan Murdoch - as Australia’s next consul-general in New York, securing one of the country’s plum diplomatic postings. McKenna, who was named in US court documents this year as the “driving force” behind the plan to reshape Rupert Murdoch’s family trust and cement his eldest son’s control of the News Corp and Fox Corporation empire, will take up the senior diplomatic posting after a career spanning corporate Australia and government boards. Siobhan McKenna, second from left, with (from left) Michelle Gunn, editor-in-chief of The Australian, as well as PM Anthony Albanese and Sky News CEO Paul Whittaker. News Corp Australia The prime minister announced her appointment while launching Australia’s bid for a seat on the United Nation’s security council in New York on Sunday (Monday AEST). She will succeed Heather Ridout, the businesswoman and former chief executive of the Australian Industry Group, whose four-year term expires in December. Albanese, who has maintained a close relationship with the younger Murdoch, defended the appointment as an “outstanding” merit-based choice, after questions from journalists, pointing to McKenna’s experience across the private and public sectors.



“Siobhan McKenna is a professional, and she will do an outstanding job representing Australia and the Australian government here in New York,” Albanese said. “The fact that she has experience in both the private sector and the public sector is a very good thing. I’m someone who supports people being employed on merit.” Australia’s current consul-general in New York Heather Ridout, pictured with actor and art collector Steve Martin, will step down in December. Andrew Kelly Acting as a senior diplomatic official under the ambassador, the consul-general leads Australia’s presence in key international cities by championing local trade and investment while driving bilateral engagement with regional government and business leaders. The position comes with a salary of around $350,000, a substantial entertainment budget as well as an official residence at One Beekman, a pre-war high-rise cooperative apartment building located near the United Nations in the Turtle Bay neighbourhood in New York. Albanese said she would move to the IS with her husband, James Flintoft, a prominent Melbourne board director and former ANZ executive, and their three children.



It is the second time Albanese has appointed the 54-year-old to a public role, having installed her as chair of Australia Post in December 2022, and reappointing her for a second term. She was widely regarded within News Corp as being the “Albo whisperer”, a source with inside knowledge said. McKenna was contacted for comment. The posting marks a significant new chapter for McKenna, who formally cut ties with News Corp in October last year after two decades as one of the most influential figures in Lachlan Murdoch’s Australian business interests. Siobhan McKenna was known inside News Corp as the “Albo whisperer”. Jeff Andersen She became News Corp’s head of broadcasting in 2017, overseeing Foxtel and Sky News Australia and playing a central role in the development of streaming services Kayo Sports and Binge. Her departure followed News Corp’s sale of its controlling stake in Foxtel to global sports streaming company DAZN in a deal that valued the Australian pay-TV business at $3.4 billion. McKenna also worked closely with Lachlan through his private investment company Illyria and Nova Entertainment, and was involved in the bitter succession battle over control of Rupert Murdoch’s global media empire.



She has also served on the boards of Network Ten and Woolworths, chaired the NBN under the former Rudd/Gillard government and served as a commissioner on the Productivity Commission. Related Article Good Weekend ‘Feared, respected and disliked’: The private powerbroker who has Lachlan Murdoch’s ear News Corp chief executive Robert Thomson last year described McKenna as a “transformational force” and said her departure represented a major turning point for the company. But it was revealed in court documents last month she had been “unbelievably candid and, frankly, indiscreet” when she told a friend and business partner of James Murdoch, Lachlan’s younger brother - Jesse Angelo - that Rupert and Lachlan were “dissatisfied” with Thomson’s leadership and were searching for his “elegantly exit stage left”. The Project Family Harmony court battle revealed that McKenna’s influence extended well beyond her formal corporate roles, with the Australian Financial Review last month reporting Lachlan Murdoch had turned to her in 2023 to devise a plan to protect his control of Fox and News Corp after his father Rupert’s death.



In his ruling on the family dispute, Nevada judge Edmund Gorman found McKenna was the “driving force” behind the plot, organising meetings, preparing agendas and liaising with lawyers. She reportedly also prepared talking points for Rupert Murdoch to use in discussions with his children and personally presented the plan to him at Fox’s Los Angeles studios. World.title: On board an epic, 6200-kilometre luxury train through travel’s new frontier
World.content:
InspirationTrain journeys On board an epic, 6200-kilometre luxury train through travel’s new frontier Jenny Hewett September 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I’m sitting on the shores of Lake Issyk Kul in Kyrgyzstan when three men on horseback thunder past with golden eagles flapping atop their raised right arms. The scene is so striking, it could have been painted on silk. Soon after, a furry missile appears on the sand. The shore of Lake Issyk Kul in Kyrgyzstan. iStock “We play football by riding a horse,” says our female Kyrgyz guide, Aisuluu. “But instead of a ball, we are using a dead goat without a head.” I’m among a small group of transfixed spectators to this exclusive private taster of the traditional nomad games of the Kyrgyz people, commonly known as the Olympic Games of Central Asia. The official World Nomad Games festival is held every two years on the shores of the eighth-deepest lake in the world. Kokburu, or horseback polo, is one of the main sports, alongside horseback archery, horseback wrestling and falconry. It’s a remarkably skilful demonstration featuring both men and women, and culminates in a fiery finish for one brave athlete, his fireproof suit set alight as he canters out of sight.



Horses are the main mode of transport in Kyrgyzstan, but I have arrived at this emerging destination in considerable comfort. I’m on a 14-day Republics of the Silk Road rail itinerary to Tashkent, which departs from Almaty in Kazakhstan and takes in four of the five Stans. The journey, with Golden Eagle Luxury Trains, is along the former trade routes of the ancient Silk Road, with visits in Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan. Sadly, Turkmenistan, which is notoriously isolated, has declined visas for Golden Eagle train passengers since 2024. 



Knowledgeable local guides and comfortable buses accompany us at each destination. On-board expert, British journalist Liam Halligan, who lived and worked in Moscow for many years, provides a series of fascinating talks about geopolitics in the region. The luxury train’s viewing car. Luxury train travel is experiencing a resurgence, with a number of operators launching new trains and itineraries in the past few years. And while many of our fellow passengers are much older than me, Littler says there’s been a significant shift in demographic. “When we started out, our average age was about 66. We never had anybody below 40, but now we have travellers in their 20s,” he says. “Slow travel is in vogue and somehow, there seems to be an awful lot more money around for experiential travel,” says Littler. This is one of the world’s more luxurious train journeys, and it comes with plenty of bells and whistles. A resident pianist plays every evening in the bar car, and table settings sparkle with crystal glassware and porcelain tableware.



Meals strike a balance between fussy and rustic: fine dining aboard the train and authentic lunches at local restaurants at most of our stops. One night we’re treated to Russian caviar and vodka tastings, the next we’re rugging up for a barbecue on the train platform. I’m in a Gold Class cabin with an en-suite. While compact, it is comfortable, although once the bunk beds are out, navigating the space with your travelling companion can feel like an awkward first dance. A pianist plays every evening in the bar car. A topic of conversation among the 50 passengers is the temperamental showers, which struggle to get hot throughout the trip. Our Russian attendants Christina and Nikita are pure sunshine, offering tea and coffee every morning, greeting us with a blue carpet (to match the train’s livery) after each stop, and eagerly bridging language barriers via the use of a smartphone. A television in our cabin has an archive of documentaries about the ancient Silk Road and the broader region, which provides additional context to the complex history of this part of the world, including the conquerors that invaded the region, and the roughly 70-year period under Soviet control.



It feels almost surreal to be travelling along this major trading route that began about 2150 years ago and ran from China’s ancient capital of Xi’an to the souks of Istanbul and merchants of Venice. What started out with the trade of silk eventually led to the exchange of ideas, technology and arts that revolutionised Europe. The bathroom in the Han Dynasty Suite on the Golden Eagle Silk Road Express. In Uzbekistan, which we enter multiple times, we tour the souks of Bukhara and the ancient fortified city of Khiva, which served as a significant caravan stop during the time of the Silk Road, and is heaving with tourists. Many of the cities are resplendent with blue and turquoise Persian architecture and tile work dating back to the 14th-century rule of Islamic conqueror Amir Temur. It can be easy to grow weary of the many mosques, mausoleums and minarets. But every now and then, the itinerary throws a curveball to reignite our attention. After rolling past desolate rural villages in Tajikistan, the poorest country in Central Asia, we arrive in the capital Dushanbe and tour the ostentatious Kohi Navruz Palace, whose sole purpose is to chest-thump at visiting heads of state: floral parquetry, a six-tonne Swarovski chandelier and a hall adorned entirely with 15,000 kilograms of precious stones including lapis lazuli. The 16th-century Barakhan Madrasah in Tashkent, Uzbekistan is renowned for its tile-decorated portal and turquoise domes.



Less polarising is the “desert of forbidden art” in the remote Uzbek autonomous region of Karakalpakstan. The world-class Nukus Museum was established by Ukrainian-born painter and archaeologist Igor Savitsky, who smuggled more than 40,000 works deemed anti-Soviet here between the 1920s and 1960s. It houses the biggest collection of Russian and Central Asian art outside of St Petersburg, and is one of the world’s most underrated cultural treasures. Dushanbe, the capital of Tajikistan. iStock Related Article Central Asia Don’t want to rough it? You can now do this intriguing part of Asia in style By the time the train reaches our destination in Tashkent, we’ve travelled 6238 kilometres, and have loaded up on handwoven silk, handmade ceramics and Uzbek robes. For nearly two weeks, we’ve rattled around on this luxurious caravan, exploring one of the world’s most intrepid regions in absolute luxury. I check out of our hotel on wheels, but mentally I’m still sipping champagne in the bar car. THE DETAILS



TRAIN

World.title: The ultimate holiday treat? Two hours away from your kids
World.content:
Reviews & adviceFamily holidays Opinion The ultimate holiday treat? Two hours away from your kids Ben Groundwater Travel writer September 21, 2026 — 5:00am

September 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There’s an immediate, shared understanding as my partner and I lie back on the cabana cushions and breathe out a big sigh. The cocktails haven’t even arrived yet. We haven’t even had a chance to get in the pool. But the holiday – or at least, a few hours of holiday – begins here. Because right now, someone else is looking after our kids. Jean-Michel Cousteau Resort Fiji. Some of you may scoff at this. But then, you’re probably happy to have someone come in and clean your room every day. You have someone else cook your dinner each night. Why not have some assistance with the duty that takes up the bulk of your life, whether on holiday or not? There’s no way you could have convinced me that childcare was an indulgence before I became a parent. Kids club, no kids club – who cares? Your kids will find something to do regardless.



I also didn’t spend a whole lot of time in the sort of places that did have childcare facilities, because I wasn’t in the market. And I didn’t care because when you don’t have kids, you can’t possibly get your head around the all-encompassing nature of looking after children. 



The only person I will take to the toilet in the next two hours will be me. They say there’s no such thing as a holiday when you have young kids – it’s just parenting in a nicer location. Quite often though it’s parenting in a more difficult location, because the hotel doesn’t have comfortable bedding for little kids, or the restaurants don’t have the right food, or a million other things that are easier to manage in your own home. Holidays begin to look more like a challenge than a pleasure. A parent once said to me, “It’s hard work making beautiful memories,” and that is so true that I have repeated it on every trip away with the family since. We will look back on these times with pleasure. But in the moment, we know how hard we’re working just to get through it. Which brings me back to the indulgence of childcare. No visions of champagne breakfasts for this parent. No hot air balloon rides or private jets. Indulgence looks like the sign-in desk at the kids’ club at Elements of Byron resort.



They only do this during school holidays, though fortunately that’s when we’re visiting. So we sign the kids in and they run inside all excited to play with toys and make arts and crafts and meet new friends. Related Article Fiji The one thing that makes Fiji unbeatable for a family holiday We slink off in the direction of the pool, knowing we have a shady cabana bagged and nothing else to do for the next couple of hours but sip pina coladas and maybe even read a few pages of the books that we optimistically decided to bring with us. The mental load diminishes for a few brief moments. The physical effort disappears. No one has made a bum joke in several minutes. This is the stuff holiday dreams are made of, the ultimate indulgence in many ways. We do go on holidays without having someone else around to help with the kids. We travelled to Japan for 10 days and everyone had a ball exploring and eating and gaping at the wonders that country has to offer. Jess and I also worked really hard every day making those beautiful memories happen.



But then we went to Fiji, to Jean-Michel Cousteau Resort, which provides one dedicated nanny per child for your entire holiday, and wow, you have never been so indulged. We went skiing in Falls Creek and the kids attended full-day lessons, which essentially function as a childcare service, and everyone had the best time. Because this is the thing about childcare when it’s done right: the kids have a really good time. They love it. They feel indulged. And we do too. Everyone has a holiday. And then we all get back together at the pool and I resume my scanning for mortal danger.

World.title: It’s the batteries, stupid. Why garbage fires are now an everyday event
World.content:
Exclusive EnvironmentSustainabilityFire It’s the batteries, stupid. Why garbage fires are now an everyday event Caitlin Fitzsimmons September 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Disposable vapes, toys, singing birthday cards and rechargeable tools are among the battery-operated devices causing thousands of fires in waste and recycling centres in a massive and escalating problem across Australia. There are an estimated 10,000 to 12,000 battery-related fires in Australia’s waste and recycling system every year, says ReTHiNK Waste Tasmania, a consumer education initiative between the Tasmanian government and the waste-management sector. Loading Staff often deal with fires, but state fire brigades have been called to hundreds of blazes at waste and recycling facilities across Australia so far this year, including 86 in NSW alone, and batteries were often suspected to be the cause. Fire Rescue Victoria said it was called to fires involving a lithium-ion battery daily across all settings and that it was a growing problem in waste management, but it was unable to provide exact figures. The fires are a safety risk for staff in the waste and recycling sector, a crippling financial burden for companies that can no longer buy insurance to protect assets, and an environmental problem because of toxic air pollution and the setback to recycling efforts.



NSW Fire and Rescue Commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell said the distinguishing feature of a battery fire was how quickly they started because of the volume of energy stored in the battery cell. “One minute, it’ll be sitting there looking very benign,” Fewtrell said. “A second or two later, it’s a very intense fire, often spitting embers and pieces of battery out, which can also spread the fire into other parts of the rubbish or the recycling pile.” Joshua Fischer, of Fire Rescue Victoria, is concerned by a rise in battery fires in garbage trucks. Chris Hopkins Fire Rescue Victoria Deputy Commissioner Joshua Fischer said the fires posed significant safety risks, and also serious environmental harms because “fires can release toxic pollutants and harmful contaminants into the air, soil and waterways”. Fire and Rescue NSW reported 86 fires at waste and recycling centres between January 1 and September 14 this year, compared with 114 for the whole of 2025. There were also 44 fires in garbage trucks so far this year, compared with 62 for the whole of last year, and the vast majority started in the garbage compactor or load-carrying compartment of the truck.



“When I was a firefighter and on the trucks [before 2011], it was very, very seldom that you would be going to a garbage truck fire, and now they’re much more prevalent,” Fewtrell said. “A large part of that is, we believe, due to lithium-ion batteries being included in the waste or the recycling streams.” Lithium-ion batteries are highly combustible under heat or pressure, while standard household batteries such as AA can also cause fires but are less volatile. West Australian Department of Fire and Emergency Services Deputy Commissioner Jon Broomhall said lithium-ion batteries that were damaged, crushed or overheated could trigger “thermal runaway” – a chain reaction in which batteries produce intense heat and release flammable gases, leading to ignition. “The conditions inside rubbish trucks or waste facilities are especially conducive for battery ignition as items are often compacted and crushed,” Broomhall said. In January 2025, Veolia’s waste-sorting centre in Cairns was destroyed by fire, thought to be caused by a lithium-ion battery, resulting in material having to be diverted to landfill. Veolia also had a facility in NSW offline for several months because of roof damage. The company has shared footage from its security cameras showing six fires in two months at one recycling plant – the Bibra Lake Materials Recovery Facility in Western Australia – in a bid to raise awareness of the problem.



Visy chief executive Mark De Wit said companies had to invest in cameras that were always manned, infrared guns to monitor heat, water cannons and fire extinguishers. The fires were particularly hard to extinguish in a recycling centre full of plastic, which was oil-based, or cardboard, he said. “We had [a fire] yesterday, we had one the day before, it’s almost a daily event and it’s always a battery,” De Wit said, when asked about the issue at the Visy Recycling Roundtable. “It is completely company-agnostic. Visy’s lost a site in the last five years. Re.Group has lost a recycling site in the last five years. Cleanaway has lost a site in the last five years. Most recycling facilities can’t get insurance any more because of the fires.” Related Article Renewables ‘Moving at light speed’: Plug-in solar and batteries are coming to Australia Cleanaway confirmed this; Re.Group was contacted for comment. Veolia chief operating officer Carmen Loecherer said the fires were a daily occurrence and that she was worried about staff safety. She knew that batteries were the culprit because video footage often showed a battery igniting, or employees had found a battery in an audit.



“In particular when there are fires in vehicles that transport waste, we pull it out and we try and find the culprit,” Loecherer said. “Usually, it’s still smouldering when we put it out, and 99 per cent of the time it’s a battery.” Both Veolia and Visy said products with embedded batteries such as disposable vapes and birthday cards, and rechargeable hardware tools or toys, were the biggest problems. The companies called for other states to copy the NSW product stewardship scheme that forced manufacturers to fund more collection points and consumer education. However, illegal vapes sit outside that system because the producer is not always identifiable. In WA, the Department of Fire and Emergency Services reported 40 fires at waste-disposal facilities across the state between January 1 and June 30, with seven proven to be caused by batteries. That compared with 70 fires over 2025, with eight proven to be caused by batteries. The department said the true number of battery fires would be higher because it was often difficult to prove the cause. World.title: ‘We have the brotherhood to offer you’: Inside the push to keep boys away from crime
World.content:
Men and boys pray at United Muslims of Australia’s western Sydney headquarters, where youth programs are designed to give boys a sense of belonging.

On a Friday night, children race their friends to the fun and games. But beyond the play, there is work to be done in a community battling fear, anxiety and stereotypes.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As the time ticks towards 7.30pm on a Friday, the bustle of young boys running through the corridor quietens to a hush; dozens of men and children trickle into the prayer room of United Muslims of Australia’s sprawling western Sydney headquarters as the evening worship begins. For 10 minutes, only the rhythm of Isha – the night’s final prayer – can be heard. As quickly as it subsides, though, the racket of the boys’ excitement returns. With their praying done, they rush out of the room, shove itchy feet into shoes, and race away into the maze of the centre; some make for the gaming consoles, while others – in the football jerseys of their sporting idols – are already halfway to the hardwood of the indoor futsal court. An evening at United Muslims of Australia youth centre in Padstow. James Brickwood Youth play computer games, handball and futsal in the basement of the centre after prayers. James Brickwood While the games serve as an incentive for the boys to gather with their peers in the Muslim community, football is just one of many items on the agenda this Friday night. Inside these walls, there is important work to be done. Hundreds of boys and girls – aged nine to 15 – flock to the Padstow centre each Friday for youth programs offering guidance for those at risk of wandering to the wrong side of the tracks, teaching them about Islam, and instilling a sense of pride in young Muslims struggling with identity in a politically charged Australia. “We want our children to be proud Muslims without compromising their faith,” says UMA founder Sheikh Shadi Alsuleiman. “I want them to be proud Australians that contribute back to their community.” Alsuleiman welcomes this masthead to the centre at a time when the question of how to keep young boys – especially those in western Sydney – off the streets and away from organised crime is at the centre of a growing challenge for community leaders and authorities trying to combat the rise of criminal networks recruiting impressionable children.



In the past 18 months, police have charged hundreds of teenage boys, some of them from Muslim families, over their involvement in Sydney’s escalating gangland conflicts. The recruitment of children, some as young as 14, to carry out targeted attacks has become a hallmark of recent underworld violence and one of the most challenging aspects of policing feuds between rival criminal groups. Last Wednesday, homicide squad detectives arrested and charged two boys, aged 14 and 16, over the mistaken-identity killing of 23-year-old university student Marco Tapia, who was shot dead lying in his bed. This month, NSW Premier Chris Minns announced proposed legislative changes designed to deter children from working for organised crime networks. Under a proposed expansion to the serious children’s indictable offences scheme, children charged with offences linked to organised crime, including those related to public shootings and firebombings, would be tried as adults in the state’s District Court and Supreme Court, where they would face longer prison terms than if they were prosecuted as juveniles. At UMA, the centre’s youth programs are designed to not only teach boys about their faith, but give them the sense of belonging many their age seek in criminal gangs. “You’ve kind of got to ask yourself what those boys are finding in those gangs,” says Zaid Omran, UMA’s youth co-ordinator. “They’re finding brotherhood, they’re finding identity, they’re finding social insurance, they’re finding a home away from home, they’re finding … people who see them, people who hear them, people who value them.” The acceptance that young boys may feel within a gang is short-lived, unsustainable and fake, says Zaid Omran, UMA’s youth co-ordinator. James Brickwood Omran says young boys’ energy can be redirected into positive action with the right guidance. James Brickwood



The key to keeping Muslim boys on the right path is offering comforts grounded in faith and community rather than crime, Omran says. “If you can win a young person’s heart, then you have the ability to redirect whatever energy he has into something productive, into being a positive impact on the rest of society,” he says. “The ability for you to hold someone’s hand from as young as nine years old, if you have the steadfastness, if you have the fortitude to follow through and stay holding that person’s hand from as young as nine, from such a young age, then you’re decreasing the possibility of that person ever even coming close to all of that stuff.” Omran says the acceptance young boys may feel within a gang is short-lived, unsustainable and fake. The second they are no longer useful to those in charge, the boys are turfed. “That’s very, very powerful, for a young person to be seen – in every sense of that word – for them to feel heard,” he says. “We have the brotherhood to offer you.” Community leaders are also facing the challenge of organised crime and criminal gangs being glorified on social media, says Ibrahim Kayellou, 26, a youth mentor at the centre. Keeping boys away from content that could set them on a path to crime has become as much a priority for youth program leaders as teaching Islamic values. “It’s hard for the parents to keep up with it,” Kayellou says. Outside the centre’s walls, Muslims face rising Islamophobia and negative stereotypes that threaten boys’ sense of identity and instil a sense of fear and anxiety within the community, Alsuleiman says. “Islamophobia’s becoming the norm,” he says. “It’s been accepted to insult Muslims, to speak against Muslims, to demonise Muslims, to vilify Muslims, and it is a huge concern across the board with the Muslim community.” Sheikh Shadi Alsuleiman arriving at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, where he said instances of Islamophobia had increased by 600 per cent since 2022. Kate Geraghty Alsuleiman says there is a sense of anxiety and fear within the Muslim community. James Brickwood



Alsuleiman, who is also the Australian National Imams Council president, has been a vocal critic of the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza. He has also attracted criticism for public comments on homosexuality. “I have previously noted passages in the holy Quran which do not support homosexuality,” Alsuleiman said in a statement to this masthead in 2016. “However, I always follow such statements with a personal commitment to tolerance and encouragement that all Muslims and all people approach all individuals, no matter their faith, race or sexuality, in a considerate and respectful way.” Now, Alsuleiman says many of the Muslim community’s most vulnerable members – women and children – feel unsafe. The bollards blocking the centre’s front door are not for decoration, he points out, adding that there is a strong sense within the community that an attack on Muslims like the Christchurch massacre in 2019 may be repeated. “It’s not about if, it’s about when,” he says. “There’s a very strong sense of anxiety in the community and fear.” Related Article Updated

Organised crime Child recruits to be tried as adults amid Sydney gangland crackdown Some community members are so concerned about their safety that they are scared to walk on the street or commute to work. Coupled with what Alsuleiman says are harmful anti-Muslim rhetoric and narratives being pushed by prominent right-wing political parties, tensions between his community and others have become inflamed. Last month, he told the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion that recorded instances of Islamophobia had increased by more than 600 per cent since 2022. “The Muslim community feels the collective blame for the actions of others, especially post-Bondi,” Alsuleiman says. “The community feels that it is a target.”

World.title: Forget the grand final, this is the hardest week in rugby league
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Opinion Forget the grand final, this is the hardest week in rugby league Roy Masters Sports Columnist September 21, 2026 — 5:22am

September 21, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Preliminary finals are to a grand final what a nervy, fumbling first date is to a comfy, content wedding anniversary. It’s edgy expectation versus partial fulfilment. The penultimate weekend of a season, where four teams fight for the right to advance to the Big Dance, often has players and coaches nervous and uptight. They are aware that a tiny slip-up could end their season days short of what could have been a premiership. Loading Grand final teams tend to be more relaxed, some clubs simply secure at having already achieved their place in history. “Players can lose their edge going from a prelim to the grand final,” says Storm coach Craig Bellamy. Even the most vigilant coach can’t counter the doorman whispering to grand final players before kick-off, “No matter what happens today boys, you have done the club proud.”



It follows that a defeat in the preliminary final can be more devastating than losing a grand final. Bellamy, coach of more preliminary and grand final teams than anyone over the past quarter-century, has been more gutted after losing preliminary finals than I have seen him after narrow defeats in deciders. In 2011, after the Warriors won in Melbourne, he isolated himself from everyone, desperately desolate. His team had been expelled from the previous year’s competition as punishment for salary cap cheating, stripped of all honours and a galaxy of star players. A grand final win would have been redemption for all the world to see. “That was the worst,” admits Bellamy. Melbourne captain Christian Welch with coach Craig Bellamy in 2023 after losing the preliminary final to Penrith. NRL Images Ten years later, a Storm winger dropped the ball with the line wide open, and it was the Panthers who advanced to the grand final against the Rabbitohs. The Panthers were still a little fragile, relying on a Stephen Crichton intercept to launch their dynasty. It denied Bellamy the one prize which eluded him – successive premierships – and he fumed at the front of the bus during the silent journey to the team’s Queensland COVID base where they had been isolated almost all season. As coach of St George in 1984, I felt a one-point loss in the preliminary final more than a one-point loss in the grand final the following year. Lose a grand final, and you can console yourself with having had the experience. Also, the disappointment is ameliorated if your two lower-grade teams win, as the Dragons did in 1985. Lose a preliminary final, and you walk away with nothing. Many a player has declared after losing a preliminary final, “I won’t watch the grand final.”



Yet, paradoxically, the culture both in the NRL and the AFL says there is only one winner in a season. Every team that failed to stand on the dais on grand final day is a loser. So how can losing a prelim be more devastating? It’s the opportunity missed factor, the nagging feeling that if you reached the big day, you would have won. It hurts more when, throughout the season, your team has dominated the team it could have met in the decider. Perhaps coaches feel the loss of preliminary finals more than players. Young players at the top clubs believe they will be back the following year. Many never are. After four straight premierships, Nathan Cleary and the Panthers were hit with preliminary final pain in 2025. Getty Images Melbourne’s Christian Welch won a grand final in 2020; lost grand finals in 2016, 2018 and 2024 and lost preliminary finals in 2021 and 2023. He counts losing grand finals as far more devastating. “Having to stand on the field watching the premiership rings being handed out, you picture yourself in their position on the stage singing the team song,” he says.



“You are so physically close to your lifelong dream but in reality, closer to the boys who won the spoon a month earlier. You can feel the euphoria of the winners; they are 10 metres away from you. A grand final loss is just so much more confronting and visceral, whereas a prelim loss you can justify in your head that you weren’t that close to premiership glory.” One thought I can’t reconcile in my head is how today’s NRL champions don’t display the prime trait of their generation. The social scientists insist the Gen Z population is the most risk-averse generation in history. They fear failure, yet today’s dressing shed disappointment is like non-stick cookware. The Dolphins will ride the emotions of preliminary finals week for the first time. Getty Images Maybe it’s the attack-focused nature of today’s rules that promotes the rocks-and-diamonds players, such as Reece Walsh and Scott Drinkwater. It follows that these preliminary finals may not be the nervous, mistake-dreading encounters they were in the past. Still, the bunker plays to the textbook Gen Z fear. The lottery luck of some of the decisions sees players concede “12-point tries”. That is when a try is denied and the opposition scores immediately afterwards. An NRL official, not authorised to speak publicly, says an incorrect bunker ruling followed by an opposition try occurs far more than is reported.



The psychiatrist’s riddle is relevant to this weekend’s finals in terms of the focus on the Sydney crowd turnout and the number of teams that progressed from week one with zero or minimal recent experience in the play-offs. Is the stadium half full or half empty? Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 The secret to DCE’s 424-game career? A ‘goldfish memory’, Ted Lasso and Dolphin days Will the newcomers be contenders or pretenders? To continue the analogy at the top of this column, will the teams like the Dolphins be nervous first daters or relaxed anniversary celebrants? By contrast, Penrith’s nucleus of playmakers are now in their seventh successive preliminary final. Maybe they will reach the altar a fifth time, but the bunker has a habit of being the disruptive, uninvited guest at a wedding. World.title: ASX eyes losses as oil prices, bond yields weigh on Wall Street
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX eyes losses as oil prices, bond yields weigh on Wall Street Stan Choe September 21, 2026 — 5:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street capped an up -and- down week with a mixed finish for US stock indexes, as elevated bond yields and oil prices weighed on the market. The S&P 500 inched 0.2 per cent higher after drifting between modest gains and losses for much of the day. The benchmark index also posted its second straight weekly loss. Wall Street drifted higher to close an uneven week. AP The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite added 0.4 per cent. The Australian sharemarket is set to slump, with futures on Saturday pointing to a loss of 57 points or 0.7 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.11¢. The majority of stocks on Wall Street fell, and helping to weaken them was rising pressure from the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed to 5 per cent from 4.94 per cent late Thursday after it topped the 5 per cent level early this week for the first time since 2023.



Higher yields slow the overall economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money, from the US government to people looking to buy houses to businesses wanting to build AI data centres. They also tend to undercut prices for stocks and other investments. Related Article Superannuation Super contributions surge more than a third after budget tax changes Yields have been climbing in a long march since the COVID pandemic knocked them nearly to zero in 2020. The ascent has accelerated recently because inflation has remained stubbornly high for years. Inflation is well above 3 per cent by several measures. It worsened due to higher oil prices caused by the war with Iran. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, got to nearly $US110 early this week, up from a little over $US70 in July. It has been seesawing since.



It briefly dropped below $US102 in overnight trading before erasing much of the loss and settling at $US103.87, down 0.9 per cent from the day before. Rising oil prices have pushed gasoline prices to $US4.47 per gallon, up from $US3.20 per gallon a year ago, according to AAA. That is tightening the squeeze on household budgets. Diesel prices are at a record $US6.45 per gallon and that has a more direct impact on shipping costs for everything from groceries to clothing. High inflation has been raising expenses for everyone, and more companies are giving details about how much. Steel maker Nucor said late Thursday that it expects to report an increase in profit from its steel mills business in the third quarter from the second because it’s able to charge higher prices. But it’s also having to absorb higher costs. It gave a forecast for overall profit in the third quarter that fell short of analysts’ expectations, and its stock sank 6.3 per cent. Berkshire Hathaway edged up 0.1 per cent after famed investor Warren Buffett said he’s giving up his role as chairman of the company. Buffett already gave up his role as CEO of the company, where he built a reputation for buying stocks at relatively cheap prices and being patient with his investments.



Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Why higher interest rates are the new normal Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor Elsewhere on Wall Street, General Motors fell 5.1 per cent and Qualcomm dropped 5.8 per cent. Among stocks that gained ground were Coinbase Global, which climbed 11.7 per cent for the biggest gain among S&P 500 stocks, and Robinhood Markets, which climbed 9.1 per cent. In stock markets abroad, indexes slumped across Europe, including drops of 1.5 per cent for the CAC 40 in Paris and 1.5 per cent for London’s FTSE 100. Wall Street will get a key update this week on the US housing market, along with a regular weekly unemployment update.

World.title: Why higher interest rates are the new normal
World.content:
BusinessBanking & financeInterest rates Opinion Why higher interest rates are the new normal Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor September 21, 2026 — 5:15am

September 21, 2026 — 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Trying to guess where interest rates might move from month to month is a favourite pastime for many people in the financial markets (not to mention finance journalists). And lately, we’ve all had plenty to speculate about. The surging oil price is making our inflation problem worse, prompting markets last week to price in up to three more Reserve Bank interest rate rises, which would push the cash rate above 5 per cent. Mortgage holders hoping for some interest rate relief are going to be disappointed. Peter Rae As dramatic as that would be, however, this column isn’t about what the RBA might do to interest rates this month or at the meeting after that. Rather, it’s about where rates are likely to gravitate in years ahead, and I’m afraid the recent news on that front is not what borrowers want to hear. Economists and market experts lately have predicted rising global interest rates in the long term, and that’s likely to mean we end up with higher rates in Australia.



Related Article Opinion

Interest rates Why the RBA won’t be coming to save the property market Clancy Yeates Deputy business editor The causes are not only increasing inflation but also global “megatrends” as the rise of artificial intelligence, growing geopolitical conflict and decarbonisation. What do these huge societal shifts mean for interest rates? Quite a bit, according to the “neutral interest rate,” an economic concept that’s big in the world of central banking. Raising interest rates is akin to hitting the economic brakes and cutting rates is like stepping on the accelerator, while the neutral rate is just that – one that neither stimulates nor slows the economy.



The dismal science of economics is known for being theoretical, but even here the concept of a neutral rate is fuzzy. It can’t be measured or observed, as with the unemployment rate can, and it changes over time. As fuel costs drive inflation higher, markets are betting on more RBA rate rises. Sitthixay Ditthavong Instead of measuring it, economists attempt to estimate where the neutral rate might be, and then use that in their analysis of whether interest rates should be more expansionary or contractionary. It can get highly technical, but the key point is this: market economists believe the neutral rate has been steadily rising in recent years. Commonwealth Bank’s senior economist Trent Saunders last week said CBA had lifted its estimate of the current neutral rate to 3.85 per cent, up from 3.7 per cent in July and 3.25 per cent last October.



These estimates have risen partly because our economy has been surprisingly resilient – it’s held up better than expected against three rate rises this year, for example. Related Article Federal budget What six failed predictions taught Australia about its future There is a much bigger global story, as estimates of “neutral” interest rates have also risen around the world since the pandemic. This is where the huge trends of our era – such as AI, increased military spending and decarbonisation – come in. Economists say that what ultimately sets global interest rates in the long term is the balance between savings and investment. If you’ve got too much saving for the amount of investment, the returns savers can expect for lending their money will be lower (that is, they’ll have to accept a lower interest rate), and the converse if you have more investment than savings.



From the late 1990s to the early 2020s, there was a long-term decline in global interest rates, and a popular explanation for this was the “savings glut”. This basically said there was too much saving compared to investment opportunities, which drove down global rates. Since the early 2020s, that trend appears to have stopped. There’s now huge demand for savings to finance the massive flows of money into artificial intelligence and data centres, the green energy transition and the lift in defence spending by governments. RBA governor Michele Bullock is desperate to rein in inflation. Louie Douvis “We expect investment demand to remain strong relative to global saving, placing continued upward pressure on neutral rates,” CBA’s Saunders says. Westpac’s chief economist Luci Ellis, who has been talking about a higher “neutral rate” for two years, lists various reasons why we’re not going back to the low-rate world of the 2010s.



There’s been a societal shift toward greater expectation of government intervention in the economy – a trend that was solidified in the pandemic – which has meant higher spending by governments. Raising interest rates is akin to hitting the economic brakes and cutting rates is like stepping on the accelerator, while the neutral rate is just that – one that neither stimulates nor slows the economy. The growing rivalry between the US and China has prompted governments to spend more on defence and on supporting “strategic” industries, such as certain types of manufacturing. The likes of AI and the energy transition are soaking up more private sector investment. Ellis’ view is that we’re not going back to the 2010s world of cheap money because it was an “aberration”. So, that is why economists are convinced that the “neutral interest rate” will be higher than in the past.



What does all this mean for borrowers? Put simply, it means the average level of interest rates in years to come is likely to be higher than it was in the low-interest rate world that preceded the COVID-19 pandemic. There will still be cycles of interest rate moves, meaning the RBA will raise and cut rates in response to shorter-term “cyclical” changes in the economy. The global surge in spending on AI and data centres is hoovering up more savings. iStock But the “structural” or deep-seated trend will be towards higher interest rates than we’ve had in the past.



And when the RBA does eventually cut interest rates in this cycle - a move some expect next year - it won’t need to cut them by very much to take its foot off the brake and move into “neutral territory.” Related Article Analysis

Finance The private credit cockroaches eating our rich-listers In short, even when the RBA is satisfied it has inflation under control, we should not expect rates to come down by much. And unless there’s a crisis, they won’t return to the rock-bottom levels of last decade. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Albanese names Murdoch’s former top lieutenant as consul-general in New York
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Albanese names Murdoch’s former top lieutenant as consul-general in New York Rob Harris September 21, 2026 — 5:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has named Siobhan McKenna - the former top lieutenant to Lachlan Murdoch - as Australia’s next consul-general in New York, securing one of the country’s plum diplomatic postings. McKenna, who was named in US court documents this year as the “driving force” behind the plan to reshape Rupert Murdoch’s family trust and cement his eldest son’s control of the News Corp and Fox Corporation empire, will take up the senior diplomatic posting after a career spanning corporate Australia and government boards. Siobhan McKenna, second from left, with (from left) Michelle Gunn, editor-in-chief of The Australian, as well as PM Anthony Albanese and Sky News CEO Paul Whittaker. News Corp Australia The prime minister announced her appointment while launching Australia’s bid for a seat on the United Nation’s security council in New York on Sunday (Monday AEST). She will succeed Heather Ridout, the businesswoman and former chief executive of the Australian Industry Group, whose four-year term expires in December. Albanese, who has maintained a close relationship with the younger Murdoch, defended the appointment as an “outstanding” merit-based choice, after questions from journalists, pointing to McKenna’s experience across the private and public sectors.



“Siobhan McKenna is a professional, and she will do an outstanding job representing Australia and the Australian government here in New York,” Albanese said. “The fact that she has experience in both the private sector and the public sector is a very good thing. I’m someone who supports people being employed on merit.” Australia’s current consul-general in New York Heather Ridout, pictured with actor and art collector Steve Martin, will step down in December. Andrew Kelly Acting as a senior diplomatic official under the ambassador, the consul-general leads Australia’s presence in key international cities by championing local trade and investment while driving bilateral engagement with regional government and business leaders. The position comes with a salary of around $350,000, a substantial entertainment budget as well as an official residence at One Beekman, a pre-war high-rise cooperative apartment building located near the United Nations in the Turtle Bay neighbourhood in New York. Albanese said she would move to the IS with her husband, James Flintoft, a prominent Melbourne board director and former ANZ executive, and their three children.



It is the second time Albanese has appointed the 54-year-old to a public role, having installed her as chair of Australia Post in December 2022, and reappointing her for a second term. She was widely regarded within News Corp as being the “Albo whisperer”, a source with inside knowledge said. McKenna was contacted for comment. The posting marks a significant new chapter for McKenna, who formally cut ties with News Corp in October last year after two decades as one of the most influential figures in Lachlan Murdoch’s Australian business interests. Siobhan McKenna was known inside News Corp as the “Albo whisperer”. Jeff Andersen She became News Corp’s head of broadcasting in 2017, overseeing Foxtel and Sky News Australia and playing a central role in the development of streaming services Kayo Sports and Binge. Her departure followed News Corp’s sale of its controlling stake in Foxtel to global sports streaming company DAZN in a deal that valued the Australian pay-TV business at $3.4 billion. McKenna also worked closely with Lachlan through his private investment company Illyria and Nova Entertainment, and was involved in the bitter succession battle over control of Rupert Murdoch’s global media empire.



She has also served on the boards of Network Ten and Woolworths, chaired the NBN under the former Rudd/Gillard government and served as a commissioner on the Productivity Commission. Related Article Good Weekend ‘Feared, respected and disliked’: The private powerbroker who has Lachlan Murdoch’s ear News Corp chief executive Robert Thomson last year described McKenna as a “transformational force” and said her departure represented a major turning point for the company. But it was revealed in court documents last month she had been “unbelievably candid and, frankly, indiscreet” when she told a friend and business partner of James Murdoch, Lachlan’s younger brother - Jesse Angelo - that Rupert and Lachlan were “dissatisfied” with Thomson’s leadership and were searching for his “elegantly exit stage left”. The Project Family Harmony court battle revealed that McKenna’s influence extended well beyond her formal corporate roles, with the Australian Financial Review last month reporting Lachlan Murdoch had turned to her in 2023 to devise a plan to protect his control of Fox and News Corp after his father Rupert’s death.



In his ruling on the family dispute, Nevada judge Edmund Gorman found McKenna was the “driving force” behind the plot, organising meetings, preparing agendas and liaising with lawyers. She reportedly also prepared talking points for Rupert Murdoch to use in discussions with his children and personally presented the plan to him at Fox’s Los Angeles studios. World.title: On board an epic, 6200-kilometre luxury train through travel’s new frontier
World.content:
InspirationTrain journeys On board an epic, 6200-kilometre luxury train through travel’s new frontier Jenny Hewett September 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I’m sitting on the shores of Lake Issyk Kul in Kyrgyzstan when three men on horseback thunder past with golden eagles flapping atop their raised right arms. The scene is so striking, it could have been painted on silk. Soon after, a furry missile appears on the sand. The shore of Lake Issyk Kul in Kyrgyzstan. iStock “We play football by riding a horse,” says our female Kyrgyz guide, Aisuluu. “But instead of a ball, we are using a dead goat without a head.” I’m among a small group of transfixed spectators to this exclusive private taster of the traditional nomad games of the Kyrgyz people, commonly known as the Olympic Games of Central Asia. The official World Nomad Games festival is held every two years on the shores of the eighth-deepest lake in the world. Kokburu, or horseback polo, is one of the main sports, alongside horseback archery, horseback wrestling and falconry. It’s a remarkably skilful demonstration featuring both men and women, and culminates in a fiery finish for one brave athlete, his fireproof suit set alight as he canters out of sight.



Horses are the main mode of transport in Kyrgyzstan, but I have arrived at this emerging destination in considerable comfort. I’m on a 14-day Republics of the Silk Road rail itinerary to Tashkent, which departs from Almaty in Kazakhstan and takes in four of the five Stans. The journey, with Golden Eagle Luxury Trains, is along the former trade routes of the ancient Silk Road, with visits in Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan. Sadly, Turkmenistan, which is notoriously isolated, has declined visas for Golden Eagle train passengers since 2024. 



Knowledgeable local guides and comfortable buses accompany us at each destination. On-board expert, British journalist Liam Halligan, who lived and worked in Moscow for many years, provides a series of fascinating talks about geopolitics in the region. The luxury train’s viewing car. Luxury train travel is experiencing a resurgence, with a number of operators launching new trains and itineraries in the past few years. And while many of our fellow passengers are much older than me, Littler says there’s been a significant shift in demographic. “When we started out, our average age was about 66. We never had anybody below 40, but now we have travellers in their 20s,” he says. “Slow travel is in vogue and somehow, there seems to be an awful lot more money around for experiential travel,” says Littler. This is one of the world’s more luxurious train journeys, and it comes with plenty of bells and whistles. A resident pianist plays every evening in the bar car, and table settings sparkle with crystal glassware and porcelain tableware.



Meals strike a balance between fussy and rustic: fine dining aboard the train and authentic lunches at local restaurants at most of our stops. One night we’re treated to Russian caviar and vodka tastings, the next we’re rugging up for a barbecue on the train platform. I’m in a Gold Class cabin with an en-suite. While compact, it is comfortable, although once the bunk beds are out, navigating the space with your travelling companion can feel like an awkward first dance. A pianist plays every evening in the bar car. A topic of conversation among the 50 passengers is the temperamental showers, which struggle to get hot throughout the trip. Our Russian attendants Christina and Nikita are pure sunshine, offering tea and coffee every morning, greeting us with a blue carpet (to match the train’s livery) after each stop, and eagerly bridging language barriers via the use of a smartphone. A television in our cabin has an archive of documentaries about the ancient Silk Road and the broader region, which provides additional context to the complex history of this part of the world, including the conquerors that invaded the region, and the roughly 70-year period under Soviet control.



It feels almost surreal to be travelling along this major trading route that began about 2150 years ago and ran from China’s ancient capital of Xi’an to the souks of Istanbul and merchants of Venice. What started out with the trade of silk eventually led to the exchange of ideas, technology and arts that revolutionised Europe. The bathroom in the Han Dynasty Suite on the Golden Eagle Silk Road Express. In Uzbekistan, which we enter multiple times, we tour the souks of Bukhara and the ancient fortified city of Khiva, which served as a significant caravan stop during the time of the Silk Road, and is heaving with tourists. Many of the cities are resplendent with blue and turquoise Persian architecture and tile work dating back to the 14th-century rule of Islamic conqueror Amir Temur. It can be easy to grow weary of the many mosques, mausoleums and minarets. But every now and then, the itinerary throws a curveball to reignite our attention. After rolling past desolate rural villages in Tajikistan, the poorest country in Central Asia, we arrive in the capital Dushanbe and tour the ostentatious Kohi Navruz Palace, whose sole purpose is to chest-thump at visiting heads of state: floral parquetry, a six-tonne Swarovski chandelier and a hall adorned entirely with 15,000 kilograms of precious stones including lapis lazuli. The 16th-century Barakhan Madrasah in Tashkent, Uzbekistan is renowned for its tile-decorated portal and turquoise domes.



Less polarising is the “desert of forbidden art” in the remote Uzbek autonomous region of Karakalpakstan. The world-class Nukus Museum was established by Ukrainian-born painter and archaeologist Igor Savitsky, who smuggled more than 40,000 works deemed anti-Soviet here between the 1920s and 1960s. It houses the biggest collection of Russian and Central Asian art outside of St Petersburg, and is one of the world’s most underrated cultural treasures. Dushanbe, the capital of Tajikistan. iStock Related Article Central Asia Don’t want to rough it? You can now do this intriguing part of Asia in style By the time the train reaches our destination in Tashkent, we’ve travelled 6238 kilometres, and have loaded up on handwoven silk, handmade ceramics and Uzbek robes. For nearly two weeks, we’ve rattled around on this luxurious caravan, exploring one of the world’s most intrepid regions in absolute luxury. I check out of our hotel on wheels, but mentally I’m still sipping champagne in the bar car. THE DETAILS



TRAIN

Golden Eagle Luxury Trains offers its 14-day Republics of the Silk Road itinerary through the five Stans in April and September, from $US26,900 ($37,796) a person twin share for a Silver Class cabin. See goldeneagleluxurytrains.com The writer travelled as a guest of Golden Eagle Luxury Trains.

World.title: The ultimate holiday treat? Two hours away from your kids
World.content:
Reviews & adviceFamily holidays Opinion The ultimate holiday treat? Two hours away from your kids Ben Groundwater Travel writer September 21, 2026 — 5:00am

September 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There’s an immediate, shared understanding as my partner and I lie back on the cabana cushions and breathe out a big sigh. The cocktails haven’t even arrived yet. We haven’t even had a chance to get in the pool. But the holiday – or at least, a few hours of holiday – begins here. Because right now, someone else is looking after our kids. Jean-Michel Cousteau Resort Fiji. Some of you may scoff at this. But then, you’re probably happy to have someone come in and clean your room every day. You have someone else cook your dinner each night. Why not have some assistance with the duty that takes up the bulk of your life, whether on holiday or not? There’s no way you could have convinced me that childcare was an indulgence before I became a parent. Kids club, no kids club – who cares? Your kids will find something to do regardless.



I also didn’t spend a whole lot of time in the sort of places that did have childcare facilities, because I wasn’t in the market. And I didn’t care because when you don’t have kids, you can’t possibly get your head around the all-encompassing nature of looking after children. 



The only person I will take to the toilet in the next two hours will be me. They say there’s no such thing as a holiday when you have young kids – it’s just parenting in a nicer location. Quite often though it’s parenting in a more difficult location, because the hotel doesn’t have comfortable bedding for little kids, or the restaurants don’t have the right food, or a million other things that are easier to manage in your own home. Holidays begin to look more like a challenge than a pleasure. A parent once said to me, “It’s hard work making beautiful memories,” and that is so true that I have repeated it on every trip away with the family since. We will look back on these times with pleasure. But in the moment, we know how hard we’re working just to get through it. Which brings me back to the indulgence of childcare. No visions of champagne breakfasts for this parent. No hot air balloon rides or private jets. Indulgence looks like the sign-in desk at the kids’ club at Elements of Byron resort.



They only do this during school holidays, though fortunately that’s when we’re visiting. So we sign the kids in and they run inside all excited to play with toys and make arts and crafts and meet new friends. Related Article Fiji The one thing that makes Fiji unbeatable for a family holiday We slink off in the direction of the pool, knowing we have a shady cabana bagged and nothing else to do for the next couple of hours but sip pina coladas and maybe even read a few pages of the books that we optimistically decided to bring with us. The mental load diminishes for a few brief moments. The physical effort disappears. No one has made a bum joke in several minutes. This is the stuff holiday dreams are made of, the ultimate indulgence in many ways. We do go on holidays without having someone else around to help with the kids. We travelled to Japan for 10 days and everyone had a ball exploring and eating and gaping at the wonders that country has to offer. Jess and I also worked really hard every day making those beautiful memories happen.



But then we went to Fiji, to Jean-Michel Cousteau Resort, which provides one dedicated nanny per child for your entire holiday, and wow, you have never been so indulged. We went skiing in Falls Creek and the kids attended full-day lessons, which essentially function as a childcare service, and everyone had the best time. Because this is the thing about childcare when it’s done right: the kids have a really good time. They love it. They feel indulged. And we do too. Everyone has a holiday. And then we all get back together at the pool and I resume my scanning for mortal danger.

He specialises in food and wine – writing about it, as well as consuming it – and at any given moment in time Ben is probably thinking about either ramen in Tokyo, pintxos in San Sebastian, or carbonara in Rome. World.title: It’s the batteries, stupid. Why garbage fires are now an everyday event
World.content:
Exclusive EnvironmentSustainabilityFire It’s the batteries, stupid. Why garbage fires are now an everyday event Caitlin Fitzsimmons September 21, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Disposable vapes, toys, singing birthday cards and rechargeable tools are among the battery-operated devices causing thousands of fires in waste and recycling centres in a massive and escalating problem across Australia. There are an estimated 10,000 to 12,000 battery-related fires in Australia’s waste and recycling system every year, says ReTHiNK Waste Tasmania, a consumer education initiative between the Tasmanian government and the waste-management sector. Loading Staff often deal with fires, but state fire brigades have been called to hundreds of blazes at waste and recycling facilities across Australia so far this year, including 86 in NSW alone, and batteries were often suspected to be the cause. Fire Rescue Victoria said it was called to fires involving a lithium-ion battery daily across all settings and that it was a growing problem in waste management, but it was unable to provide exact figures. The fires are a safety risk for staff in the waste and recycling sector, a crippling financial burden for companies that can no longer buy insurance to protect assets, and an environmental problem because of toxic air pollution and the setback to recycling efforts.



NSW Fire and Rescue Commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell said the distinguishing feature of a battery fire was how quickly they started because of the volume of energy stored in the battery cell. “One minute, it’ll be sitting there looking very benign,” Fewtrell said. “A second or two later, it’s a very intense fire, often spitting embers and pieces of battery out, which can also spread the fire into other parts of the rubbish or the recycling pile.” Joshua Fischer, of Fire Rescue Victoria, is concerned by a rise in battery fires in garbage trucks. Chris Hopkins Fire Rescue Victoria Deputy Commissioner Joshua Fischer said the fires posed significant safety risks, and also serious environmental harms because “fires can release toxic pollutants and harmful contaminants into the air, soil and waterways”. Fire and Rescue NSW reported 86 fires at waste and recycling centres between January 1 and September 14 this year, compared with 114 for the whole of 2025. There were also 44 fires in garbage trucks so far this year, compared with 62 for the whole of last year, and the vast majority started in the garbage compactor or load-carrying compartment of the truck.



“When I was a firefighter and on the trucks [before 2011], it was very, very seldom that you would be going to a garbage truck fire, and now they’re much more prevalent,” Fewtrell said. “A large part of that is, we believe, due to lithium-ion batteries being included in the waste or the recycling streams.” Lithium-ion batteries are highly combustible under heat or pressure, while standard household batteries such as AA can also cause fires but are less volatile. West Australian Department of Fire and Emergency Services Deputy Commissioner Jon Broomhall said lithium-ion batteries that were damaged, crushed or overheated could trigger “thermal runaway” – a chain reaction in which batteries produce intense heat and release flammable gases, leading to ignition. “The conditions inside rubbish trucks or waste facilities are especially conducive for battery ignition as items are often compacted and crushed,” Broomhall said. In January 2025, Veolia’s waste-sorting centre in Cairns was destroyed by fire, thought to be caused by a lithium-ion battery, resulting in material having to be diverted to landfill. Veolia also had a facility in NSW offline for several months because of roof damage. The company has shared footage from its security cameras showing six fires in two months at one recycling plant – the Bibra Lake Materials Recovery Facility in Western Australia – in a bid to raise awareness of the problem.



Visy chief executive Mark De Wit said companies had to invest in cameras that were always manned, infrared guns to monitor heat, water cannons and fire extinguishers. The fires were particularly hard to extinguish in a recycling centre full of plastic, which was oil-based, or cardboard, he said. “We had [a fire] yesterday, we had one the day before, it’s almost a daily event and it’s always a battery,” De Wit said, when asked about the issue at the Visy Recycling Roundtable. “It is completely company-agnostic. Visy’s lost a site in the last five years. Re.Group has lost a recycling site in the last five years. Cleanaway has lost a site in the last five years. Most recycling facilities can’t get insurance any more because of the fires.” Related Article Renewables ‘Moving at light speed’: Plug-in solar and batteries are coming to Australia Cleanaway confirmed this; Re.Group was contacted for comment. Veolia chief operating officer Carmen Loecherer said the fires were a daily occurrence and that she was worried about staff safety. She knew that batteries were the culprit because video footage often showed a battery igniting, or employees had found a battery in an audit.



“In particular when there are fires in vehicles that transport waste, we pull it out and we try and find the culprit,” Loecherer said. “Usually, it’s still smouldering when we put it out, and 99 per cent of the time it’s a battery.” Both Veolia and Visy said products with embedded batteries such as disposable vapes and birthday cards, and rechargeable hardware tools or toys, were the biggest problems. The companies called for other states to copy the NSW product stewardship scheme that forced manufacturers to fund more collection points and consumer education. However, illegal vapes sit outside that system because the producer is not always identifiable. In WA, the Department of Fire and Emergency Services reported 40 fires at waste-disposal facilities across the state between January 1 and June 30, with seven proven to be caused by batteries. That compared with 70 fires over 2025, with eight proven to be caused by batteries. The department said the true number of battery fires would be higher because it was often difficult to prove the cause.
