World.title: ‘We have the brotherhood to offer you’: Inside the push to keep boys away from crime
World.content:
Men and boys pray at United Muslims of Australia’s western Sydney headquarters, where youth programs are designed to give boys a sense of belonging.

On a Friday night, children race their friends to the fun and games. But beyond the play, there is work to be done in a community battling fear, anxiety and stereotypes.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As the time ticks towards 7.30pm on a Friday, the bustle of young boys running through the corridor quietens to a hush; dozens of men and children trickle into the prayer room of United Muslims of Australia’s sprawling western Sydney headquarters as the evening worship begins. For 10 minutes, only the rhythm of Isha – the night’s final prayer – can be heard. As quickly as it subsides, though, the racket of the boys’ excitement returns. With their praying done, they rush out of the room, shove itchy feet into shoes, and race away into the maze of the centre; some make for the gaming consoles, while others – in the football jerseys of their sporting idols – are already halfway to the hardwood of the indoor futsal court. An evening at United Muslims of Australia youth centre in Padstow. James Brickwood Youth play computer games, handball and futsal in the basement of the centre after prayers. James Brickwood While the games serve as an incentive for the boys to gather with their peers in the Muslim community, football is just one of many items on the agenda this Friday night. Inside these walls, there is important work to be done. Hundreds of boys and girls – aged nine to 15 – flock to the Padstow centre each Friday for youth programs offering guidance for those at risk of wandering to the wrong side of the tracks, teaching them about Islam, and instilling a sense of pride in young Muslims struggling with identity in a politically charged Australia. “We want our children to be proud Muslims without compromising their faith,” says UMA founder Sheikh Shadi Alsuleiman. “I want them to be proud Australians that contribute back to their community.” Alsuleiman welcomes this masthead to the centre at a time when the question of how to keep young boys – especially those in western Sydney – off the streets and away from organised crime is at the centre of a growing challenge for community leaders and authorities trying to combat the rise of criminal networks recruiting impressionable children.



In the past 18 months, police have charged hundreds of teenage boys, some of them from Muslim families, over their involvement in Sydney’s escalating gangland conflicts. The recruitment of children, some as young as 14, to carry out targeted attacks has become a hallmark of recent underworld violence and one of the most challenging aspects of policing feuds between rival criminal groups. Last Wednesday, homicide squad detectives arrested and charged two boys, aged 14 and 16, over the mistaken-identity killing of 23-year-old university student Marco Tapia, who was shot dead lying in his bed. This month, NSW Premier Chris Minns announced proposed legislative changes designed to deter children from working for organised crime networks. Under a proposed expansion to the serious children’s indictable offences scheme, children charged with offences linked to organised crime, including those related to public shootings and firebombings, would be tried as adults in the state’s District Court and Supreme Court, where they would face longer prison terms than if they were prosecuted as juveniles. At UMA, the centre’s youth programs are designed to not only teach boys about their faith, but give them the sense of belonging many their age seek in criminal gangs. “You’ve kind of got to ask yourself what those boys are finding in those gangs,” says Zaid Omran, UMA’s youth co-ordinator. “They’re finding brotherhood, they’re finding identity, they’re finding social insurance, they’re finding a home away from home, they’re finding … people who see them, people who hear them, people who value them.” The acceptance that young boys may feel within a gang is short-lived, unsustainable and fake, says Zaid Omran, UMA’s youth co-ordinator. James Brickwood Omran says young boys’ energy can be redirected into positive action with the right guidance. James Brickwood



The key to keeping Muslim boys on the right path is offering comforts grounded in faith and community rather than crime, Omran says. “If you can win a young person’s heart, then you have the ability to redirect whatever energy he has into something productive, into being a positive impact on the rest of society,” he says. “The ability for you to hold someone’s hand from as young as nine years old, if you have the steadfastness, if you have the fortitude to follow through and stay holding that person’s hand from as young as nine, from such a young age, then you’re decreasing the possibility of that person ever even coming close to all of that stuff.” Omran says the acceptance young boys may feel within a gang is short-lived, unsustainable and fake. The second they are no longer useful to those in charge, the boys are turfed. “That’s very, very powerful, for a young person to be seen – in every sense of that word – for them to feel heard,” he says. “We have the brotherhood to offer you.” Community leaders are also facing the challenge of organised crime and criminal gangs being glorified on social media, says Ibrahim Kayellou, 26, a youth mentor at the centre. Keeping boys away from content that could set them on a path to crime has become as much a priority for youth program leaders as teaching Islamic values. “It’s hard for the parents to keep up with it,” Kayellou says. Outside the centre’s walls, Muslims face rising Islamophobia and negative stereotypes that threaten boys’ sense of identity and instil a sense of fear and anxiety within the community, Alsuleiman says. “Islamophobia’s becoming the norm,” he says. “It’s been accepted to insult Muslims, to speak against Muslims, to demonise Muslims, to vilify Muslims, and it is a huge concern across the board with the Muslim community.” Sheikh Shadi Alsuleiman arriving at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, where he said instances of Islamophobia had increased by 600 per cent since 2022. Kate Geraghty Alsuleiman says there is a sense of anxiety and fear within the Muslim community. James Brickwood



Alsuleiman, who is also the Australian National Imams Council president, has been a vocal critic of the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza. He has also attracted criticism for public comments on homosexuality. “I have previously noted passages in the holy Quran which do not support homosexuality,” Alsuleiman said in a statement to this masthead in 2016. “However, I always follow such statements with a personal commitment to tolerance and encouragement that all Muslims and all people approach all individuals, no matter their faith, race or sexuality, in a considerate and respectful way.” Now, Alsuleiman says many of the Muslim community’s most vulnerable members – women and children – feel unsafe. The bollards blocking the centre’s front door are not for decoration, he points out, adding that there is a strong sense within the community that an attack on Muslims like the Christchurch massacre in 2019 may be repeated. “It’s not about if, it’s about when,” he says. “There’s a very strong sense of anxiety in the community and fear.” Related Article Updated

Organised crime Child recruits to be tried as adults amid Sydney gangland crackdown Some community members are so concerned about their safety that they are scared to walk on the street or commute to work. Coupled with what Alsuleiman says are harmful anti-Muslim rhetoric and narratives being pushed by prominent right-wing political parties, tensions between his community and others have become inflamed. Last month, he told the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion that recorded instances of Islamophobia had increased by more than 600 per cent since 2022. “The Muslim community feels the collective blame for the actions of others, especially post-Bondi,” Alsuleiman says. “The community feels that it is a target.”

World.title: Supermarket debate shift 'encouraging' as Labour, National campaign on reform
World.content:
RNZ national

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is speaking to Morning Report shortly. Listen live on the player above, the RNZ app or your local RNZ frequency.

Consumer NZ is pleased the political debate on the grocery sector has shifted towards finding solutions and away from debating whether or not there is a problem.

On Sunday, Labour revealed its plans to increase competition in the grocery sector by focusing on the wholesale side.

It follows National and New Zealand First's plans to split up Foodstuffs, and the Greens' policy to create a state-owned KiwiMart.

If elected, Labour would force Foodstuffs and Woolworths to run their wholesale arms independently from their retail arms.

The party would give smaller stores guaranteed access to wholesale products, preventing wholesalers cutting off supply.

It would also remove restraint of trade laws that prevent smaller retailers such as Four Square from lowering prices if they want, or from choosing to go independent.

Labour announces new supermarket policy Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said when even The Warehouse was struggling to access wholesale, it showed something needed to change.

"There are small businesses up and down the country that want to really compete, that want to give a better deal to their consumers, who can't at the moment because they can't access the wholesale that allows them to do that."

Labour's commerce and consumer affairs spokesperson Arena Williams. Sam Rillstone

Announcing the policy at Plenty Foods grocer in Upper Hutt, Labour's commerce and consumer affairs spokesperson Arena Williams said Labour would essentially create a "different team, under a different model" to incentivise wholesalers to "go out and win" customers.

"We want the wholesalers to behave like any other business. To win retail customers like this grocer, to make sure their deals work for a grocer like this."

The policy, Williams said, would see more "small, hard-nosed, tough" businesspeople getting into the grocery business, offering more products and competition.

The policy has found tentative support from the Greens, and vehement criticism from ACT.

David Seymour responds to supermarket policy announcements Morning Report Download MP3 8m

National is pointing to advice commissioned by the previous Labour government as to why the policy would not work.

Foodstuffs and Woolworths, meanwhile, are watching closely, while insisting they are already doing what they can to support competition.

Consumer NZ chief executive Jon Duffy presents Finance Minister Nicola Willis with a petition on accurate supermarket pricing (file photo). Anneke Smith

Consumer NZ encouraged by debate shift

While Hipkins and Williams were confident Labour could achieve its reforms in its first 100 days in government, advocacy group Consumer NZ did not think any of the proposals political parties had put forward could be done quickly.

But its chief executive Jon Duffy said it was clear there needed to be structural intervention.

"What is really encouraging is that we seem to be now not having a debate around whether the government needs to step in and do something about this sector, it's how they should do that. So that means the debate has really moved forward to implementing solutions rather than still debating whether there's a problem. So that's a good thing."

Labour's Arena Williams discusses new supermarket policy Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Duffy said creating two independent wholesalers looked like a good idea, but he wanted to see more detail on its structure.

"In order for those entities to be genuinely independent of the retail arms, there's going to have to be pretty firm structures in place separating them out. So I'm interested to see the detail on how that would work."

Greens co-leaders Marama Davidson and Chlöe Swarbrick announcing the party's KiwiMart policy. RNZ

Greens 'stoked' at more supermarket policies

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said she was "stoked" to see both Labour and National wanted to force structural change to increase competition.

Swarbrick said the Greens, which earlier this month announced they would create a state-owned KiwiMart to force a third player, had "put on the agenda" the need for more affordable groceries.

"A lot of it does feel, albeit like clearly a step in the right direction, none go as far as securing the future of affordable groceries as introducing that third player owned in the public interest for and by New Zealanders in the form of KiwiMart."

In April, New Zealand First proposed splitting Foodstuffs in the same way as National would pursue, but without a Commerce Commission review first.

National's deputy leader Nicola Willis. RNZ/Nick Monro

National warns of consequences

National is campaigning on pursuing splitting up Foodstuffs, subject to a Commerce Commission review.

If re-elected, National would legislate to break up Foodstuffs so Pak'nSave became one chain and Four Square and New World another.

National's deputy leader Nicola Willis said Labour's policy was light on detail, with the idea already having been examined and rejected as complex, costly and high-risk.

Willis pointed to a 2022 market study by the Commerce Commission warning that separating wholesale and retail operations was not "necessary or desirable" and would create "practical challenges and transaction costs".

"The commission warned that government facilitation of a new independent wholesaler would be 'complex, potentially expensive' and carry a 'high risk of failure'," she said.

"The subsequent independent assessment commissioned under the previous Labour government went further, finding wholesale ownership separation was 'fundamentally flawed' and warning that forced divestment could cause significant disruption and impose costs that could ultimately be borne by consumers."

Willis said Labour was announcing an intervention first "and the consequences are worked out later".

Labour's Williams acknowledged that the Commerce Commission had identified "potential problems" with the separation, but said Labour's policy would fix them by ensuring small grocers had a guaranteed route of access to a range of essential goods "on fair terms".

"Prices don't rise in the short term under this model," she said.

ACT Party leader David Seymour. Zachary Cornelisen

ACT takes aim at bureaucracy

The ACT Party, which earlier came out swinging against National's plan to pursue a Foodstuffs split, was similarly critical of Labour's proposal.

Leader David Seymour said he felt a sense of déjà vu, and that the policy was unworkable.

"It would take an army of bureaucrats to decide what a fair price is, larger than the army that we currently have."

With four parties now campaigning on major structural change, Seymour said the campaign was descending into hysteria.

"As soon as it becomes acceptable to attack a legitimate business for short-term political gain, the only question left is, who's next?"

Seymour said ACT's plan was to make it easier to get a consent for a new supermarket, which he admitted was "more subtle" than what others were proposing but "more honest".

Foodstuffs and Woolworths respond

A Foodstuffs spokesperson said Foodstuffs would take time to consider the detail of Labour's announcement.

"As we've said previously, we support any discussion focused on improving outcomes for grocery customers at the checkout. The key questions for any proposal are whether it will deliver lower prices, better choice and better service for New Zealanders, how long any benefits would take to flow through, and how those benefits would be achieved in practice," the spokesperson said.

"Both Foodstuffs cooperatives are already committed to expanding and strengthening their wholesale offers, and we continue to look for ways to improve choice and access across the grocery sector."

Woolworths said it remained committed to a competitive and sustainable grocery sector, and it understood the cost-of-living pressure Kiwi families were under.

"We have worked constructively with the government and the Commerce Commission for a number of years to implement significant, structural changes across our business to support greater competition. This includes working with the Grocery Supply Code and establishing a dedicated wholesale business, New Zealand Grocery Wholesalers, to provide wholesale grocery items to a growing number of independent retailers," a spokesperson said.

"We will work through these policies carefully and continue to engage constructively and transparently with the Commerce Commission and the government to ensure that they have all of the information they need as they consider these issues. As shared previously, any proposal aimed at lowering prices for customers needs to consider all of the factors that impact the cost of groceries."

World.title: Forum leaders to advocate for Pacific issues at United Nations General Assembly
World.content:
Pacific leaders will put a "strong, unified regional voice" at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York this week, the Pacific Islands Forum says.

The UNGA's 81st session will take place from 21 to 28 September, with several Pacific leaders set to be in attendance.

In a statement over the weekend, the Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat (PIFS) said Palau's President Surangel Whipps Jr together with other Forum leaders would lead the PIFs high-level engagements in New York. They will advance shared Pacific priorities agreed by Forum leaders at its 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting in Palau earlier this month.

The secretariat said the annual PIF leaders' dialogue with the UN secretary-general António Guterres will take place on Friday (Saturday NZT).

"Forum Leaders' presence at UNGA81 offers an important opportunity to project a strong, unified regional voice on issues central to the Pacific's future, including climate change, sustainable development, ocean governance, development finance, and the escalating threat posed by sea-level rise," the PIFS statement said.

"Forum Leaders will reinforce the importance of a multilateral system that is responsive to Pacific priorities and our lived realities."

Pacific leaders' efforts to advocate for and strengthen visibility around the Pacific Resilience Facility (PRF) to reach its target of US$500 million by the end of this year is expected to be central to their engagements at UNGA.

"This work is particularly timely as the region builds momentum towards Pre-COP31 in Fiji and Tuvalu in October and COP31 in Türkiye and November," the PIFS said.

PIF secretary-general Baron Waqa said the Forum's message to the UN is clear.

"[The] challenges facing our region are inseparable from the global challenges before us," he said.

World.title: The rise of 'accidental landlords'
World.content:
Could I run out of money in retirement and other questions experts wish you'd ask No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 15m

Some would-be house sellers who have not been able to get the price they want are deciding instead to rent their properties out - but there is a warning they should take care.

Data from Cotality shows there was an increase in the number of properties that were listed for sale but did not sell, and were then rented, in both the market peak of 2021 and again in recent months.

Cotality chief property economist Kelvin Davidson said the 2021 peak could be because more people thought that being a property investor was an appealing prospect.

"I suspect more recently the upturn would have been because of developers not being able to sell at a sufficient price so renting out instead, or accidental 'Mum and Dad' landlords - as opposed to what might have been a conscious choice for someone to become a landlord back in 2021. This time there's probably been some people hoping to sell, but can't get a decent price or can't actually get a deal at all, so are holding on to it as a rental instead."

Recent Real Estate Institute data showed a 13 percent drop in the number of sales nationwide, year-on-year.

In recent months, properties have been withdrawn from sale and then listed for rent within three months at a rate of about 3000 a year.

At the peak of the market, it was 5500, but that fell to fewer than 2000 in 2023.

Sarina Gibbon of Tenancy Advisory - which provides advice to property managers, landlords and tenants - said she was encountering more people who had ended up as landlords because their plans to sell had failed.

Some were people who could afford to hold on and hope for a better price in future, she said, or people who had to move for work.

But she said it was not always a wise financial decision. "The propensity for Kiwi investors to use their first home as a rental property is a pretty bad habit… just because it's a great first home doesn't mean it's a great investment."

She said many had not given sufficient thought to the rules for rentals, such as the Residential Tenancies Act or the healthy homes rules.

Gibbon said she had spoken to one woman who believed that because she had been able to buy a property, it should be compliant as a rental. She was being taken to the Tenancy Tribunal because of health homes breaches.

"Rental law is traditionally not taken seriously and just treated as a bit of an afterthought. People get themselves in trouble because they don't realise that it's both a business undertaking and a legal undertaking."

She said anyone considering it should work with professional property managers.

Infometrics managing director Gareth Kiernan said it could be the case that properties that were not originally intended as investments would not get the same yield as those that were bought for the purpose of renting out.

"Generally speaking, investors tend to concentrate their purchases down towards the lower quarter of the property spectrum, whereas owner-occupier is median or higher.

"It comes down to the question of how much is a tenant prepared to pay for a house with x bedrooms… you might pay a bit more for a two-bedroom house or a three-bedroom house when it's a nice home as opposed to a lower quality one but it's probably not going to be commensurate to the value of the property. But obviously if they are worried about selling it and making a loss then perhaps having it tenanted and achieving some sort of return is a preferable outcome. A good second best outcome."

Property coach Steve Goodey said there were properties available for sale that never even registered on the market. He said a developer might have ten units available and decide to only advertise one to cut costs. That could mean the scale of unsold properties was understated, he said.

World.title: Alzheimer's disease starting to be considered a treatable condition - study
World.content:
Alzheimer's disease is starting to be considered as a treatable and preventable condition, a major new report says.

The World Alzheimer Report 2026, released today from Alzheimer's Disease International, says despite years of slow progress, clinical trials are now on the brink of diagnostic and medical breakthroughs.

The number of people living with dementia globally is projected to surpass 139 million by 2050, the report said, becoming one of the leading causes of death throughout the world.

But while a cure is still far away, medical research is radically shifting the understanding of the disease.

"I think for a long time there's been a fairly nihilistic view in the dementia world, that it is something that can just happen as you age for example, and that we can't do anything about," neurologist, neuroscientist and Alzheimers NZ spokesperson Dr Campbell Le Heron said.

"These trials are showing us that we can potentially do something about it - at least in certain situations - but I think our biological understanding of the condition is identifying ways we can actually prevent it," he added.

Dr Campbell Le Heron. Supplied

In the past several years, drugs that slow the progression of the disease have entered the market internationally.

Le Heron said the drugs target and remove the amyloid plaque that's been developing in the brains of sufferers years before they get symptoms.

Trials are underway - some involving New Zealand - which are treating people before they have symptoms to see if cognitive impairment can be prevented.

"We don't know if that's going to be the case yet or not, but I think we have to have a mind on the future because that's what we're hoping we will be able to show," Le Heron explained.

"And if that's the case, then we really need to...be improving diagnostic pathways for people with cognitive impairment, but also thinking about how we can identify people at risk of developing cognitive impairment from Alzheimer's disease."

The emergence of blood tests to diagnose the disease is also a major development in detecting Alzheimer's earlier, the report said.

Trials are underway in the UK and Australia developing the tests.

Le Heron said the disease was currently diagnosed through specialist brain imaging and lunbar punctures in the lower back - but these were hard for people to access.

The tests were still not perfect, he added, and would need to be one part of a full, clinical assessment.

"In my mind, one of the really important things in these tests is hopefully they're going to be a whole lot cheaper than the current tests that we have, and because it is a blood test it will be much more accessible for everybody in the country, compared to just being seen at a specialist centre."

Given these rapid developments, Le Heron said the government needed to improve access to diagnostic tools, boost its specialist workforce, train up primary care clinicians, and put funding into community-based dementia services.

"We cannot allow these advances to become available only to people who live near specialist services or have the knowledge, money and connections needed to access them."

Māori, pacific peoples and rural communities shouldn't be left behind, he said.

Associate minister for health and minister for seniors Casey Costello was approached for comment.

Can you prevent Alzheimer's disease through lifestyle choices?

The report referenced clinical trials which look at how lifestyle choices can alter the trajectory of cognitive decline - not in laboratories, but in kitchens, gyms and community centres.

One study, originating in Finland in 2009, set out to test whether lifestyle could protect the ageing brain. Participants aged between 60 and 77 enrolled in a two-year lifestyle programme including a focus on healthy diet, physical activity, brain exercises, and social activity.

Those who implemented the lifestyle benefits gained about 25 per cent more cognitive improvements compared to the group which didn't, he said.

Le Heron recommended exercising five days a week to the point you "get puffed", eating a mediterranean-style diet with lots of fruit and vegetables, and prioritising socialising.

So what about crosswords, or brain puzzles?

World.title: NZ Warriors NRL playoff exit leaves sour taste, as fans turn on referee, officials
World.content:
Analysis - Neither the NZ Warriors nor their fans should have ended such a historic season in this manner.

While the Auckland-based team fumbled or were burgled of their best chance of an NRL championship in more than a decade, depending on your perspective, a record crowd of 48,511 at Eden Park was brought into disrepute by the reaction of a few poor losers after the final whistle.

The scoreboard will show the Warriors stumbled to a 12-10 defeat against Newcastle Knights, capping a demoralising two-and-out exit from the playoffs, after coming so close to the regular season minor premiership.

They had more than enough chances to dictate their own fate, but instead left themselves and their fans lamenting some late officialling decisions that could have gone either way, but went against the home side.

Referee Ashley Klein and his onfield team bore the brunt of that outrage, booed from the field, and dodging what appeared to be plastic bottles or cans thrown from the stands.

Those actions drew the disgust of Warriors legend Shaun Johnson in TV commentary.

"It leaves a bit of a sour taste in your mouth, after what's been an unbelievable night," he told Sky Sport.

"The colours, the energy, the happiness, the celebration... but there's just no need for it. It's just embarrassing.

"Ashley Klein probably reffed the best game of rugby league I've seen in a long time tonight. He didn't take any gamesmanship in terms of people laying down.

"He didn't let people approach him winging, he didn't make the game about him. He let the players come and play, and essentially, they dictated the outcome."

That said, three calls in the final 10 minutes enraged the fans.

Down by two, the Warriors appeared to force a handling error from the Knights in their own half. Klein ruled a knock on, but Newcastle challenged the call and review official Chris Butler overruled it, apparently finding a minute touch from Warriors centre Ali Leiataua that escaped most other onlookers.

Moments later, the Knights again mishandled deep in their own territory, but Klein ruled Warriors halfback Te Maire Martin stripped the ball, as he bounced out of the tackle. The Warriors challenged and lost.

Referee Ashley Klein disallows a Warriors try against Newcastle Knights. Brett Phibbs/Photosport

Finally, in the dying seconds, Warriors centre Leka Halasima chased a high kick towards the Knights goalposts and was sent crashing to the ground before he could leap for the contest.

The fans waited for a possible escort call from Klein, but he waved play on and the visitors were allowed to survive to the final siren.

"It was frustrating," admitted Warriors coach Andrew Webster. "I thought they were trying to find ways to take it off us.

"Like, the rotation of the ball [on Leiataua's touch], he said, 'I can't find any evidence, but hang on, I'll have one more look'.

"He has a look and, 'Ooops, there it is'. He looked at it 20 times.

"On the last one [Halasima's collision], when two points would have drawn the game, he's going across Leka pretending to try and catch the ball, which they told us you can't do."

Webster wasn't sold on Martin's alleged strip either, but conceded his team did more than enough to take those decisions out of the equation and could not deliver the final blow.

Leka Halasima scores one of his two tries for the Warriors against Newcastle. PhotoSport / Brett Phibbs

"At the end of the day, you make your own luck in this game and we had enough opportunities to win that game," he said.

"We created plenty of momentum, plenty of good looks, but we missed two poor tackles that led to tries. Big games are about moments, but it wasn't just those two moments - there were lots of others.

"We had a good opportunity to dominate and we didn't."

The Warriors had other chances. Leiataua had a second-half try taken away for obstruction in the defensive line, while fullback Taine Tuaupiki was allowed to narrowly miss his attempted sideline conversion of Halasima's second try - a kick that would have levelled the scores - before the NRL doctors pulled him from the field for a concussion check.

"It hurts," Webster reflected. "You give yourself an opportunity and you don't take it, so it hurts.

"It's harder than when you think you're a pretender and kind of making up the numbers. We didn't think that, we were very confident in our abilities.

"We won some big games this year and dominated some big teams, so it's in us and we know it. Top two was no fluke and we had the right for two [home] semis, but we couldn't get the job done and that's hard to take."

The Warriors completed the regular season with a club-record 18 wins, scoring more than 700 points for the first time, while selling out their home fixtures and drawing massive support to away games.

None of that means much to them right now, but maybe later, when the ache subsides.

"It's hard to look back at what we've achieved, but there is an element of motivation and we don't want to feel this pain again," Webster said. "It's tough to go through it, but we've definitely come a long way as a club and a country.

"That crowd tonight was ridiculous how good they were. There's so many good things happening in our place, how many young players coming through...

"Obviously we've achieved a lot, but not what we wanted to."

Among those feeling the Warriors' pain was rugby league legend and Fox Sport commentator Gordon Tallis.

"I felt the fans walked away just a little bit robbed tonight," he told RNZ. "I felt like they didn't get any calls tonight.

World.title: 'His life was worth nothing to them' - Heartbroken families speak out against work safety rule changes
World.content:
More than 700 people have been killed in work-related deaths in the past decade, despite the Key government's overhaul of workplace health and safety laws following the Pike River Mine disaster. The coalition government has again changed the law, this time to cut red tape and ease compliance costs, but critics say more New Zealanders will die at work as a result. South Island correspondent Timothy Brown reports.

Working in a timber yard was not Ethyn McTier's idea of a dream job.

His role at Timaru's Point Lumber was just a means to an end and a way to raise some money for his real dream of moving to Australia and becoming a builder.

Instead, the 23-year-old went to that job on 1 November 2022 and never came home.

McTier was trapped by an unguarded conveyor belt and crushed to death at the yard.

The conveyor belt that killed Ethyn McTier. Supplied

Before his death, McTier had expressed concerns to his family about the working conditions at Point Lumber.

His mother said he borrowed money from the company's director Sean Sloper to fix his teeth. McTier's integrity meant he would never walk away from the job without repaying the loan.

An independent safety consultant recommended installing a guard on the conveyor belt in 2017, but it was not there when McTier was killed.

A three-year-old boy was crushed to death after a stack of logs collapsed and rolled on him while he was visiting his father at the same yard in 2016.

WorkSafe investigated and prosecuted Point Lumber over the boy's death but the regulator was not aware of the conveyor belt or concerns about its safety until after McTier died.

Point Lumber RNZ / Tim Brown

Point Lumber was under no obligation to disclose the information and WorkSafe only dealt with the company on one occasion between the two deaths about an unrelated matter.

There have been more than 700 work-related deaths since John Key's government overhauled workplace health and safety laws in 2015 in response to the 2010 Pike River mine disaster that killed 29 people.

There are about 70 people work-related deaths every year with primary industries, transport, construction and manufacturing accounting for almost 60 percent.

McTier's family now fears that the coalition government's law changes mean more workers will face an increased risk of death or injury, an assessment shared by New Zealand First leader and government minister Winston Peters.

The government said the law changes focused businesses on critical workplace risks.

Workplace Relations and Safety Minister Brooke van Velden said the government wanted everyone to get home from work safely and the changes intended to clarify and simplify the law had been misunderstood.

She said WorkSafe would continue to target businesses flouting the law or neglecting workers' safety, with the amendments due to come into effect next April.

Groups as diverse as the Law Association, Business Leaders' Health and Safety Forum, Woolworths, Institute of Safety Management and Council of Trade Unions have raised concerns the government's changes weaken worker protections and increase health and safety risks.

Some worry that they create a two-tier system with small businesses having fewer responsibilities, others fear they narrow the focus on potential risks and some say they prioritise economic concerns over worker safety.

McTier's sister Daria McTier said it felt like his death was in vain and her family did not want anyone else to die at work.

"It does, kind of for us, feel like it was all for nothing," she said.

Daria McTier said they wanted the law strengthened rather than weakened.

"If changes can happen and no one else has to go through what we've gone through, I think we'd be really happy," she said.

Ethyn McTier's family Amber Farmer, Sheryl Clark and Daria McTier RNZ/LouisDunham

McTier's mother Sheryl Clark said legislative change to better protect workers would be a legacy fitting of her son's life.

"He would have died for something. Something good has come from this. It wasn't just a waste of his death, because that's how I feel if it stays the same," she said.

Daria McTier said her family also struggled to understand how WorkSafe had failed to ensure the safety of the yard before her brother's death.

"There is obviously a lot of fault with Point Lumber and Sean, obviously, but change needs to happen at that top level," she said.

"We have these rules and regulations, but what is the point if they're not being enforced until after the fact? Then somebody's lost their life, the damage is done.

"The circumstances around this incident in particular are quite hard to accept because there had already been a death at the workplace, WorkSafe were involved then, they surely would have known that the working conditions weren't safe but nothing was done.

"Then we have this independent person coming in, also again saying, 'this isn't up to scratch, these are the things you can do to improve it'. Again, nothing was done, and look what it's led to.

"Everybody has the right to go to work and come home safe but there needs to be people enforcing that and making sure that these workplaces are safe."

The Timaru District Court awarded the family $140,000 in reparations for McTier's death.

Fines of $310,000 had to be paid to the government, an amount more than twice that awarded to the family.

Clark said it felt like the government was rewarded for failing to keep her son safe.

"That is not justice. That seems to me that they're making money off his death," she said.

"I didn't want any money. I wanted [Sloper] to go to jail so that he was taken away from his comfort zone and paying for what happened. I feel like shelling out money for someone's death, that didn't hurt him, not like we had to suffer.

"That's all it comes down to, money. He still gets to run his business. It didn't really cost him anything like it cost us."

Ethyn McTier as a child. Supplied

Council of Trade Unions president Sandra Grey described the circumstances of McTier's death as an outrage.

"No family should lose a son, a brother, a family member when it is completely avoidable," she said.

"We should all be absolutely outraged that for the lack of a guard someone did not get to go home.

"What we often see with guards around machinery is it sometimes can slow the process up slightly. People go, 'well, we could get through our work quicker if we didn't have the guard, it's expensive, it costs us time'.

"Never should the profit motive drive unsafe procedures and we should have seen after the first death an absolute eagle eye on that mill. In any workplace where there has been a death, there should be a relentless move to make sure they have complied with every single compliance order and every single safety measure that's needed because no family ever gets over that sort of tragic death.

"This doesn't just end a young man's life. It ruins the future for all the people around him.

"We need to be outraged that we've got a government that thinks business concerns about paperwork are more problematic than people dying. They've weighed the scales up and they've said, 'we'll accept there'll be some deaths because businesses just don't like compliance'. This is not about compliance. This is about saving lives."

As a company with fewer than 20 employees, Point Lumber is considered a "small PCBU" - or person conducting a business or undertaking - and subject to less onerous expectations under the government's law changes.

Point Lumber director Sean Sloper declined to be interviewed by RNZ and instead provided written answers to questions.

He said extensive and ongoing improvements had been made to the business since McTier's death, with $120,000 spent on securing the area where he died.

Sloper said McTier's sleeve had been caught in the conveyor belt weeks before he died and it appeared McTier had told a senior staff member about the close call.

But McTier's family disputed that and said Ethyn McTier had told them about a fortnight before his death another staff member got their sleeve caught while clearing out the conveyor belt.

Asked if any other staff had raised concerns about the conveyor belt, Sloper said: "I can't recall without digging through those records."

Sloper said a guard was fitted to the conveyor belt as recommended by the 2017 audit but it was not in place at the time of McTier's death because it had been removed during a re-engineering of the site.

"The conveyor belt was always seen as a low-risk operation for the industry. It is in a hard to access area," he said.

"We don't know why or what Ethyn was doing in this area on the day of the accident. We were doing extra-long poles at the time and the only way to access the conveyor drum was on your hands and knees."

Asked if there were any other incidents of concern at the business, Sloper said: "Risk management is a constant - it doesn't start or stop at specific times, it is an ongoing process."

Point Lumber used a reputable Christchurch safety consultant for its audits before McTier's death and had since employed a qualified and experienced local woman who was herself audited annually, Sloper said.

"We acknowledge we don't have the necessary in-house expertise to do our own health and safety systems," he said.

Since McTier's death WorkSafe had issued five improvement notices to Point Lumber. all of which had been complied with.

The regulator said it had also issued two directive letters, which were an informal, lower level of intervention.

"Point Lumber had no obligation to disclose its private audits to WorkSafe. Businesses hold the primary duty of care to keep their workers safe. Safety audits and improvements, staff training and so on are all part of that duty of care and are good business practice. WorkSafe does not need to be involved," a WorkSafe spokesperson said.

McTier's death echoed Wes Tomich's death less than a year later in Tauranga.

Wes Tomich. Supplied

The 37-year-old was cleaning a running conveyor belt at Ballance Agri-Nutrients' Mount Maunganui site when he tried to step over it, slipped and was pulled into the machine.

His mother Lee-ann Tomich said her son had spoken to her about the risks at the plant.

"Just before the accident he had come to us and said to us he wanted to leave Ballance. He said to [his father] Anthony, he's not happy with a few things that are going on there. If we had known how bad it was, we would have told him to walk out of the job," she said.

His father Anthony Tomich was shocked by safety standards at the plant.

"I've been in the game a long time. I've been over working in Australia, working in New Zealand, all over South Island, North Island. I'm a contractor, so I know a bit about what goes on around the place and I was really, really, really gobsmacked as to what they were doing," he said.

"It wasn't an accident really, at the end of the day. It's something that was foreseen. He should still be here. It's such an unnecessary death really because all they had to do was just heed warnings that they had been given. Unfortunately they didn't do that and this is the result."

A 2015 risk assessment of Ballance Agri-Nutrients' sites identified the danger of workers being caught in belts as well as a lack of guards or non-compliant guards and a lack of emergency stops within easy access of operators.

Ballance Agri-Nutrients asked Beca Group to translate and review the risk assessment, which was done in 2022, seven years after the initial assessment and before Tomich's death.

Beca's report referred to the risk of cleaning and maintaining the belt that ultimately caused Tomich's death and non-compliant guarding.

WorkSafe said it only became aware of the risk of the conveyor belt following Tomich's death.

Its old file management system showed 370 files relating to Ballance Agri-Nutrients with 52 compliance actions, but some interactions would have generated multiple files.

WorkSafe could not say how many of its interactions with Ballance Agri-Nutrients related to the Mount Maunganui site but its predecessor, the Department of Labour, had issued the company with an improvement notice for a conveyor belt at another site in 2009.

In 2012 the department investigated after a worker's hand was trapped between a spanner he was holding and a conveyor belt at the company's Mt Maunganui site, although it was not the same belt that caused Tomich's death.

A letter was sent to Ballance Agri-Nutrients but no further enforcement action was taken.

When asked if the regulator should have done more to protect Tomich and other workers - considering McTier's death the year before as a result of a known hazard and the known hazards at Ballance Agri-Nutrients - a WorkSafe spokesperson said the companies had been warned about safety risks.

"Both Ballance and Point Lumber had been told by independent health and safety experts that the conveyor belts which caused the fatalities were dangerous before the fatalities occurred. WorkSafe became aware of the dangers of the conveyor belts only when it was notified of the deaths. In the case of both these businesses WorkSafe acted promptly when it became aware of other safety risks, issuing notices and following up as needed to ensure worker safety," they said.

Wes Tomich. Supplied

Anthony Tomich said he believed WorkSafe had failed to keep his son safe.

"When they came here the guy said to me that they can't force them to make changes. What's the point then? It's like a guard dog with no teeth. It's just unbelievable," he said.

The Tauranga District Court fined Ballance Agri-Nutrients $420,000 and $287,202.86 was paid to the family, although almost three-quarters of that sum came from Wes Tomich's employee scheme life insurance policy.

In October 2023, less than three months after his death, Ballance Agri-Nutrients' then-chief executive Mark Wynne was recognised with a lifetime achievement award at the NZ Co-op Awards.

"Wes had been buried for not even two months and then I was reading reports that the company's CEO at the time, Mark Wynne, just received a lifetime achievement award," Anthony Tomich said.

"How do you get a lifetime achievement award when someone died on your watch?" Lee-ann Tomich said.

The Tomich family said the recognition was disrespectful and workplace health and safety would only improve when business leaders were held responsible for the safety of those working under them.

"If the CEOs were held more accountable for their companies we would see less deaths. If they had to go to jail when someone got killed unnecessarily then we'd see change in safety in the workplace. But their CEO didn't show up for court, nothing. So it was just like washed off his hands. He just walked away. Nothing," Lee-ann Tomich said.

RNZ asked Ballance Agri-Nutrients why it did not address lacking and non-compliant guards and the lack of easily accessible emergency stops following the 2015 assessment or the 2022 report and when improvements were finally made.

The company did not address the questions and instead sent a statement attributed to chief executive Kelvin Wickham.

"In late July 2023 the Ballance team lost a team member in a sudden and tragic accident. All who knew the individual were immensely impacted by his death," the company said.

"Ballance fully co-operated with WorkSafe NZ during its lengthy investigation and we are committed to recognising the failures and learning from this tragedy wherever we can.

"We have put additional measures and new training programmes in place to ensure an incident like this does not happen again."

The statement was largely similar to previous statements sent to journalists inquiring about Tomich's death, with the only notable amendment the removal of Tomich's name with "the individual" in its place.

RNZ also attempted to contact Wynne, who now sits on the boards of Alliance Group and Quayside Holdings, although no response has been received.

Workplace Relations and Safety Minister Brooke van Velden declined RNZ's interview request and instead asked to respond to written questions.

"As a government our hope for every family is that their loved ones return home from work at the end of each workday. We want workers safe at work," she said in a statement.

"There has been a lot of misunderstanding about what the health and safety reforms introduced by this coalition government will do. The changes we made are about ensuring that people understand what health and safety law requires of them, to actually be able to prioritise what it is that they need to do at work to keep themselves and others safe.

"The reforms focus all businesses and workers on the critical risks they must manage in their workplace - those are the risks that are likely to result in death, serious injury and illness. WorkSafe will continue to prosecute in cases where there has clearly been significant or negligent disregard for health and safety law, repeated non-compliance or where serious harm has occurred and deterrence is necessary.

"I have been informed that at the time of these incidents, WorkSafe had not clearly identified manufacturing as a priority sector. In 2023 WorkSafe strengthened its focus on the high-risk areas of manufacturing, forestry, agriculture and construction. This of course does nothing to reduce the tragedy of the workers who were killed and whose deaths were completely preventable but it highlights the importance of WorkSafe concentrating on sectors where serious injury or death are most likely to occur, including manufacturing."

Workplace Relations and Safety Minister Brooke van Velden. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

The minister did not directly respond to RNZ's questions about industry and worker concerns her law changes would cause further deaths and injuries.

Grey said New Zealand had an appalling health and safety record and the coalition's amendments would only make the situation worse, particularly for companies with 20 or fewer workers that would be subject to a less onerous regime.

"This government has changed legislation so that there's a two-tier system. Big companies have full compliance around health and safety, have to do the rigorous processes required. The new law means that small businesses just don't have to do the same level of detail around their compliance. It was always sold as that they find it really, really hard to do the compliance. What we're talking about is matters of life and death or serious injury for many, many workers," she said.

Grey was also concerned the new regime would not provide enough emphasis on the negative effects of work on mental health.

"For many workers it's not physical harm immediately that is the problem, it is actually psychosocial harm and we think that has been watered down in this new legislation," she said.

"That's all the things around workplace stress, fatigue, and that sometimes does lead to physical harm but also the hidden part is WorkSafe estimated around 70 workers a year die by suicide as a result of workplace stress. We don't want our health and safety law to miss out this huge part of what work does to workers, to humans, to families, which is it creates stress, it creates problems and we should have all companies addressing those problems.

"This legislation didn't have the support of the experts, didn't have the support of workers, many businesses argued against it and yet for some reason this government thinks they should take a lighter hand in this space. It's not good enough and we are going to see more workers dying if we don't tackle this issue properly."

The families of Ethyn McTier and Wes Tomich have been left to pick up the pieces of shattered lives.

Daria McTier said the loss of her brother was the worst day of her life and had turned the family's life upside down.

Her sister called her at work to tell her there had been an accident.

"I couldn't believe it. I just was in complete shock and then I had to ring and deliver that news to mine and Ethan's dad, which was just also incredibly hard to do. After I got off the phone to our dad, I think it just really hit me that he wasn't here any more.

"Our lives will never be the same and everyone else just carries on as normal," she said.

"It just kind of makes us feel like it didn't matter. He didn't matter. Our lives now don't matter."

Daria McTier said her brother had five siblings and was everyone's favourite, at the heart of a big family.

"I don't think anyone in this world had bad things to say about that kid," Clark said.

"He was an extremely hard worker. He was always there for his friends. He was always there for all of us. He was always there."

As the government worked on changes to workplace health and safety laws, the McTier family said no one reached out to seek their views.

The McTiers still had questions about why WorkSafe did not put a larger focus on Point Lumber following the first death at the yard and why the regulator did not know about the threat posed by the conveyor belt.

"WorkSafe had said to us that they didn't have the resources to do this," Daria McTier said.

"Before we had the sentencing WorkSafe had given us a show through of the improvements that had been done at the workplace, after the fact of course, and it was just kind of shocking to think that they weren't there all along."

"For me to make any of this okay, WorkSafe has to stand up and take accountability for these deaths," Clark said.

"Ultimately they are there to uphold safety at work, are they not? They did not do that."

WorkSafe said the family's recollection of the conversations differed from its understanding.

"If WorkSafe had been aware of the conveyor belt hazard at the time, it would have assessed the matter and considered the appropriate response. We are open to a further discussion if the family would benefit from it," a spokesperson said.

Wes Tomich's mother Lee-ann Tomich said the family moved from South Africa to New Zealand in 1997 to give the children a better life.

"There's no greater pain than losing a child. The suffering never stops," she said.

"It's like you had a life before he passed and then a life after and the lives are totally different.

"We brought him out here from South Africa to give him a better life and he loved it. He absolutely loved it. He thrived. He loved the country. He loved everything about it. He loved the All Blacks. He was just such an awesome character."

The family wanted the coroner to hold an inquest into Tomich's death but the request was declined, leaving them with many unanswered questions about his death.

"When people say to you 'have you got closure?', there's no closure," Lee-ann Tomich said.

"Every day of our life you wake up in the morning, first thing on my mind, it's Wes. When we're going to bed at night. Wes. I don't even sleep at night. I wake up like every two hours or every three hours and it's just running through my head. I still cannot to this day believe that he's not with us.

World.title: Ashfall-hit communities in Penama receive Vanuatu government support
World.content:
Ashfall-hit communities in Vanuatu set for a major aid boost Pacific Waves Download MP3 2m

Vanuatu's cabinet ministers have approved just over US$1 million (VU$126 million) in aid to communities in Penama Province affected by volcanic ashfall.

The ashfall comes from activity at the Manaro Voui volcano on Ambae Island.

The approval follows recent ground assessments on Ambae, for which the Council of Ministers had earlier approved US$170,000.

The final assessment reports confirmed widespread impact on food gardens, water sources, and shelter due to heavy ashfall, requiring immediate government intervention.

The government said help would be delivered quickly, with public funds used transparently and responsibly.

The cabinet also approved funding for El Niño response packages for islands in Torba and Penama Provinces, and more funding for the MV Matui search and rescue mission and an upcoming commemoration ceremony.

The Penama Provincial Government in Vanuatu has welcomed the aid funds.

Penama government spokesperson Gibson Bani said the money would help implement a regional response they have been trying to get approved for a long time.

World.title: Alex de Minaur fires as Aussie pair clicks in Davis Cup triumph
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Alex de Minaur has returned to form to seal Australia's Davis Cup progression, with the hosts beating Poland 3-1 in Brisbane also thanks to some earlier doubles brilliance.

The world No.9 found top gear on Sunday at Pat Rafter Arena, beating Kamil Majchrzak 6-3 6-3 to clinch a 3-1 result that sends Australia into the Cup's penultimate round next year.

With his backhand and serve firing, de Minaur followed up his 57-minute annihilation of Maks Kasnikowski on Saturday with another therapeutic response to a disappointing second-round US Open exit earlier this month.

Earlier, Max Purcell's scintillating tiebreak tennis alongside rock-solid Rinky Hijikata swung their doubles match, and the tie, in Australia's favour.

The pair's 7-6 (7-3) 6-3 defeat of Jan Zielinski and Karol Drzewiecki followed the win and the loss posted in singles by de Minaur and James Duckworth respectively on Saturday.

Purcell, on the comeback from a controversial 18-month anti-doping ban, turned the match on its head after a tight first set progressed to an inevitable tie break.

He drilled a backhand return to win the opening point on the Polish serve, then produced a pair of aces to shoot the hosts clear 3-0.

De Minaur wins Davis Cup opener After a long and winding road to Brisbane in 2026, Alex de Minaur rides a partisan home crowd to an impressive victory in the first rubber of Australia's Davis Cup tie against Poland.

An unforced error from Poland was followed by two more Purcell winners, and he then held his nerve on a series of low volleys to eventually clinch the set.

Hijikata then held impressively and, after missing two break-point chances, nailed a forehand return to nab the match's only service break.

That was all Australia needed, with the composed pair energising the sold-out Pat Rafter Arena to secure a pressure-relieving victory in 77 minutes.

Australia's win followed a shock loss on the road to Ecuador earlier this year that plunged it into the must-win encounter against Poland.

The Aussies still need to win next year's qualifying round, against an opponent still to be decided, to progress to the finals in Italy in November, 2027.

AAP

World.title: Lions star to challenge grand final ban, Hawks duo handed massive fines
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The Brisbane Lions will challenge a one-match ban handed to Lachie Neale, which would rule the two-time premiership captain out of the AFL grand final.

Neale was offered the suspension after being charged with striking during the Lions' controversial nine-point win over Hawthorn in Saturday night's preliminary final at the MCG.

Hawks fans throw bottles at umpires Hawthorn fans are condemned for their behaviour after the siren following a heart-stopping preliminary final against the Brisbane Lions at the MCG.

Meanwhile, Hawks pair James Sicliy and Tom Barrass have been fined $10,000 and $5,000 respectively for abusing umpire Hayden Meyer following the frenetic finish to the match.

Neale's off-the-ball incident involved a gut punch to the Hawks' Jack Ginnivan in the first quarter.

Vision showed Ginnivan wrestling with Lions forward Eric Hipwood, before Neale jogs over and hits the Hawks player with a left-handed punch to the stomach.

It was graded intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact.

Within minutes of the AFL releasing the match review findings on Sunday, the Lions confirmed they will challenge the ban.

Neale will front the tribunal but, if unsuccessful, will miss Saturday's grand final against Fremantle at the MCG.

New match review guidelines state intentional strikes to the stomach are automatically graded as medium impact rather than low, resulting in one-match bans.

Lachie Neale has won two flags with the Lions. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Robert Cianflone)

Neale may attempt to lean on the "exemplary record" clause to clear himself for the grand final.

He has never been suspended in his 320-match career and could use the same clause that helped Scott Pendlebury escape suspension for his bump on Adelaide's Josh Worrell this season.

Under AFL regulations, "a player with an exemplary record may argue that their good record constitutes exceptional and compelling circumstances".

Players can no longer use the so-called "good bloke" defence that helped Brisbane's Charlie Cameron overturn a ban in 2024.

Neale's other option is to attempt to have the impact grading reduced, though that route would be unlikely to be successful.

A suspension would also mean Neale may have played his final match for the Lions.

The 33-year-old, who has twice won the Brownlow Medal, is expected to make an off-season move to Collingwood as a free agent.

Neale and Harris Andrews were co-captains when the Lions won the 2024 and 2025 premierships.

Should the Lions defeat the Dockers, they will match the feat of the club's 2001-03 squad, which won three straight flags.

James Sicily was fined $10,000 by the AFL. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Sicily and Barrass were handed their massive fines for misconduct after their heated conversation with Meyer immediately after the final siren.

It followed a controversial finish, in which a holding-the-ball free kick paid against Hawthorn's Jarman Impey gifted Brisbane's Hugh McCluggage the match-clinching goal in the dying stages.

Sicily and Barrass were not offered an early plea.

The AFL determined the fixed financial sanction for abusive language towards an umpire was inadequate, and so charged Sicily and Barrass under the "other misconduct'' provision.

Hawks midfielder Jai Newcombe was cleared over his first-quarter contact with Neale in a collision that involved opponents pushing the two players into each other.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Crows prevail in fiery AFLW clash with Lions
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Brisbane's wait to ignite its AFLW season will continue, as an ugly moment contributed to its nine-point loss to Adelaide.

Last year's grand finalists entered Sunday's clash at Springfield Central Stadium to find form after suffering their third loss in four games with a five-point defeat to West Coast last Saturday.

But an outburst in the third quarter by Lions defender Lily-Rose Williamson, wrapping her arms around the neck of Teah Charlton inside the forward 50, severely damaged their chances.

The midfielder scored from the ensuing free kick and the Lions didn't recover until late in the final term as the visitors secured a 5.9 (39) to 4.6 (30) victory.

The Lions (2-4) were left stunned as the Crows held them goalless in the first quarter while kicking two majors of their own.

But Brisbane stepped up as midfielders Orla O'Dwyer and Shanae Davison slotted settling goals to reduce the visitors' lead to two points at half-time.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

The visitors restored their advantage when forward Hannah Munyard poked the ball through the middle before Charlton scored.

Crows forward India Rasheed grabbed a major, but teenager Asher Fearn-Wannan and midfielder Catherine Svarc kicked consolation goals.

Suns surge to victory, Tigers survive Giants comeback

The Suns notched a third-straight AFLW win with victory over the Bombers. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Gold Coast's band of youngsters have strengthened their grip on a third AFLW finals berth, beating Essendon by 41 points at Windy Hill.

The Suns have surprised many this season after starting the campaign as one of the more youthful and inexperienced sides in the league.

Their 7.9 (51) to 1.4 (10) win over Essendon on Sunday was their third consecutive victory and moved them into fifth spot, just four points behind second-placed defending champions North Melbourne.

Gold Coast's defence was resolute in the blustery conditions, and the Bombers did not score a point until late in the second quarter.

At the same time, the visitors were dominating territory and snagged three goals courtesy of a trio of players all aged under 21.

After leading by 20 points at half-time, Suns forward Anne Hatchard and midfielder Charlie Rowbottom added their names to the scoresheet, before Emily Gough found the Bombers' only major late in the third period.

The visitors grabbed another two goals in the final term to complete the win.

Defender Niamh McLaughlin (33 disposals, 506 metres gained) and Rowbottom (36 disposals, one goal) were busy for Gold Coast (4-2), while Hatchard and Havana Harris scored two majors each.

The loss kept the Bombers (0-6) winless, although midfielder Madison Prespakis was outstanding with a game-high 38 disposals

North's record winning streak over after shock loss to Hawks North Melbourne has lost for the first time in almost three years, with the two-time defending AFLW premier falling to a shock 7-point defeat to Hawthorn in Cairns.

At Manuka Oval, Richmond survived an almighty scare to claim a stirring 9.14 (68) to 10.1 (61) win over a pinpoint-accurate GWS.

Fresh off a 15-point win over St Kilda last Sunday, the Tigers (4-2) raced out of the gates and led by 16 points at quarter-time in Canberra.

Richmond continued to run riot in the second term, booting five goals in 12 minutes to balloon their advantage to 55-18 at the main break.

But the Giants completely transformed after half-time, scoring six majors, including a double from Georgia Garnett, to give themselves a glimmer of hope at three-quarter time.

Leading by eight points, the visitors sprayed a flurry of opportunities wide, but their defence held off the Giants' desperate attack to claim the win and go equal with the Suns on victories.

Finals hopes are fading for the Giants (1-5), but midfielders Alyce Parker (27 disposals) and Rebecca Beeson (23 disposals, two goals) were prolific, while Garnett finished with three goals.

Forward Gabby Seymour (16 hit outs) posted a career-best three majors for Richmond, while Olivia Wolmarans also had three goals.

At Moorabbin Park, West Coast notched a second win of the season with an 11-point victory over St Kilda.

The Eagles kicked on after a tight first half, with key forward Amy Franklin kicking two goals.

Ella Roberts was industrious in midfield for West Coast, completing 25 disposals, as her side rose to 13th with the 5.6 (36) to 3.7 (25) victory.

AAP/ABC

World.title: AFL bans loom for bottle-throwing Hawks fans
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The AFL has condemned the behaviour of Hawthorn fans and warned they face minimum five-year bans if identified after they "crossed the line" throwing bottles at umpires.

The match officials had bottles thrown at them from the stands as they walked off the MCG playing arena following the Hawks' nine-point loss to the Brisbane Lions in Saturday night's preliminary final at the MCG.

"The AFL and MCC [Melbourne Cricket Club] security will work with Vic Pol to identify the bottle throwers directed at the umpires last night," the league said in a statement.

"If identified they will be banned from games and the stadium for a minimum five years.

"The passion for footy is unmatched in Australian sport, however, what transpired last night by a number of individuals was dangerous and crossed the line."

At the heart of Hawthorn's collective rage was a holding-the-ball free paid against Jarman Impey in the last minute of the match.

Hawks fans throw bottles at umpires Hawthorn fans are condemned for their behaviour after the siren following a heart-stopping preliminary final against the Brisbane Lions at the MCG.

It was the most controversial of a succession of contentious umpiring calls during the game.

Brisbane's Hugh McCluggage then kicked the match-clinching goal, which put the Lions in front by three points.

Hawks players James Sicily, Tom Barrass and Jack Ginnivan had a heated conversation with the umpires immediately after the full-time siren.

Sicily ($10,000) and Barrass ($5,000) have since been fined by the AFL.

On Saturday night, Hawks coach Sam Mitchell said he did not know about Sicily, Barrass and Ginnivan speaking to the umpires, but he was aware of the bottles being thrown onto the ground.

"At the end of the game, part of me wanted to break down in tears, part of me wanted to scream with rage, part of me wanted to throw chairs, you don't know how to react," Mitchell said post-match.

"So when you're in the stand, you need to continue to be feeling that emotion, because that's why we love it, but how it manifests itself. We shouldn't be throwing things on the field and doing those types of things.

"But the passion in the stand and the passion of the game is why we love it so much, so I hope that for the vast majority it was felt responsibly."

Bottles and cans could be seen on the playing area after the match. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: James Wiltshire)

On Sunday, Premier Ben Carroll condemned the behaviour, telling reporters that it was not the "Victorian way".

"I think these people should be made an example of," he said.

"This could have had catastrophic injuries if one of those bottles or cans hit an umpire on the head.

"You've always got to respect the umpire's decision."

AFL Fans Association president Ron Issko said he understood the passion, disappointment and frustration of Hawthorn supporters, but denounced their throwing of objects at the umpires.

"It is never, ever an excuse to throw bottles or cans on to the ground or at the umpires. What we saw was an ugly look for our game," he said.

"There is an even more serious concern when objects are thrown towards people.

"A bottle, or can, could cause a serious injury to a player, umpire, security staff, ground staff or another spectator.

"When a bottle is thrown towards an umpire and comes close to hitting them, that crosses an even more serious line.

"No-one should have to fear being struck by a projectile simply because they are doing their job."

AAP

World.title: Ugly scenes as refs have projectiles hurled at them after NRL semifinal
World.content:
Projectiles have been thrown at the NRL refereeing crew following Newcastle's upset semifinal win over the New Zealand Warriors.

Newcastle, last season's wooden spooners, silenced the huge 48,511-strong crowd at Auckland's Eden Park to secure a nail-biting 12-10 win, advancing to the NRL preliminary finals for the first time in 13 years.

Some in that large Eden Park crowd hurled projectiles at referee Ashley Klein and his team, while Warriors coach Andrew Webster described three late decisions that went against his side as "frustrating".

Warriors centre Leka Halasima was knocked to the ground before he could contest a high kick in the 79th minute, with Klein clearing the contact made by Knights prop Tyson Frizell and not giving the home side a chance to send the match into extra time with a penalty goal.

Frizell had his eyes on the ball, but did appear to cut across Halasima's line, allowing Fletcher Sharpe to leap high and catch the ball for Newcastle.

Minutes earlier, the Warriors were left fuming when Bunker official Chris Butler overturned a Knights knock-on but did not overturn a strip penalty against them, with the home side believing the ball was dropped because of a loose carry.

"It was frustrating. I feel like they were trying to find ways to take it off us," Webster said in reference to the two Bunker reviews.

"The last one, and two points would have drawn the game, he's [Tyson Frizell] going across Leka [Halasima], pretending to try and catch the ball, which they [NRL] have told us you can't do."

Webster made it clear those decisions were not the reason his side will not be facing Penrith next Sunday in Sydney, while Knights coach Justin Holbrook said he thought the officials made the right calls late.

World.title: Rollers capture first wheelchair basketball world title in 12 years
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Australia has defeated Italy 81-57 to win the men's IWBF World Championships final in Canada, giving the Rollers their third title in the tournament's history.

The result capped an unbeaten campaign for the Rollers in Ottawa, with the Australians proving again they are a giant of international wheelchair basketball by adding to their previous triumphs in 2010 and 2014.

Jaylen Brown played a starring role, scoring a game-high 28 points.

Jaylen Brown (left) was brilliant for the Rollers in their victory over Italy. (IWBF)

Captain Tom O'Neill-Thorne made a significant contribution on the scoreboard with a 20-point haul.

O'Neill-Thorne also managed 16 assists and seven rebounds in an outstanding all-around display.

Bill Latham provided valuable support with 12 points, seven rebounds and two assists.

The Rollers had an answer to every challenge posed by the Italians. (IWBF)

Italy had entered the gold-medal game with an undefeated record.

But the Rollers were in command from the opening quarter and led at every break.

They dominated Italy with 29 assists to 19 and out-rebounded their opponents 35-25.

The Rollers' defensive intensity shone through as they forced 13 turnovers and only conceded nine of their own.

World.title: Wallaroos collapse against France as bus fire delays game
World.content:
Australia's Wallaroos have been left frustrated by a potentially massive Test win that got away as undisciplined France somehow escaped with a 29-26 win after being 19 points down and reduced at one point to just 11 players.

On an extraordinary day of Test rugby, exacerbated by off-field drama when the second half had to be delayed due to a bus on fire adjacent to the Stade Maurice David, home fans were left almost in disbelief at how their imploding and depleted side somehow still conjured a win.

The French were at one point in the first half down to 11 players after three yellow cards, including one upgraded to a 20-minute red, and a straight red.

A bus fire near the ground delayed the start of the second half. (Getty Images: David Ramos)

It enabled the Wallaroos to power into a 19-0 lead, but that was not enough to stop France fighting back with three second-half tries, even while suffering a sixth card after the break.

Australia, who also had Michaela Leonard sent to the bin in the second half to complete the card chaos, did not help itself as the French reeled off 17 unanswered points in the final 25 minutes to turn a 26-12 deficit into the most unlikely win.

Ultimately, the four Australian tries from Britanny Merlo, Tania Naden, Caitlyn Halse and Piper Duck were not enough for them to follow up last week's comprehensive defeat by England with a morale-boosting win.

The craziness began early, with the French being hit with four cards in 20 minutes, with Ambre Mwayembe, Lea Champon and Lea Murie all binned for high tackles — Mwayembe's being upgraded to a 20-minute red — before Chloe Correa got a straight red for eye-gouging in the maul.

Australia cashed in, with Merlo rolling over from the maul for her second international try after 17 minutes, Naden peeling off to score against a side left helpless when down to 11 and Halse then scoring the Wallaroos' slickest effort after a fine team move.

But when France started getting its numbers back, it became a very different game, as it reduced the deficit to 19-12 by half-time.

After Duck's early score five minutes into the delayed second half, Pauline Bourdon went over to narrow the gap.

When Leonard was binned for a high tackle, the hosts became increasingly encouraged, only to be checked again as Charlotte Escudero got penalised for 10 minutes for her own high challenge.

France then used its maul power to go over for a 68th-minute try through hooker Elisa Riffonneau before Teani Feleu crashed over in the corner for the clincher.

The Wallaroos play in Edinburgh next week against a Scotland side that lost 66-14 to 10-try New Zealand.

Tech.title: No one is surprised that Nvidia’s Jensen Huang thinks AI fears are overblown.
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

The man who may stand to make the most money from the AI boom seems to think he knows better than anyone else, including researchers who have studied and worked on AI for decades. In an interview with CBS Sunday Morning, he claimed there was a “0% chance” of AI being the end of the world. He also said of people sounding the alarm about the dangers of AI that, “Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible.”

He also claims that calls from CEOs like Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman to slow down the development of AI are “not grounded in science.” He even argued that there was no need for new rules, laws, or guidelines, in the face of several high-profile cases in which models escaped containment and hacked other companies.

It’s not surprising that Huang was dismissive of the dangers posed by rogue AI and concerns about selling chips to China, or that he adamantly opposed new regulation. He is the CEO of the world’s most valuable company and number seven on Forbes’ list of the richest people in the world. Just as importantly, his wealth has skyrocketed from an estimated $21 billion in 2023 to over $192 billion in 2026. Any hiccup in the unchecked expansion of the AI industry could slow his ascent.

Watch the full interview below.

He posted that his administration “will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!”
